כמו שראיתם שעשה לי להושיעני שהוחלתי לו:
rashi.eng: *Strengthen yourselves, and He will give your heart courage.* as you see that He did for me, to save me because I hoped for Him.

notes.1113: (tn): The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 34:9; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15). Here it refers to the relief that one experiences when one’s sins are forgiven.

rashi.heb:
*לדוד משכיל.* 
אמרו חכמים כל מזמור שנאמר בו משכיל ע"י מתורגמן אמרו:
rashi.eng:
*Of David, a maskil.* 
The Sages said (Pes. 117a): Every Psalm in which “maskil” is mentioned was said through an interpreter.

rashi.heb:
*אשרי נשוי פשע.* 
שהקב"ה נושא פשע ומכסה חטאיו נשוי אנפורדוני"ץ בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *Praiseworthy is he whose transgression is forgiven.* Whose transgression the Holy One, Blessed Be He, forgives, and He conceals his sins. (נשוי is anpardone in Old French, pardoned. The implication is forgiveness, because the forgiveness of iniquity represents [the sin] being lifted up and withdrawn from upon a person.)

notes.1116: (tn, Heb): “man.” The word choice reflects the perspective of the psalmist, who is male. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, the gender and age specific “man” has been translated with the more neutral “one.”
notes.1117: (tn, Heb): “blessed [is] the man to whom the Lord does not impute wrongdoing.”
notes.1118: (sn): In whose spirit there is no deceit. The point is not that the individual is sinless and pure. In this context, which focuses on confession and forgiveness of sin, the psalmist refers to one who refuses to deny or hide his sin, but instead honestly confesses it to God.

rashi.heb:
*ולא יחשב לו עון.* 
ובלבד שלא תהיה ברוחו רמיה להיות בדעתו לשוב אל קיאו:
rashi.eng: *to whom the Lord ascribes no iniquity.* provided that in his spirit there is no guile, thinking to revert to his “vomit.”

notes.1120: (tn, Heb): “my bones became brittle.” The psalmist pictures himself as aging and growing physically weak. Trying to cover up his sin brought severe physical consequences.

rashi.heb:
*כי החרשתי.* 
כאשר החרשתי מלהתודות על פשעי לפניך:
rashi.eng: *When I was silent.* When I was silent, [when I refrained] from confessing my transgressions before You.

rashi.heb:
*בלו עצמי.* 
מרוב אנחותי ודאגותי כל היו' שהייתי דואג מפני הפורענות:
rashi.eng: *my bones decayed.* because of my many sighs and my worries all day, that I was worrying about the punishment.

notes.1121: (tn, Heb): “your hand was heavy upon me.”
notes.1122: (tc, Heb): “my [?] was turned.” The meaning of the Hebrew term לְשַׁד (l�shad) is uncertain. A noun לָשָׁד (lashad, “cake”) is attested in Num 11:8, but it would make no sense to understand that word in this context. It is better to emend the form to לְשֻׁדִּי (l�shuddiy, “to my destruction”) and understand “your hand” as the subject of the verb “was turned.” In this case the text reads, “[your hand] was turned to my destruction.” In Lam 3:3 the author laments that God’s “hand” was “turned” (הָפַךְ, hafakh) against him in a hostile sense. You tried to destroy me. The psalmist’s statement reflects his perspective. As far as he was concerned, it seemed as if the Lord was trying to kill him.
notes.1123: (tn): The translation assumes that the plural form indicates degree. If one understands the form as a true plural, then one might translate, “in the times of drought.”
notes.1124: (sn): Summer. Perhaps the psalmist suffered during the hot season and perceived the very weather as being an instrument of divine judgment. Another option is that he compares his time of suffering to the uncomfortable and oppressive heat of summer.

rashi.heb:
*כי יומם ולילה.* 
היה כבד עלי מורא ידך וגזרותיך:
rashi.eng: *For [both] day and night.* the fear of Your hand and Your decrees was heavy upon me.

rashi.heb:
*נהפך לשדי.* 
לחלוח שלי, וכן לשד השמן (במדבר י״א:ח׳), לחלוח שמן כך פירשו דונש, ומנחם חבר לשון שדידה כמו משוד עניים (לעיל י"ב), רשעים זו שדוני (לעיל י"ז):
rashi.eng: *my freshness was transformed.* Heb. לשדי, my moisture, and so (in Num. 11:8): “the moisture (לשד) of oil,” the moisture of oil. This is how Dunash explained it (p. 14). Menachem (p. 171) associates [it with] an expression of plunder as (above 12:6): “from the plunder (משד) of the poor;” (above 17:9) “Because of the wicked who have robbed me (שדוני).”

rashi.heb:
*בחרבוני קיץ.* 
עד שייבש בחורב הקיץ מפני דאגת כובד ידך שהייתי דואג על חטאתי ולפיכך:
rashi.eng: *as in the droughts of summer.* Until it dries up as the drought of summer out of my worry of the heaviness of Your hand, that I was worrying about my sins; therefore…

notes.1125: (tn): The Hiphil of ידה normally means “give thanks, praise,” but here, as in Prov 28:13, it means “confess.”
notes.1126: (tn, Heb): “the wrongdoing of my sin.” By joining synonyms for “sin” in this way, the psalmist may be emphasizing the degree of his wrongdoing.

rashi.heb:
*חטאתי אודיעך.* 
תמיד ולשון הווה הוא כי אמרתי טוב שאודה עלי פשעי לה' ועתה כשהודיתי ואמרתי לנתן הנביא חטאתי (שמואל ב י״ב:י״ג):
rashi.eng: *I would inform You of my sin.* always. This is a present tense. For I said, It is good that I should confess my transgressions to the Lord, and now that I confessed and said to Nathan the prophet, “I have sinned,” (as in II Samuel 12:13)…

rashi.heb: *נשאת עון חטאתי.* כענין שנאמר (שם) גם ה' העביר חטאתך וגו':
rashi.eng: *You forgave the iniquity of my sin.* as the matter that is stated there (verse 13): “Also the Lord has removed your sin, etc.”

notes.1127: (tn): A “faithful follower” (חָסִיד, khasid) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see Pss 4:3; 12:1; 18:25; 31:23; 37:28; 86:2; 97:10).
notes.1128: (tn, Heb): “at a time of finding.” This may mean, “while there is time to ‘find’ [the Lord]” and seek his forgiveness (cf. NIV). Some emend the text by combining מְצֹא (m�tso’, “finding”) with the following term רַק (raq, “only, surely”) and read either ר[וֹ]מָצ (matsor, “distress”; see Ps 31:22) or ק[וֹ]מָצ (matsoq, “hardship”; see Ps 119:143). In this case, one may translate “in a time of distress/hardship” (cf. NEB, NRSV).
notes.1129: (tn): The Hebrew term רַק (raq) occasionally has an asseverative force.
notes.1130: (sn): The surging water is here a metaphor for trouble that endangers one’s life.
notes.1131: (tn, Heb): “him.” The translation uses the plural “them” to agree with the plural “every one of your faithful followers” in the first line of v. 6.

rashi.heb:
*לעת מצוא.* 
בהמצאך לקבל תפלתו ומה היא זאת:
rashi.eng: *at the time that You are found.* When You are found to accept his prayer, and what is this?…

rashi.heb:
*רק לשטף מים רבים.* 
אשר לא יגיעו אליו שלא יפול ביד האומות שהם כמים שוטפים וכן מצינו שהתפלל דוד על זאת ואמר נפלה נא ביד ה' כי רבים רחמיו וביד אדם אל אפולה (שמואל ב כ״ד:י״ד):
rashi.eng: *only about a flood of vast waters.* that they should not reach him, that he should not fall into the hands of enemies, who are like flooding waters. And so we find that David prayed for this and said (II Sam. 24:14): “Let us fall now into the hand of the Lord, for His mercies are great; but into the hand of man let me not fall.”

notes.1132: (tn, Heb): “[with] shouts of joy of deliverance you surround me.”

rashi.heb:
*אתה סתר לי.* 
להסתר בצלך מפני פחד אויב:
rashi.eng: *You are a shelter for me.* to hide in Your shadow from before the enemy.

rashi.heb:
*תצרני.* 
כמו תשמרני:
rashi.eng: *You guard me.* Heb. תצרני, like תשמרני.

rashi.heb:
*רני פלט.* 
רנה של הצלה:
rashi.eng: *songs of deliverance.* A song of rescue.

rashi.heb:
*תסובבני.* 
לשון הוה הוא סבבתני תמיד רני פלט וכך אמרת לי
rashi.eng: *You encompass me.* Heb. תסובבני. This is the present tense. You always encompassed me with songs of deliverance. And so You said to me…

notes.1133: (tn): The second person pronominal forms in this verse are singular. The psalmist addresses each member of his audience individually (see also the note on the word “eye” in the next line). A less likely option (but one which is commonly understood) is that the Lord addresses the psalmist in vv. 8-9 (cf. NASB “I will instruct you and teach you…I will counsel you with My eye upon you”).
notes.1134: (tn, Heb): “I will instruct you and I will teach you in the way [in] which you should walk.”
notes.1135: (tn, Heb): “I will advise, upon you my eye,” that is, “I will offer advice [with] my eye upon you.” In 2 Chr 20:12 the statement “our eye is upon you” means that the speakers are looking to the Lord for intervention. Here the expression “my eye upon you” may simply mean that the psalmist will teach his pupils directly and personally.

rashi.heb:
*אשכילך ואורך.* 
דרך ללכת.
rashi.eng: *I will enlighten you and instruct you which way.* to go.

rashi.heb:
*איעצה.* 
ארמוז לך בעיני רמז מה תעשה, איעצה לשון קריצת עין כמו עוצם עיניו לחשוב תהפוכות (משלי ט״ז:ל׳):
rashi.eng: *I will wink.* With My eye; I will hint to you what to do. איעצה is an expression of winking the eye, as (in Prov. 16:30): “He winks (עצה) his eyes to think perverse thoughts.”

notes.1136: (tn): The verb form is plural (i.e., “do not all of you be”); the psalmist addresses the whole group.
notes.1137: (tn, Heb): “like a horse, like a mule without understanding.”
notes.1138: (tn, Heb): “with a bridle and bit, its [?] to hold, not to come near to you.” The meaning of the Hebrew noun עֲדִי (’adiy) is uncertain. Normally the word refers to “jewelry,” so some suggest the meaning “trappings” here (cf. NASB). Some emend the form to לְחֵיהֶם (l�khehem, “their jawbones”) but it is difficult to see how the present Hebrew text, even if corrupt, could have derived from this proposed original reading. P. C. Craigie (Psalms 1-50 [WBC], 265) takes the form from an Arabic root and translates “whose gallop.” Cf. also NRSV “whose temper must be curbed.”

rashi.heb:
*אל תהיו כסוס כפרד.* 
שאינו מבין בין העושה לו טובה לעושה לו רעה כשאתה ממתגם בו במתג הוא בולם פיו ומכסכס ברסנו וכשאתה מקרדו ומקרצפו אתה צריך לבלום ולסגור פיו ולייסרו במתג ורסן כשאתה מעדהו עדי ומיפהו:
rashi.eng: *Be not like a horse, like a mule.* which does not discern between one who benefits him and one who does him harm, for when you insert a bit into his mouth, he closes his mouth and shakes his bridle, and when you curry him and brush him, you must close his mouth and chastise him with a bit and bridle while you adorn him and groom him.

rashi.heb:
*בל קרב אליך.* 
שלא יקרב אליך, להזיקך כשאתה מיפהו במתג ורסן עדיו לבלום. בשעת עדיו שאתה מקרדו ומקרצפו אתה צריך לסוגרו במתג ורסן שלא יקרב אליך, בלימה בלשון משנה לשון מסגר, פיו בלום רגליו מבולמות (במסכת בכורו'), ומנחם חבר לבלום וכן על בלימ' (איוב כ"ז) לשון תוכן (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *so that… he does not come near you.* So that he should not come near you to hurt you while you groom him, with bit and bridle (when he is being groomed, to close his mouth. When he is being groomedwhile you curry him and brush him you must close his mouth with a bit and bridle so that he does not come near you.) בלימה is an expression of closing in the language of the Mishnah: Its mouth is closed (בלום), its feet are closed (מבלמות), in Tractate Bechoroth (40b). (Menachem associated לבלום, and also בלימה [Job 26:7] as an expression of regulating [p. 45].)

notes.1139: (tn, Heb): “many [are the] pains of evil [one].” The singular form is representative here; the typical evildoer, representative of the larger group of wicked people, is in view.
notes.1140: (tn, Heb): “but the one who trusts in the Lord, faithfulness surrounds him.”

notes.1141: (tn, Heb): “all [you] pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 36:10; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).
notes.1142: (sn): Psalm 33. In this hymn the psalmist praises the Lord as the sovereign creator and just ruler of the world who protects and vindicates those who fear him.

rashi.heb:
*בנבל עשור.* 
של עשר מיני נעימה:
rashi.eng: *with a lyre of ten melodies.* Heb. בנבל עשור, of ten kinds of melody.

notes.1143: (sn): A new song is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the lives of his people in fresh and exciting ways.
notes.1144: (tn, Heb): “play skillfully with a loud shout.”

notes.1145: (sn): For the Lord’s decrees are just… After the call to praise (vv. 1-3), the psalmist now gives a series of reasons why the Lord is worthy of praise.
notes.1146: (tn, Heb): “word.” In this context, which depicts the Lord as the sovereign creator and ruler of the world, the Lord’s “word” refers to the decrees whereby he governs his dominion.
notes.1148: (tn, Heb): “and all his work [is] in faithfulness.”

notes.1149: (tn, Heb): “loves.” The verb “loves” is here metonymic; the Lord’s commitment to principles of equity and justice causes him to actively promote these principles as he governs the world.

notes.1152: (tn, Heb): “and by the breath of his mouth all their host.” The words “were created” are added in the translation for stylistic reasons; they are understood by ellipsis (note “were made” in the preceding line). The description is consistent with Gen 1:16, which indicates that God spoke the heavenly luminaries into existence.

notes.1153: (tn, Heb): “[he] gathers like a pile the waters of the sea.” Some prefer to emend נֵד (ged, “heap, pile”; cf. NASB) to נֹד (nod, “bottle”; cf. NRSV; NIV “into jars”), but “pile” is used elsewhere to describe water that the Lord confines to one place (Exod 15:8; Josh 3:13, 16; Ps 78:13). This verse appears to refer to Gen 1:9, where God decrees that the watery deep be gathered to one place so that dry land might appear. If so, the participles in this and the following line depict this action with special vividness, as if the reader were present on the occasion. Another option is that the participles picture the confinement of the sea to one place as an ongoing divine activity.
notes.1154: (tn): Or “watery depths.” The form תְּהוֹמוֹת (t�homot, “watery depths”) is the plural form of תְּהוֹם (t�hom, “great deep”; see Gen 1:2).

rashi.heb:
*כנד.* 
לשון גובה, וכן תרגום אונקלוס נצבו כמו נד (שמות ט״ו:ח׳) קמו כשור, וכן פירש מנחם ואין נד ונאד שוין:
rashi.eng: *as a mound.* Heb. כנד, an expression of height, and so did Onkelos render (Exod. 15:8): נצבו כמו נד, they stood up like a wall, and so did Menachem (p. 121, missing) explain it. נד and נאד do not have the same meaning.

rashi.heb:
*נותן באוצרות תהומות.* 
תחת הארץ:
rashi.eng: *He puts the deeps into treasuries.* under the earth.

notes.1155: (tn): In this context “fear” probably means “to demonstrate respect for the Lord’s power and authority by worshiping him and obeying his commandments.”

notes.1156: (tn): That is, “all the earth” in the first line of v. 8. The apparent antecedent of the masculine subject of the verbs in v. 9 (note וַיֶּהִי [vayyehiy] and וַיַּעֲמֹד [vayya’amod]) is “earth” or “world,” both of which are feminine nouns. However, כָּל (kol, “all”) may be the antecedent, or the apparent lack of agreement may be explained by the collective nature of the nouns involved here (see GKC 463 �145.e).

notes.1158: (tn, Heb): “breaks” or “destroys.” The Hebrew perfect verbal forms here and in the next line generalize about the Lord’s activity.

notes.1160: (tn, Heb): “the thoughts of his heart for generation to generation.” The verb “abides” is supplied in the translation. The Lord’s “decisions” and “plans” here refer to his decrees and purposes.

notes.1161: (tn): The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1; 2:12; 34:9; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).

notes.1163: (tn): The Hebrew perfect verbal forms in v. 13 state general facts.

rashi.heb:
*השגיח.* 
הביט:
rashi.eng: *He oversees.* He looks.

notes.1165: (tn, Heb): “the one who forms together their heart[s].” “Heart” here refers to human nature, composed of intellect, emotions and will. The precise force of יָחַד (yakhad, “together”) is unclear here. The point seems to be that the Lord is the creator of every human being.

rashi.heb:
*היוצר יחד לבם.* 
לב כלם יחד ויודע כל המחשבות ורבותינו הסיבוהו אל ממכון שבתו השגיח היוצר יחד לבם, ודרשו מכאן שכולן נסקרין בסקירה אחת:
rashi.eng: *He Who forms their hearts together.* All of their hearts together and knows all the thoughts. Our Sages, however, explain that it refers back to “From His dwelling place, the Creator oversees their hearts together,” and they derived from here that all are examined with a single glance (Rosh Hashana 18a).

notes.1166: (tn, Heb): “a lie [is] the horse for victory.”

notes.1167: (tn, Heb): “look, the eye of the Lord [is] toward the ones who fear him.” The expression “the eye…[is] toward” here indicates recognition and the bestowing of favor. See Ps 34:15. The one who fears the Lord respects his sovereignty and obeys his commandments. See Ps 128:1; Prov 14:2.
notes.1168: (tn, Heb): “for the ones who wait for his faithfulness.”

notes.1169: (tn, Heb): “to save from death their live[s].”
notes.1170: (tn, Heb): “and to keep them alive in famine.”

notes.1171: (tn): Or “our lives.” The suffixed form of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “being, life”) is often equivalent to a pronoun in poetic texts.

notes.1174: (tn, Heb): “let your faithfulness, O Lord, be on us.”
notes.1176: (sn): Psalm 34. In this song of thanksgiving the psalmist praises God for delivering him from distress. He encourages others to be loyal to the Lord, tells them how to please God, and assures them that the Lord protects his servants. The psalm is an acrostic; vv. 1-21 begin with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. (Verse 6 begins with the letter he (ה) and v. 7 with the letter zayin (ז). The letter vav (ו), which comes between ה and ז, seems to be omitted, although it does appear at the beginning of v. 6b. The final verse of the psalm, which begins with the letter pe (פ), is outside the acrostic scheme.
notes.1177: (tn, Heb): “By David, when he changed his sense before Abimelech and he drove him away and he went.” Pretended to be insane. The psalm heading appears to refer to the account in 1 Sam 21:10-15 which tells how David, fearful that King Achish of Gath might kill him, pretended to be insane in hopes that the king would simply send him away. The psalm heading names the king Abimelech, not Achish, suggesting that the tradition is confused on this point. However, perhaps “Abimelech” was a royal title, rather than a proper name. See P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 (WBC), 278.

notes.1179: (tn, Heb): “continually [will] his praise [be] in my mouth.”

rashi.heb:
*בשנותו את טעמו.* 
כענין שנאמר (ש"א כ"א) ויתו על דלתות השער וגו' וישנה את טעמו בעיניהם ששנה דברו וטעמו ועשה עצמו שוטה והוריד רירו על זקנו (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *when he disguised his sanity.* as the matter that is stated (in I Sam. 21:14): “And he changed his speech before their eyes, etc. And he scribbled upon the doors of the gates.” That he disguised his speech and his sanity and feigned madness and let his saliva run down upon his beard.

rashi.heb:
*לפני אבימלך.* 
כך כל מלכי פלשתים נקראים וכל מלכי מצרים פרעה ואע"פ ששמו אכיש קורין לו אבימלך, ומדרש אגדה שהיה צדיק כאבימלך (שנכתב בתורה אצל שרה) שלא רצה להרגו ואנשיו אומרים לו (שם) הלא זה דוד מלך הארץ כדאיתא במדרש תהלים:
rashi.eng: *before Abimelech.* All Philistine kings were called thus, and all Egyptian kings [were called] Pharaoh. Although his name was Achish, he was called Abimelech. The Midrash Aggadah explains that he was as righteous as Abimelech (mentioned in the Torah in relation to Sarah), for he did not want to kill him although his men said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land?” As is stated in Midrash Psalms (34:1).

notes.1180: (tn, Heb): “my soul will boast”; or better, “let my soul boast.” Following the cohortative form in v. 1, it is likely that the prefixed verbal form here is jussive.
notes.1181: (tn): The two prefixed verbal forms in this verse are best taken as jussives, for the psalmist is calling his audience to worship (see v. 3).

rashi.heb:
*בה' תתהלל נפשי.* 
מתפאר אני ומתהלל שיש לי פטרון כזה להושיע ולהגן תתהלל נפשי שפורוונ"טרא בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *My soul boasts of the Lord.* I boast, and praise myself that I have a patron like this to save me and protect me. Se porvantera in French, I will boast.

rashi.heb:
*ישמעו ענוים.* 
נפלאות שעשה לי מתוך מהללי יבינו אותם וישמחו:
rashi.eng: *may the humble hear.* the wonders that He did for me. Through my praise, they will understand it and rejoice.

notes.1184: (tc, Heb): “they look to him and are radiant and their faces are not ashamed.” The third person plural subject (“they”) is unidentified; there is no antecedent in the Hebrew text. For this reason some prefer to take the perfect verbal forms in the first line as imperatives, “look to him and be radiant” (cf. NEB, NRSV). Some medieval Hebrew mss and other ancient witnesses (Aquila, the Syriac, and Jerome) support an imperatival reading for the first verb. In the second line some (with support from the LXX and Syriac) change “their faces” to “your faces,” which allows one to retain more easily the jussive force of the verb (suggested by the preceding אַל [’al]): “do not let your faces be ashamed.” It is probable that the verbal construction in the second line is rhetorical, expressing the conviction that the action in view cannot or should not happen. See GKC 322 �109.e.

rashi.heb:
*מגורותי.* 
לשון פחד כמו ויגר מואב, (במדבר כ"ב):
rashi.eng: *my terrors.* Heb. מגורותי, an expression of fear, as (in Num. 22:3): “and Moab became terrified (ויגר).”

notes.1185: (tn): The pronoun refers back to “this oppressed man,” namely, the psalmist.

rashi.heb:
*הביטו אליו.* 
כל אותם שהביטו אליו מתוך צרתם:
rashi.eng: *They looked to Him.* All those who looked to Him out of their trouble.

rashi.heb:
*ונהרו.* 
האירו פניהם:
rashi.eng: *and they became radiant.* Their faces shone.

rashi.heb:
*יחפרו.* 
יתביישו כמו (ישעיהו כ״ד:כ״ג) וחפרה הלבנה ובושה החמה:
rashi.eng: *be ashamed.* Heb. יחפרו, they will be ashamed, as (in Isa. 24:23): “And the moon shall be ashamed (וחפרה) and the sun shall be abashed.”

notes.1186: (tn, Heb): “his”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.1188: (tn): The prefixed verb with vav (ו) consecutive here carries the same generalizing force as the active participle in the first line. See GKC 329 �111.u.

notes.1189: (tn): This verb is normally used of tasting or savoring food. The metaphor here appears to compare the Lord to a tasty meal.
notes.1190: (tn): The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).
notes.1191: (tn, Heb): “man.” The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the more neutral “one.”
notes.1192: (tn): “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 2:12; 5:11-12; 31:17-20; 34:21-22).

rashi.heb:
*טעמו וראו כי טוב ה'.* 
טעמו דברו:
rashi.eng: *Comprehend and see that the Lord is good.* Comprehend His word.

rashi.heb:
*יראו.* 
יהיו יראים לשון צווי:
rashi.eng: *Fear.* Heb. יראו. Be afraid, the imperative form.

notes.1196: (tn, Heb): “the fear of the Lord I will teach you.” In vv. 13-14 the psalmist explains to his audience what it means to “fear” the Lord.

rashi.heb:
*רשו.* 
ל' דלות:
rashi.eng: *suffer want.* Heb. רשו, an expression of poverty.

rashi.heb:
*כל טוב.* 
ניסו"ן בי"ין בלע"ז, כמו כל מלאכה (שמות י"ב):
rashi.eng: *no good.* Heb. כל טוב, nient bon, any good, as (in Exod. 12:16): “any work (כל-מלאכה).”

notes.1197: (tn, Heb): “Who is the man who desires life?” The rhetorical question is used to grab the audience’s attention. “Life” probably refers here to quality of life, not just physical existence or even duration of life. See the following line.
notes.1198: (tn, Heb): “[Who] loves days to see good?”

notes.1200: (tn, Heb): “and your lips from speaking deception.”

notes.1203: (tn, Heb): “the eyes of the Lord [are] toward the godly, and his ears [are] toward their cry for help.”

rashi.heb:
*בקש שלום.* 
במקומך:
rashi.eng: *seek peace.* in your place.

rashi.heb:
*ורדפהו.* 
במקום אחר:
rashi.eng: *and pursue it.* elsewhere.

notes.1204: (tn, Heb): “the face of the Lord [is] against the doers of evil to cut off from the earth memory of them.”

notes.1205: (tn, Heb): “they” (i.e., the godly mentioned in v. 15).
notes.1206: (tn): The three perfect verbal forms are taken in a generalizing sense in v. 17 and translated with the present tense (note the generalizing mood of vv. 18-22).

rashi.heb:
*פני.* 
פנים של זעם לישאריא"ש בלע"ז, כמו (ויקר' ב') ושמתי פני באיש ההוא, כך חברו מנחם:
rashi.eng: *The face of the Lord.* His angry face, les ires in Old French, ire, as (in Lev. 20:5): “And I will direct My face, etc.” So did Menachem (p. 143) associate it.

notes.1207: (tn): The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the oppressed and needy.

rashi.heb:
*צעקו.* 
הצדיקים וה' שמע:
rashi.eng: *They cry out.* i.e., the righteous, and the Lord hearkens.

notes.1209: (tn): The Hebrew text uses the singular form; the representative or typical godly person is envisioned.
notes.1211: (tn): The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the godly.
notes.1212: (tn, Heb): “him,” agreeing with the singular form in the preceding line.

notes.1213: (tn): The Hebrew participial form suggests such protection is characteristic.
notes.1214: (tn): That is, he protects the godly from physical harm.
notes.1215: (sn): Not one of them is broken. The author of the Gospel of John saw a fulfillment of these words in Jesus’ experience on the cross (see John 19:31-37), for the Roman soldiers, when they saw that Jesus was already dead, did not break his legs as was customarily done to speed the death of crucified individuals. John’s use of the psalm seems strange, for the statement in its original context suggests that the Lord protects the godly from physical harm. Jesus’ legs may have remained unbroken, but he was brutally and unjustly executed by his enemies. John seems to give the statement a literal sense that is foreign to its original literary context by applying a promise of divine protection to a man who was seemingly not saved by God. However, John saw in this incident a foreshadowing of Jesus’ ultimate deliverance and vindication. His unbroken bones were a reminder of God’s commitment to the godly and a sign of things to come. Jesus’ death on the cross was not the end of the story; God vindicated him, as John goes on to explain in the following context (John 19:38-20:18).

rashi.heb:
*רבות רעות צדיק.* 
הרבה רעות ופחדים באות עליו ומכלם נצול:
rashi.eng: *Many evils befall the righteous.* Many evils and terrors befall him, and he is saved from all of them.

notes.1216: (tn, Heb): “evil kills the wicked [one].” The singular form is representative; the typical evil person is envisioned. The Hebrew imperfect verbal form draws attention to the typical nature of the action.
notes.1217: (tn, Heb): “are guilty,” but the verb is sometimes used metonymically with the meaning “to suffer the consequences of guilt,” the effect being substituted for the cause.

rashi.heb:
*שומר.* 
הקב"ה כל עצמותיו:
rashi.eng: *He guards.* The Holy One, blessed be He, [guards] all his bones.

notes.1218: (tn, Heb): “redeems the life of his servants.” The Hebrew participial form suggests such deliverance is characteristic.
notes.1219: (tn): “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 2:12; 5:11-12; 31:19).
notes.1220: (sn): Psalm 35. The author, who faces ruthless enemies who seek his life for no reason, begs the Lord to fight his battles for him and to vindicate him by annihilating his adversaries.

rashi.heb:
*תמותת רשע רע.* 
תמותת את הרשע הרעה שהוא עושה:
rashi.eng: *Evil will kill the wicked.* The evil that the wicked man does will kill him.

rashi.heb:
*תמותת.* 
תמית:
rashi.eng: *will kill.* Heb. תמותת, [equivalent to] תמית.

rashi.heb:
*לא יאשמו.* 
לא יתחרטו לאמר אשמנו שחסינו בך ריפונטירונ"ט בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *shall not be accounted guilty.* They will not regret saying, “We are guilty, because we took shelter in You.” Repontiront in Old French, se repentiront: they repent.

rashi.heb:
*ריבה ה' את יריבי.* 
עשה מריבה עם אותם שעושים מריבה עמי:
rashi.eng: *O Lord, strive with those who strive against me.* Make a quarrel with those who make quarrels with me.

rashi.heb:
*לחם.* 
לשון מלחמה וכן לוחמי הלחם עם הנלחמים עמו:
rashi.eng: *battle.* Heb. לחם an expression of war (מלחמה), and so לחמי, battle those who battle with me.

notes.1222: (tn): Two different types of shields are mentioned here. See also Ezek 38:4. Many modern translations render the first term (translated here “small shield”) as “buckler” (cf. NASB “buckler and shield”; the order is often reversed in the translation, apparently for stylistic reasons: cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV “shield and buckler”). The English term “buckler,” referring to a small round shield held on the arm to protect the upper body, is unfamiliar to many modern readers, so the term “small shield” was used in the present translation for clarity.

notes.1223: (tn): Or “javelin.” On the meaning of this word, which occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, see M. Dahood, Psalms (AB), 1:210-11.
notes.1224: (tn, Heb): “draw out spear and lance to meet.”
notes.1225: (tn, Heb): “say to me,” or “say to my soul.”

rashi.heb:
*והרק חנית.* 
הזדיין כמו אריק חרבי (שמות ט״ו:ט׳), וירק את חניכיו (בראשית י״ד:י״ד):
rashi.eng: *And arm Yourself with a spear.* Heb. והרק. Arm Yourself, as (in Exod. 15:9) “I will arm myself (אריק) with my sword;” (Gen. 14:14), “And he armed (וירק) his trained men.”

rashi.heb:
*וסגר לקראת רדפי.* 
הגן ביני וביניהם כמחיצ':
rashi.eng: *and bar the way before my pursuers.* Protect between me and them, as a barrier.

rashi.heb:
*לנפשי.* 
אימוימאימא"ש בלע"ז, כמו כרו שוחה לנפשי (ירמיהו י״ח:כ׳):
rashi.eng: *to my soul.* A moi meme in French, to myself, as (in Jer. 18:20): “for they have dug a pit for me (לנפשי).”

notes.1226: (tn): The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse are understood as jussives. The psalmist is calling judgment down on his enemies. See also the distinct jussive form in v. 6.

notes.1227: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive. See v. 4.
notes.1228: (sn): See the mention of the Lord’s angel in Ps 34:7.

notes.1230: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is distinctly jussive, indicating this is a prayer.

rashi.heb:
*חשך והלקלקות.* 
שניהם יחד כדי שיחליקו רגליה' בחלקלקות והחשך אינו מניחם להשמר מן החלקלקות כד"א (שם כ"ג) לכן יהיה דרכם להם כחלקלקות באפלה ידחו ויפלו בה:
rashi.eng: *dark and slippery.* Both together, so that their feet should slip on the slippery places and the darkness should not allow them to beware of the slippery places, as it is written (in Jer. 23:12): “Therefore, their way shall be for them like slippery places in the dark: ‘let them be thrust and fall therein.’”

notes.1231: (tc, Heb): “for without cause they hid for me a pit of their net, without cause they dug for my life.” It appears that the words “pit” and “net” have been transposed. “Net” goes with the verb “hid” in the first line (see v. 8, as well as Pss 9:15; 31:4), while “pit” goes with the verb “dug” in the second line (see Ps 7:15).

rashi.heb:
*חפרו לנפשי.* 
שוחה ליפול בה:
rashi.eng: *they have dug it for my soul.* they have dug a pit into which I should fall.

notes.1232: (tn, Heb): “let destruction [which] he does not know come to him.” The singular is used of the enemy in v. 8, probably in a representative or collective sense. The psalmist has more than one enemy, as vv. 1-7 make clear.
notes.1233: (tn): The psalmist’s prayer for his enemies’ demise continues. See vv. 4-6.

rashi.heb:
*שואה.* 
חשך ברואינ"ה בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *darkness.* Heb. שואה, darkness, broine in Old French, obscurity.

rashi.heb:
*ורשתו אשר טמן.* 
כן דרך לטמון הרשת ולכסותו בקש או בעפר כדי שלא ירגיש בה העובר עליה עד שנלכד בה:
rashi.eng: *and his net that he hid.* So is the custom to hide the net and to cover it with straw or with earth, in order that the one who passes over it should not notice it until he is trapped in it.

notes.1234: (tn, Heb): “then my soul will rejoice in the Lord and be happy in his deliverance.”

rashi.heb:
*ונפשי תגיל.* 
כשאראה במפלתם:
rashi.eng: *And my soul shall exult.* when I see their downfall.

notes.1236: (tn, Heb): “[the one who] rescues.” The substantival participle in the Hebrew text characterizes God as one who typically rescues the oppressed.
notes.1237: (tn, Heb): “from [the one who is] too strong for him.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense. The typical oppressed individual and typical oppressor are in view.
notes.1238: (tn, Heb): “the oppressed [one] and needy [one] from [the one who] robs him.” As in the previous line, the singular forms are used in a representative sense.

rashi.heb:
*כל עצמותי.* 
יקלסוך על כך כי עתה:
rashi.eng: *All my bones.* will praise You for everything, for now…

notes.1240: (tn, Heb): “[that] which I do not know they ask me.”

rashi.heb:
*יקומון.* 
עלי תמיד עדי חמס וגו':
rashi.eng: *False witnesses rise up.* constantly against me, etc.

notes.1241: (tn, Heb): “they repay me evil instead of good.”
notes.1242: (tn, Heb): “[there is] bereavement to my soul.”

notes.1243: (tn, Heb): “as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth.” Sackcloth was worn by mourners. When the psalmist’s enemies were sick, he was sorry for their misfortune and mourned for them.
notes.1244: (sn): Fasting was also a practice of mourners. By refraining from normal activities, such as eating food, the mourner demonstrated the sincerity of his sorrow.
notes.1245: (tn, Heb): “and my prayer upon my chest will return.” One could translate, “but my prayer was returning upon my chest,” but the use of the imperfect verbal form sets this line apart from the preceding and following lines (vv. 13a, 14), which use the perfect to describe the psalmist’s past actions.

rashi.heb:
*ותפלתי על חיקי תשוב.* 
כלומר ואם יאמרו לא עניתי נפשי אלא לרעתם שיכבד עליהם חליים תפלתי שהתפללתי עליהם תשוב עלי:
rashi.eng: *and may my prayer return upon my bosom.* That is to say: If they say that I afflicted myself only for their detriment, that their illness should become more serious, may my prayer that I prayed for them return to me.

notes.1246: (tn, Heb): “like a friend, like a brother to me I walked about.”
notes.1247: (sn): I bowed down. Bowing down was a posture for mourning. See Ps 38:6.
notes.1248: (tn, Heb): “like mourning for a mother [in] sorrow I bowed down.”

rashi.heb:
*כרע כאח לי התהלכתי.* 
כאילו היו לי אחי ורעי התהלכתי מיצר עליהם על צרת':
rashi.eng: *I walked about as though it were a friend or as though it were my own brother.* As though it were my brother or my friend; I walked about depressed because of their distress.

rashi.heb:
*כאבל.* 
אם כבן המתאבל על אמו או כאם המתאבלת על בנה:
rashi.eng: *as the mourning of a mother.* As a son who mourns for his mother or as a mother who mourns for her son.

rashi.heb:
*קודר.* 
לשון שחרות:
rashi.eng: *with gloom.* Heb. קדר, an expression of blackness.

rashi.heb:
*שחותי.* 
לשון שפלות:
rashi.eng: *I was bowed.* An expression of humility.

notes.1249: (tn, Heb): “they gathered together against me, stricken [ones], and I did not know.” The Hebrew form נֵכִים (nekhim, “stricken ones” ?) is problematic. Some suggest an emendation to נָכְרִים[כְ] (k�nokh�rim, “foreigners”) or “like foreigners,” which would fit with what follows, “[like] foreigners that I do not recognize.” Perhaps the form should be read as a Qal active participle, נֹכִים (nokhim, “ones who strike”) from the verbal root נָכָה (nakhah, “to strike”). The Qal of this verb is unattested in biblical Hebrew, but the peal (basic) stem appears in Old Aramaic (J. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Inscriptions of Sefire [BibOr], 114; DNWSI 1:730.) In this case one might translate, “attackers gathered together against me though I was not aware of it” (cf. NASB “smiters”; NEB, NRSV “ruffians”; NIV “attackers”).
notes.1250: (tn, Heb): “they tore and did not keep quiet.” By using the verb “tear,” the psalmist likens his enemies to a wild animal (see Hos 13:8). In v. 17 he compares them to hungry young lions.

rashi.heb:
*ובצלעי שמחו ונאספו.* 
וכשאני צולע ששבר בא עלי שמחו ונאספו:
rashi.eng: *And, when I limped, they rejoiced and gathered.* And when I limped because I suffered a fracture, they rejoiced and gathered [around me].

rashi.heb:
*נאספו עלי נכים.* 
אנשי' פסחי' כמו שאנו מתרגמינן נכה חגירא, ומנחם חברו כמו נכאי' (ישעיה ט"ז) אימנויישי"ץ בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *lame people gathered about me.* Heb. נכים, lame people, as we translate “Pharaoh-neco,” חגירא, lame. Menachem (p. 122f.) associated it with (Isa. 16:7), נכאים, broken-hearted, amenuyze in Old French, crushed.

rashi.heb:
*קרעו ולא דמו.* 
אילו היו קורעין את בשרי לא היה דמי שותת לארץ כשמלבינין פני:
rashi.eng: *Were they to tear, they would not draw blood.* Were they to tear my flesh, my blood would not flow to the ground when they embarrass me [lit. make my face white].

notes.1251: (tc): The MT reads “as profane [ones] of mockers of food,” which is nonsensical. The present translation assumes (1) an emendation of בְּחַנְפֵי (b�khanfey, “as profane men”) to בְּחַנְפִי (bekhanfiy, “when I tripped”; preposition + Qal infinitive construct from II חָנַף [“limp”] + first common singular pronominal suffix) and (2) an emendation of לַעֲגֵי מָעוֹג (la’agey ma’og, “mockers of food”) to עָגוּ[ם]לַעְגָּ (la’gam ’agu, “[with] taunting they taunted”; masculine plural noun with enclitic mem + Qal perfect third common plural from לַּעַג [la’ag, “taunt”]).
notes.1252: (tn, Heb): “gnashing at me with their teeth.” The infinitive absolute adds a complementary action – they gnashed with their teeth as they taunted.

rashi.heb:
*בחנפי לעגי מעוג וגו'.* 
בשביל חניפות של ליצנות אכילה ושתיה שמחניפין לשאול בשביל שיאכילם וישקם חורקים עלי שיניהם:
rashi.eng: *Because of the flattery of scorn for food, they gnash, etc..* Because of the flattery of scorn of eating and drinking, that they flatter Saul in order that he give them to eat and drink, they gnash their teeth against me.

rashi.heb:
*מעוג.* 
לשון אכילה כמו אם יש לי מעוג דאליהו (מלכים א י״ז:י״ב), ומנחם פתר אותו לשון עוגה קטנה (שם) וכן אם יש לי מעוג:
rashi.eng: *food.* Heb. מעוג, an expression of eating, as (in I Kings 17:12): “if I have food (מעוג),” written regarding Elijah, but Menachem (p. 130) interpreted it as an expression of a loaf of bread, and so “if I have a cake (מעוג).”

notes.1253: (tn, Heb): “O Lord, how long will you see?”
notes.1256: (tn, Heb): “my only one.” The psalmist may mean that his life is precious, or that he feels isolated and alone (see Ps 22:20). The verb “guard” is supplied in the translation, because the verb “rescue” is understood by ellipsis (see the previous line).

rashi.heb:
*כמה תראה.* 
כמה ארך אפים יש לפניך לראות כל אלה:
rashi.eng: *how long will You look on?.* How much patience do You have to look upon all these?

rashi.heb:
*משואיהם.* 
מחשך שלהם:
rashi.eng: *from their darkness.* Heb. משאיהם, from their darkness.

rashi.heb:
*מכפירים יחידתי.* 
מוסב על השיבה נפשי השיבה מכפירים יחידתי, (יחידתי נשמתי סא"א):
rashi.eng: *my only one from young lions.* This refers to “Return my soul.” Return my only one from young lions.

notes.1257: (sn): The great assembly is also mentioned in Ps 22:25.

notes.1259: (tn, Heb): “[with] a lie.” The Hebrew noun שֶׁקֶר (sheqer, “lie”) is used here as an adverb, “falsely, wrongfully” (see Ps 38:19).
notes.1261: (tn, Heb): “[do not let] those who hate me without cause pinch [i.e., wink] an eye.” The negative particle is understood in the second line by ellipsis (see the preceding line). In the Book of Proverbs “winking an eye” is associated with deceit and trickery (see 6:13; 10:10; 16:30).

rashi.heb:
*אויבי שקר.* 
ששונאין אותי על דבר שקר שמעידין עלי מה שלא עלה במחשבתי מעולם אל ישמחו במפלתי:
rashi.eng: *those who are my enemies for an unjust cause.* who hate me because of a false matter, that they testify against me what never entered my mind. Let them not rejoice at my downfall.

rashi.heb:
*שונאי.* 
ששונאי' אותי אל יקרצו עלי עין וללעוג בעיניהם על מפלתי יקרצו צינאנ"ט בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *who hate me.* Let those who hate me not wink their eyes at me, to mock my downfall with their eyes. יקרצו means seynt in Old French, signal.

notes.1262: (tn, Heb): “for they do not speak peace.”
notes.1263: (tn, Heb): “but against the quiet ones of the land words of deceit they plan.” The imperfect verbal forms in v. 20 highlight their characteristic behavior.

rashi.heb:
*על רגעי ארץ.* 
על דכאי ארץ, וכן רוגע הים (ירמיהו ל״א:ל״ה) עורי רגע (איוב ז׳:ה׳), וכן פירש דונש:
rashi.eng: *and against the crushed people of the earth.* Heb. רגעי, on the crushed people of the earth, and so (in Jer. 31:34): “Who stirs up (רגע) the sea;” (Job 7:5), “my skin wrinkled (רגע).” And so did Dunash explain it.

notes.1264: (tn, Heb): “and they cause their mouth to be wide against me.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) consecutive here carries on the generalizing mood of the previous verse. For other examples of this use of the prefixed verbal form with vav consecutive, see GKC 329 �111.t.
notes.1265: (tn, Heb): “our eye sees.” Apparently this is an idiom meaning to “look in triumph” or “gloat over” (see Ps 54:7).

rashi.heb:
*האח האח.* 
לשון שמחה מתהלל בתאות לבו מרוב שמחת' שרואים תאותם מתקיימת:
rashi.eng: *Aha! Aha!.* Heb. האח, an expression of joy of one who boasts with the lust of his heart, out of their [sic] great joy, that they see their lust gratified.

notes.1266: (tn, Heb): “you see, O Lord.” There is a deliberate play on words. In v. 21 the enemies say, “our eye sees,” but the psalmist is confident that the Lord “sees” as well, so he appeals to him for help (see also v. 17).

notes.1267: (sn): Though he is confident that the Lord is aware of his situation (see v. 22a), the psalmist compares the Lord’s inactivity to sleep and urges him to wake up.

rashi.heb:
*העירה והקיצה.* 
פמליא של מעל' לשפוט משפטי מאויבי:
rashi.eng: *Arouse Yourself and awaken.* the heavenly retinue to judge my cause from my enemies.

notes.1272: (tn, Heb): “Aha! Our desire!” The “desire” of the psalmist’s enemies is to triumph over him.

notes.1273: (tn, Heb): “may they be embarrassed and ashamed together, the ones who rejoice over my harm.”
notes.1274: (tn, Heb): “may they be clothed with shame and humiliation, the ones who magnify [themselves] against me.” The prefixed verbal forms in v. 26 are understood as jussives (see vv. 24b-25, where the negative particle אַל (’al) appears before the prefixed verbal forms, indicating they are jussives). The psalmist is calling down judgment on his enemies.

notes.1275: (tn): The prefixed verbal forms in v. 27a are understood as jussives (see vv. 24b-26).
notes.1276: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, “may the Lord be magnified [in praise].” Another option is to take the verb as an imperfect, “the Lord is great.”
notes.1277: (tn, Heb): “the one who desires the peace of his servant.”

notes.1278: (tn, Heb): “and my tongue will proclaim your justice.”
notes.1279: (tn, Heb): “all the day your praise.” The verb “proclaim” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the previous line).
notes.1280: (sn): Psalm 36. Though evil men plan to harm others, the psalmist is confident that the Lord is the just ruler of the earth who gives and sustains all life. He prays for divine blessing and protection and anticipates God’s judgment of the wicked.
notes.1281: (tn): In the Hebrew text the word נאם (“oracle”) appears at the beginning of the next verse (v. 2 in the Hebrew text because the superscription is considered v. 1). The resulting reading, “an oracle of rebellion for the wicked [is] in the midst of my heart” (cf. NIV) apparently means that the psalm, which foresees the downfall of the wicked, is a prophetic oracle about the rebellion of the wicked which emerges from the soul of the psalmist. One could translate, “Here is a poem written as I reflected on the rebellious character of evil men.” Another option, followed in the translation above, is to attach נאם (n�’um, “oracle”) with the superscription. For another example of a Davidic poem being labeled an “oracle,” see 2 Sam 23:1.

notes.1282: (tn, Heb): “[the] rebellion of an evil man [is] in the midst of my heart.” The translation assumes a reading “in the midst of his heart” (i.e., “to the core”) instead of “in the midst of my heart,” a change which finds support in a a few medieval Hebrew mss, the Hebrew text of Origen’s Hexapla, and the Syriac.
notes.1283: (tn, Heb): “there is no dread of God before his eyes.” The phrase “dread of God” refers here to a healthy respect for God which recognizes that he will punish evil behavior.

notes.1284: (tn, Heb): “for it causes to be smooth to him in his eyes to find his sin to hate.” The meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear. Perhaps the point is this: His rebellious attitude makes him reject any notion that God will hold him accountable. His attitude also prevents him from recognizing and repudiating his sinful ways.

rashi.heb:
*נאם פשע לרשע בקרב לבי וגו'.* 
הרי זה מקרא מסורס יש בקרב לבי שהפשע הוא יצר הרע אומר לרשע שלא יהא פחד אלהים לנגד עיניו:
rashi.eng: *The word of the transgression to the wicked man, in the midst of my heart, etc..* This is a transposed verse. I feel within my heart that the transgression, i.e., the evil inclination, says to the wicked man that the fear of God should not be before his eyes.

rashi.heb:
*ובקרב לבי.* 
כאדם שאומר כמדומה אני:
rashi.eng: *in the midst of my heart.* Like a person who says, “It seems to me.”

notes.1285: (tn, Heb): “he ceases to exhibit wisdom to do good.” The Hiphil forms are exhibitive, indicating the outward expression of an inner attitude.

rashi.heb:
*כי החליק.* 
הפשע על הרשע בחלקלקות בעיניו כדי שימצא הקב"ה את עונו לשנוא אותו:
rashi.eng: *For it smoothed.* The transgression made smooth places appear to his eyes in order that the Holy One, blessed be He, find his iniquity to hate him.

notes.1286: (tn, Heb): “he takes a stand in a way [that is] not good.” The word “way” here refers metaphorically to behavior or life style.
notes.1287: (tn): The three imperfect verbal forms in v. 4 highlight the characteristic behavior of the typical evildoer.

rashi.heb:
*חדל להשכיל להיטיב.* 
מנע עצמי מהשכיל להיטיב מעשיו:
rashi.eng: *he refrained from learning to improve.* He refrained from contemplating to improve his deeds.

notes.1289: (sn): The Lord’s loyal love/faithfulness is almost limitless. He is loyal and faithful to his creation and blesses mankind and the animal kingdom with physical life and sustenance (vv. 6-9).

rashi.heb:
*יתיצב על דרך לא טוב.* 
הקב"ה נתן לפניו דרך הטוב ודרך המות והוא בוחר לו דרך לא טוב:
rashi.eng: *he stands on a way that is not good.* The Holy One, blessed be He, placed before him the good way and the way of death, yet he chooses for himself a way that is not good.

notes.1290: (tn, Heb): “mountains of God.” The divine name אֵל (’el, “God”) is here used in an idiomatic manner to indicate the superlative.
notes.1292: (sn): God’s justice/fairness is firm and reliable like the highest mountains and as abundant as the water in the deepest sea. The psalmist uses a legal metaphor to describe God’s preservation of his creation. Like a just judge who vindicates the innocent, God protects his creation from destructive forces.

rashi.heb:
*ה' בהשמים חסדך.* 
בשביל רשעים הללו אתה מסלק חסד מן התחתונים ומגביה אמונתך עד שחקי' לסלקה מבני אדם:
rashi.eng: *O Lord, Your kindness is in the heavens.* Because of these wicked men, You remove [Your] kindness from the earth creatures and raise up Your faith until the sky to remove it from the sons of men.

notes.1294: (tn, Heb): “and the sons of man in the shadow of your wings find shelter.” The preservation of physical life is in view, as the next verse makes clear.

rashi.heb:
*צדקתך.* 
יקרה מן הבריות כהררי אל בשביל מעשי הרשעים ומשפטיך באים לעול' עד תהום רבה, ד"א צדקתך כהררי אל מי שאתה רוצה לעשות צדקה עמו אתה מגביהו ומתקפו כהררי אל, לשון תוקף כמו (יחזקאל י״ז:י״ג) ואת אילי הארץ לקח:
rashi.eng: *Your charity.* is as scarce to the creatures as the mighty mountains because of the deeds of the wicked, and Your judgments come upon the world until the vast deep. Another explanation:

rashi.heb:
*צדקתך כהררי אל.* 
מי שאתה רוצה לעשות צדקה עמו אתה מגביהו ומתקפו כהררי אל, לשון תוקף כמו (יחזקאל י״ז:י״ג) ואת אילי הארץ לקח:
rashi.eng: *Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains.* The one with whom You wish to deal charitably, You raise up and strengthen like the mighty mountains. אל is an expression of strength, as (in Ezek. 17:13): “and he has taken away the mighty of (אילי) the land.”

rashi.heb:
*משפטיך תהום רבה.* 
מי שאתה רוצה לדון אותו וליקח נקמתך ממנו אתה מורידו עד תהו' רב':
rashi.eng: *Your judgments are the vast deep.* Whomever You wish to judge, and wreak vengeance upon, You humble him to the vast deep.

rashi.heb:
*משפטיך.* 
יושטיצ"א בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *Your judgments.* Heb. משפטיך, joustiza in Old French, justice.

rashi.heb:
*אדם ובהמה תושיע ה'.* 
בני אדם שהם ערומים בדעת כאדם הראשון ומשימין עצמן כבהמה בענוה תושיע ה':
rashi.eng: *You save both man and beast.* People who are as astute as Adam, but who make themselves as humble as beasts, You save, O Lord.

rashi.heb:
*מה יקר חסדך.* 
אינו כדאי להמשך על הרשעים הללו אבל בני אדם אשר בצל כנפיך יחסיון הם ירויון מדשן ביתך וגו':
rashi.eng: *How precious is Your kindness.* It is not fitting that it be extended to these wicked, but the children of men who take refuge in the shadow of Your wings, they will be sated from the fat of Your house, etc.

notes.1295: (tn, Heb): “for with you is the fountain of life, in your light we see light.” Water (note “fountain”) and light are here metaphors for life.

notes.1297: (tn, Heb): “to those who know you.” The Hebrew verb יָדַע (yada’, “know”) is used here of those who “know” the Lord in the sense that they recognize his royal authority and obey his will (see Jer 22:16).
notes.1298: (tn, Heb): “and your justice to.” The verb “extend” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the previous line).
notes.1299: (tn, Heb): “the pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).

notes.1300: (tn, Heb): “let not a foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of the evil ones cause me to wander as a fugitive.”

notes.1301: (tn, Heb): “there the workers of wickedness have fallen.” The adverb שָׁם (sham, “there”) is used here for dramatic effect, as the psalmist envisions the evildoers lying fallen at a spot that is vivid in his imagination (BDB 1027 s.v.).
notes.1302: (tn): The psalmist uses perfect verbal forms in v. 12 to describe the demise of the wicked as if it has already taken place.
notes.1303: (sn): Psalm 37. The psalmist urges his audience not to envy the wicked, but to trust in and obey the Lord, for he will destroy sinners and preserve the godly. When the smoke of judgment clears, the wicked will be gone, but the godly will remain and inherit God’s promised blessings. The psalm is an acrostic; every other verse begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

rashi.heb:
*אל תבואני רגל גאוה.* 
אל תבוא עמי רגל הרשעים הללו בעת קבול שכר להיות חלקם עם הצדיקים, (ל' חלק אהלא פרט"יאה בלע"ז סא"א):
rashi.eng: *Let the foot of haughtiness not come with me.* Let the foot of these wicked men not come with me at the time of the reception of reward, [because] their lot should [not] be with the righteous.

rashi.heb:
*ויד רשעים אל תנדני.* 
ממקומי בבואי לירש משנה חלקי וחלקו (של רשע) בטובה כענין שנאמר (ישעיהו ס״א:ז׳) לכן בארצם משנה יירשו ואז:
rashi.eng: *neither shall the hand of the wicked cause me to wander.* from my place when I return to inherit a double [portion]: my portion and the portion of the wicked man, in the goodness, as the matter that is stated (in Isa. 61:7): “Therefore, in their land they shall inherit twofold.” And then…

rashi.heb:
*שם נפלו פועלי און.* 
שם יבינו במפלתם ושם דוחו ולא יכלו קום:
rashi.eng: *There the workers of iniquity have fallen.* There they will understand their downfall, and there they were thrust away and were unable to rise.

notes.1304: (tn): The verb form is singular (see vv. 3-10 as well, where the second person verbs and pronouns are also singular). The psalmist’s exhortation has a wisdom flavor to it; it is personalized for each member of his audience.
notes.1305: (tn, Heb): “over sinners.” The context indicates that the psalmist has in mind the apparent power and success of sinners. See v. 7b.

rashi.heb:
*אל תתחר במרעים.* 
מוכיח את ישראל הוא שלא יתחרו בהצלחת המרעים לעשות כמעשיה' כמו (ירמיה י"ב) ואיך תתחרה את הסוסים לרוץ במרוצתם, האטיר בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *Do not compete with the evildoers.* He reproves Israel that they should not compete with the success of the evildoers to do as their deeds, as (in Jer. 12:5): “how will you compete (תתחרה) with horses,” to run as they run, a atir in Old French, to compete.

rashi.heb:
*אל תקנא בעושי עולה.* 
לעשות עולה כמותם:
rashi.eng: *do not envy those who commit injustice.* to commit injustice like them.

rashi.heb:
*ימלו.* 
שרו"נט טראנקיי"ץ בלע"ז, ל' כריתה:
rashi.eng: *they will be… cut off.* Heb. ימלו, seront tronke in Old French, they will be cut off, an expression of cutting off.

notes.1307: (tn, Heb): “tend integrity.” The verb רָעָה (ra’ah, “tend, shepherd”) is probably used here in the sense of “watch over, guard.” The noun אֱמוּנָה (’emunah, “faithfulness, honesty, integrity”) is understood as the direct object of the verb, though it could be taken as an adverbial accusative, “[feed] securely,” if the audience is likened to a flock of sheep.

rashi.heb:
*בטח בה'.* 
ואל תאמר אם לא אגזול ואגנוב או אתן לעני צדקה במה אתפרנס:
rashi.eng: *Trust in the Lord.* and do not say, “If I do not rob and steal,” or “If I give charity to a poor man, how will I sustain myself?”

rashi.heb:
*ועשה טוב.* 
ואז תשכון ארץ לאורך ימים:
rashi.eng: *and do good.* Then you will dwell in the land for a long time.

rashi.heb:
*ורעה אמונה.* 
תאכל ותתפרנס משכר האמונה שהאמנת בהקדוש ברוך הוא לסמוך עליו ולעשות טוב:
rashi.eng: *and be nourished by faith.* You will eat and be sustained from the reward of [your] faith, that you believed in the Holy One, blessed be He, to rely on Him and do good.

notes.1308: (tn): Following the imperatives of v. 3 the prefixed verbal forms with vav (ו) in v. 4 indicate result. Faith and obedience (v. 3) will bring divine blessing (v. 4).
notes.1309: (tn, Heb): Or “and he will give you what you desire most.” “and he will grant to you the requests of your heart.”

rashi.heb:
*והתענג על ה'.* 
התענג בתפנוקי' על משענתו של הקדוש ברוך הוא:
rashi.eng: *So shall you delight in the Lord.* Enjoy delights by being supported by the Holy One, blessed be He.

notes.1310: (tn, Heb): “roll your way upon the Lord.” The noun “way” may refer here to one’s activities or course of life.
notes.1311: (tn, Heb): “he will act.” Verse 6 explains what is meant; the Lord will vindicate those who trust in him.

rashi.heb:
*גול על ה' דרכך.* 
גלגל עליו כל צרכיך:
rashi.eng: *Commit your way to the Lord.* Commit all your needs to Him.

notes.1312: (tn, Heb): “and he will bring out like light your vindication, and your just cause like noonday.”

notes.1314: (tc): The Hebrew text has וְהִתְחוֹלֵל (v�hitkholel, Hitpolel of חִיל, khil, “writhe with fear, suffer”) but this idea fits awkwardly here. The text should be changed to וְתוֹחֵל (v�tokhel; Hiphil of יָחַל, yakhal, “wait”). It appears that the Hebrew text is the product of dittography: (1) the initial וה (vav-he) is accidentally repeated from the preceding word (יְהוָה, y�hvah) and (2) the final lamed (ל) is accidentally repeated (note the preceding lamed and the initial lamed on the following form, לו).
notes.1315: (tn, Heb): “over one who causes his way to be successful.”

rashi.heb:
*דום לה'.* 
המתן לישועתו כמו (שמואל א י״ד:ט׳) אם כה יאמרו אלינו דומו דיהונתן, ומנחם חברו לשון דממה כמו וידם אהרן (ויקרא י׳:ג׳) וגם כן פתר טוב ויחיל ודומם (איכה ג׳:כ״ו) ודונש מודה לו:
rashi.eng: *Wait for the Lord.* Heb. דום. Wait for His salvation, as (in I Sam. 14:9): “If they say thus to us, ‘Wait (דמו)!’ ” mentioned regarding Jonathan. Menachem (p. 64), however, associates it as an expression of silence, as (in Lev. 10:3): “and Aaron was silent (וידם).” He likewise interpreted (Lam. 3:26): "It is good that one should wait quietly (ודומם) in this manner, and Dunash (p. 27) concurs with him.

rashi.heb:
*והתחולל.* 
לשון תוחלת:
rashi.eng: *and hope.* Heb. והתחולל, an expression of hope (תוחלת).

rashi.heb:
*אל תתחר.* 
לאמר ארשיע כמותו ואצליח כמותו:
rashi.eng: *do not compete.* saying, “I will be as wicked as he, and I will prosper as he does.”

rashi.heb:
*הרף מאף.* 
הרף מהרשיע שלא יבא עליך אף:
rashi.eng: *Desist from anger.* Desist from being wicked so that anger does not come upon you.

rashi.heb:
*ועזוב.* 
דבר המביא עליך חמתו של הקב"ה:
rashi.eng: *and forsake.* a matter that will bring upon you the wrath of the Holy One, blessed be He.

notes.1317: (tn, Heb): “for evil men.” The conjunction כִּי (ki, “for”) relates to the exhortations in v. 8; there is no reason to be frustrated, for the evildoers will be punished in due time.
notes.1319: (tn, Heb): “and those who wait on the Lord, they will possess the land.”

rashi.heb:
*כי מרעים.* 
שאתה רואה עתה מצליחים הם יכרתון:
rashi.eng: *For evildoers.* whom you now see prospering, they will be cut off.

notes.1320: (tn, Heb): “and yet, a little, there will be no wicked [one].”
notes.1321: (tn, Heb): “and you will carefully look upon his place, but he will not be [there].” The singular is used here in a representative sense; the typical evildoer is in view.

rashi.heb:
*ועוד מעט.* 
כשתמתין עוד מעט תראה כי אין הרשע:
rashi.eng: *A short while longer.* When you wait a little longer, you will see that the wicked man is not here.

rashi.heb:
*והתבוננת על מקומו.* 
ותסתכל על מקום שהיה שם ואיננו כי מת ואבד:
rashi.eng: *and you shall look at his place.* and you shall look at the place where he was, and he is not there, because he has died and has perished.

notes.1322: (tn, Heb): “and they will take delight in (see v. 4) abundance of peace.”

notes.1323: (tn): Or “innocent.” The singular is used here in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and the typical godly individual are in view.
notes.1324: (tn, Heb): “and gnashes at him with his teeth” (see Ps 35:16). The language may picture the evil men as wild animals. The active participles in v. 12 are used for purposes of dramatic description.

rashi.heb:
*וחרק.* 
כמו חרקו שן ארקי"נט בלע"ז, (איכה יד):
rashi.eng: *and gnashes.* Heb. וחרק, as (in Lam. 2:16): “and gnashed (ויחרקו) their teeth”; e rechineynt in Old French.

notes.1325: (tn, Heb): “laughs.” As the next line indicates, this refers to derisive laughter (see 2:4). The Hebrew imperfect verbal form describes the action from the perspective of an eye-witness who is watching the divine response as it unfolds before his eyes.
notes.1326: (tn, Heb): “for he sees that his day is coming.” As the following context makes clear (vv. 15, 17, 19-20), “his day” refers to the time when God will destroy evildoers.

notes.1328: (tn, Heb): “the upright in way,” i.e., those who lead godly lives.

rashi.heb:
*חרב פתחו.* 
הרשעי' פתחו, אנקומנצירנט בלע"ז תגר וחרום מתחילים הרשעים מאליהם:
rashi.eng: *initiated war.* the wicked initiated quarrel and strife without previous provocation.

notes.1330: (tn, Heb): “Better [is] a little to the godly one than the wealth of many evil ones.” The following verses explain why this is true. Though a godly individual may seem to have only meager possessions, he always has what he needs and will eventually possess the land. The wicked may prosper for a brief time, but will eventually be destroyed by divine judgment and lose everything.

rashi.heb:
*טוב מעט לצדיק.* 
טובים מעט אנשים שהולכים לעזרת הצדיקים:
rashi.eng: *The few of the righteous are better.* The few men who go to the aid of the righteous are better.

rashi.heb:
*מהמון רשעים רבים.* 
אמרפל וחביריו שהתחילו מלחמ' בעולם בשביל לשבות את לוט ולהתגרות באברהם מעט אנשים שהיו עם אברה' הצליחו והרגו כל אותן האוכלסין:
rashi.eng: *than the multitude of many wicked men.* Amraphel and his allies initiated a war in the world for the purpose of capturing Lot and provoking Abraham, but the few who were with Abraham succeeded and wiped out all those armies.

notes.1331: (tn, Heb): “for the arms of the evil ones will be broken.”
notes.1332: (tn): The active participle here indicates this is characteristically true.

notes.1333: (tn, Heb): “the Lord knows the days of the innocent ones.” He “knows” their days in the sense that he is intimately aware of and involved in their daily struggles. He meets their needs and sustains them.

rashi.heb:
*יודע ה' ימי תמימים.* 
מכי' את מעשי ימיהם ונחלתם וקבול שכר' מאתו לעול' תהיה:
rashi.eng: *The Lord knows the days of the innocent.* He recognizes the deeds of their days, and their inheritance and the reception of their reward from Him shall be forever.

notes.1336: (tn, Heb): “in days of famine they will be satisfied.”

notes.1337: (tn): Or “for,” but Hebrew כי in this case would have to extend all the way back to v. 17a. Another option is to understand the particle as asseverative, “surely” (see v. 22).
notes.1338: (tc): The meaning of the MT (כִּיקַר כָּרִים [kiqar karim], “like what is precious among the pastures/rams”) is uncertain. One possibility is to take the noun כָּרִים as “pastures” and interpret “what is precious” as referring to flowers that blossom but then quickly disappear (see v. 2 and BDB 430 s.v. יָקָר 3). If כָּרִים is taken as “rams,” then “what is precious” might refer to the choicest portions of rams. The present translation follows a reading in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpPs37), כיקוד כורם (“like the burning of an oven”). The next line, which pictures the Lord’s enemies being consumed in smoke, supports this reading, which assumes confusion of the Hebrew letters resh (ר) and dalet (ד) at the end of the first word in the sequence.
notes.1339: (tn, Heb): “they perish in smoke, they perish.” In addition to repeating the verb for emphasis, the psalmist uses the perfect form of the verb to picture the enemies’ demise as if it had already taken place. In this way he draws attention to the certitude of their judgment.

rashi.heb:
*כיקר כרים.* 
כאור ענן בקר הנראה שחרית מלבין על מרחבי בקעה שאינו מתקיים, כרים מישור כמו כר נרחב (ישעיה ל') כיקר לשון אור יקרות (זכריה י״ד:ו׳), ויש פותרין כיקר כרים, ככבוד כבשים שמפטמין אותן לטבח:
rashi.eng: *like disappearing light on the plains.* Heb. כרים כיקר, like the light of the morning cloud, which appears at dawn and glistens on the broad plains, which does not last. כרים means a plain, as (in Isa. 30:23): “a wide plain (כר נרחב).” כיקר is an expression of “disappearing light (אור יקרות)” (as in Zech. 14:6). Others interpret כיקר כרים: like the glory of lambs that are fattened for the slaughter.

notes.1340: (tn, Heb): “an evil [man] borrows and does not repay; but a godly [man] is gracious and gives.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and godly individual are in view. The three active participles and one imperfect (“repay”) draw attention to the characteristic behavior of the two types.

rashi.heb:
*לוה רשע ולא ישלם וצדיק חונן ונותן.* 
הקב"ה שהוא צדיקו של עולם חונן משלו ונותן לזה שהלוה מה שהוא גוזל ממנו:
rashi.eng: *A wicked man borrows and does not pay, but the Righteous is gracious and gives.* The Holy One, blessed be He, Who is the Righteous One of the world, is gracious with His own and gives it to the one who lent what he [the borrower] stole from him.

notes.1341: (tn): The particle כִּי is best understood as asseverative or emphatic here.
notes.1342: (tn, Heb): “those blessed by him.” The pronoun “him” must refer to the Lord (see vv. 20, 23), so the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*כי מבורכיו.* 
של צדיקו של עולם יירשו ארץ:
rashi.eng: *For those blessed by Him.* By the Righteous One of the world, shall inherit the land.

notes.1345: (tn, Heb): “from the Lord the steps of a man are established, and in his way he delights.” The second line qualifies the first. The man whose behavior is commendable in God’s sight is the one whose ways are established by God. Another option is that the second line refers to the godly man delighting in God’s “way,” namely the lifestyle which he prescribes for men. In this case one might translate, “The Lord grants success to the one who desires to obey his commands.”

rashi.heb:
*מצעדי גבר.* 
מי שהוא גבור ביראת הקדוש ברוך הוא ליש פאש דופורט בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *a mighty man’s steps.* He who is mighty in the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He; les pas du fort in French, the steps of the strong one.

rashi.heb:
*כוננו.* 
פורי"נט אפיטייץ בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *are established.* Fureut afettetes in French, are prepared for reality.

notes.1346: (tn): Other translation options for כִּי in this context are “when” (so NASB) or “though” (so NEB, NIV, NRSV).
notes.1348: (tn): The active participle indicates this is characteristically true. See v. 17.

rashi.heb:
*יפול.* 
לבורג"א בלע"ז, לשון ותפול מעל הגמל (בראשית כ״ד:ס״ד):
rashi.eng: *If he falls.* Heb. יפל, aluverjera in Old French, falters, an expression of (Gen. 24: 64): “and she fell off the camel.”

rashi.heb:
*כי.* 
כמו אם:
rashi.eng: *If.* Heb. כי, like אם.

rashi.heb:
*לא יוטל.* 
לא יושלך להיות נעזב:
rashi.eng: *he will not be cast down.* He will not be cast away to be forsaken.

notes.1350: (tn, Heb): “or his offspring searching for food.” The expression “search for food” also appears in Lam 1:11, where Jerusalem’s refugees are forced to search for food and to trade their valuable possessions for something to eat.

rashi.heb:
*נער הייתי.* 
פסוק זה שר העולם אמרו דאילו דוד לא קשיש כולי האי:
rashi.eng: *I was young.* This verse was recited by the Prince of the World (the chief angel), for if it was David, he was not so old.

notes.1351: (tn): The active participles describe characteristic behavior.

rashi.heb:
*כל היום.* 
הצדיק חונן עניים ומלוה להם:
rashi.eng: *All day long.* the righteous man is gracious to the poor and lends to them.

rashi.heb:
*וזרעו.* 
זה שהוא זורע לצדקה סופו לברכה:
rashi.eng: *and his seed.* This seed that he sows with his charity will ultimately be blessed.

notes.1353: (tn): Or “Do good!” The imperatives are singular (see v. 1).
notes.1354: (tn, Heb): “and dwell permanently.” The imperative with vav (ו) is best taken here as a result clause after the preceding imperatives.

notes.1355: (tn, Heb): “loves.” The verb “loves” is here metonymic; the Lord’s commitment to principles of justice causes him to actively promote these principles as he governs the world. The active participle describes characteristic behavior.
notes.1356: (tn): The imperfect verbal form draws attention to this generalizing statement.
notes.1359: (tn): Or “cut off”; or “removed.” The perfect verbal forms in v. 28b state general truths.

notes.1360: (tn, Heb): “The mouth of the godly [one] utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.” The singular form is used in a representative sense; the typical godly individual is in view. The imperfect verbal forms draw attention to the characteristic behavior of the godly.

rashi.heb:
*פי צדיק יהגה.* 
תחלה בלבו חכמה לראות דין שפסקה תורה לכל דבר, ואח"כ לשונו תדבר משפט:
rashi.eng: *The righteous man’s mouth utters.* at first words of wisdom in his heart to see the law that the Torah decided for each thing, and afterwards his tongue speaks judgment.

notes.1361: (tn, Heb): “the law of his God [is] in his heart.” The “heart” is here the seat of one’s thoughts and motives.
notes.1362: (tn, Heb): “his.” The pronoun has been translated as plural to agree with the representative or typical “godly” in v. 30.

rashi.heb:
*לא תמעד אשוריו.* 
לא יחליקו צעדיו:
rashi.eng: *his feet do not falter.* His steps do not slip.

notes.1363: (tn, Heb): “an evil [one] watches the godly [one] and seeks to kill him.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and godly individual are in view. The active participles describe characteristic behavior.

notes.1364: (tn, Heb): “the Lord does not abandon him into his hand or condemn him when he is judged.” The imperfects draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic behavior in this regard.

notes.1366: (tn, Heb): “keep his way.” The Lord’s “way” refers here to the “conduct required” by the Lord. In Ps 25 the Lord’s “ways” are associated with his covenantal demands (see vv. 4, 9-10). See also Ps 119:3 (cf. vv. 1, 4), as well as Deut 8:6; 10:12; 11:22; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9; 30:16.
notes.1367: (tn, Heb): “and he will lift you up.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) is best taken here as a result clause following the imperatives in the preceding lines.
notes.1368: (tn, Heb): “when evil men are cut off you will see.”

notes.1369: (tn): The Hebrew uses the representative singular again here.
notes.1370: (tn, Heb): “being exposed [?] like a native, luxuriant.” The Hebrew form מִתְעָרֶה (mit’areh) appears to be a Hitpael participle from עָרָה (’arah, “be exposed”), but this makes no sense in this context. Perhaps the form is a dialectal variant of מִתְעָלָה (“giving oneself an air of importance”; see Jer 51:3), from עָלָה (’alah, “go up”; see P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 [WBC], 296). The noun אֶזְרָח (’ezrakh, “native, full citizen”) refers elsewhere to people, but here, where it is collocated with “luxuriant, green,” it probably refers to a tree growing in native soil.

rashi.heb:
*ומתערה.* 
משריש כמו (ישעיהו י״ט:ז׳) ערות על יאור, ובלשון משנה יש הרבה אילן שנפשח ומעורה בקליפה:
rashi.eng: *well-rooted.* Heb. ומתערה, rooted, as (in Isa. 19:7): “the well-rooted plants (ערות) by the stream.” In the language of the Mishnah there are many [examples]: e.g. (Oktzin 3:8): “A tree that was cut off but is yet rooted by its bark.”

rashi.heb:
*כאזרח רענן.* 
כאחד מאזרחי הארץ הנשרשין וממולאים בנכסים וכן פירש מנחם כאזרח רענן מתלחלח ומתצמח כאשל הנשרש ואזרח מאזרחי בני אדם אנשי שרשים המה (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *as a native who is fresh.* As one of the natives of the land who are well-rooted and abounding with property. And so did Menachem (p. 20) explain it: כאזרח רענן moist and growing like a well-rooted tree, and the native (אזרח) of the natives (מאזרחי) of humans are men of roots.

notes.1371: (tn, Heb): “and he passes by and, look, he is not [there].” The subject of the verb “passes by” is probably indefinite, referring to any passerby. Some prefer to change the form to first person, “and I passed by” (cf. NEB; note the first person verbal forms in preceding verse and in the following line).

notes.1373: (tn, Heb): “for [there is] an end for a man of peace.” Some interpret אַחֲרִית (’akharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see the next verse and Ps 109:13; cf. NEB, NRSV).

rashi.heb:
*שמר תם.* 
הסתכלו בדרכי התמימים ללמוד ממעשיהם:
rashi.eng: *Observe the innocent.* Scrutinize the ways of the innocent to learn from their deeds.

rashi.heb:
*כי אחרית לאיש שלום.* 
אם ראשית אין לו אחרית יש לו, אבל פושעים וחטאים ורשעים אחרית' נכרת' ונשמדו יחדיו:
rashi.eng: *for there is a future for the man of peace.* If he has no beginning, he has a future, but the transgressors, the sinners and the wicked their future has been cut off and they have been destroyed together.

notes.1374: (tn): Or “destroyed together.” In this case the psalmist pictures judgment sweeping them away as a group.
notes.1375: (tn, Heb): “the end of evil men is cut off.” As in v. 37, some interpret אַחֲרִית (’akharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see Ps 109:13). The perfect verbal forms in v. 38 probably express general truths. Another option is that they are used emphatically to state with certitude that the demise of the wicked is as good as done.

notes.1376: (tn, Heb): “and the deliverance of the godly [ones] [is] from the Lord.”
notes.1377: (tn, Heb): “[he is] their place of refuge in a time of trouble.”

notes.1378: (tn): The prefixed verbal forms with vav (ו) consecutive carry on the generalizing tone of the preceding verse.
notes.1379: (sn): Psalm 38. The author asks the Lord to deliver him from his enemies. He confesses his sin and recognizes that the crisis he faces is the result of divine discipline. Yet he begs the Lord not to reject him.
notes.1380: (tn): The Hebrew text reads simply, “to cause to remember.” The same form, the Hiphil infinitive of זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”), also appears in the heading of Ps 70. Some understand this in the sense of “for the memorial offering,” but it may carry the idea of bringing one’s plight to God’s attention (see P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 [WBC], 303).

notes.1381: (tn): The words “continue to” are supplied in the translation of both lines. The following verses make it clear that the psalmist is already experiencing divine rebuke/punishment. He asks that it might cease. Compare Ps 38:1 with Ps 6:1, which has similar wording.

rashi.heb:
*מזמור לדוד להזכיר.* 
לאומרו בשעת צרה להזכיר צרתם של ישראל לפני הקב"ה וכנגד כל ישראל אמרו:
rashi.eng: *A song of David, to make remembrance.* To recite it in time of distress, to make remembrance of the distress of Israel before the Holy One, blessed be He, and he recited it as relating to all Israel.

notes.1382: (tn): The verb Hebrew נָחַת (nakhat) apparently here means “penetrate, pierce” (note the use of the Qal in Prov 17:10). The psalmist pictures the Lord as a warrior who shoots arrows at him (see Ps 7:12-13).
notes.1383: (tn, Heb): “and your hand [?] upon me.” The meaning of the verb נָחַת (nakhat) is unclear in this context. It is preferable to emend the form to וַתָּנַח (vattanakh) from the verb נוּחַ (nuakh, “rest”). In this case the text would read literally, “and your hand rests upon me” (see Isa 25:10, though the phrase is used in a positive sense there, unlike Ps 38:2).

notes.1384: (tn, Heb): “there is no soundness in my flesh from before your anger.” “Anger” here refers metonymically to divine judgment, which is the practical effect of God’s anger at the psalmist’s sin.
notes.1385: (tn, Heb): “there is no health in my bones from before my sin.”

rashi.heb:
*נחתו.* 
נזרקו ל' נחת נופל בנטיית קשת ולפי שעל ידי דריכת הקשת נזרקים החצים כתיב נחתו בי וכן (שמות ט״ו:ט׳) אריק חרבי היה לו לכתוב אריק תערי אלא לפי שכשמוציאין חרב מתערה התער ריק ממנה לכך תולה הריקות בחרב וכן (לעיל י"ח) ונחתה קשת נחושה ואין הנו"ן שורש בתיבה שאם היתה שורש היה לו לומ' ננחתו בי אבל נו"ן של נחתו וכן של ותנחת אינ' שורש ונופל' לפרקים כמו ונו"ן של נגף, נשך, נדר, נקם, כשמתפעל יאמר ניגף נישך נידר ניקם כמו ננגף ננשך ננדר ננקם שהדגש בא בתיבה במקום נו"ן, וכן עלה נדף (ויקרא כ"ז), עיני נגרה (איכה ג׳:מ״ט) כמו ננדף ננגרה כן יאמר נחתו כמו ננחתו וכן ונחתה קשת נחושה (ש"ב כ"ה) כמו וננחתה שדרך החי"ת להתנהג כמנהג דגשות ברוב מקומות כגון כחש לו וממשקל דגוש כמו דבר מגזרת וידבר כך כחש מגזרת ותכחש שרה (בראשית י״ח:ט״ו) ולא יאמר כיחש כאשר יאמר מן המברך ברך ולא יאמר בירך כאשר יאמר דיבר לפי שאין דגשות ניכר ברי"ש אבל בחי"ת ניכר דגשות וכן (דברים ל"ב) שיחת כמו כיפר דיבר אף כאן יאמר נחתו כמו נגשו נתנו מגזר' נחת נתן נגש והנו"ן יסוד נופל לכנס דגש במקומה כשהיא מתפעל וכן (שמואל א ב׳:ד׳) קשת גבורי' חתים מגזרת נחת וחתת כאשר יאמר מן נסב סבב מן נשם שמם ונשמו דרכיהם (ויקרא כ״ו:ל״ב) ושממו עליה (שם) וכן בלל נבל כי שם בלל ה' ונבלה שם שפתם (בראשית י״א:ז׳) כן יאמר נחת וחתת בלשון פעל:
rashi.eng: *have been shot.* Heb. נחתו, have been cast. The expression of נחת applies to the bending of a bow, and since the arrows are shot by bending the bow, he wrote נחתו בי [literally] “were bent in me.” Similarly, (in Exod. 15:9): “I will unsheath my sword חרבי) (אריק,” [lit. I emptied my sword.] The Torah should have written: אריק תערי, I will empty my sheath, but because when they draw the sword from its sheath, the sheath is emptied of it, he therefore relates the emptying to the sword. Similarly, (above 18:35): “a copper bow was bent (ונחתה).” The “nun” is not a radical, because, if it were a radical, it would have to be ננחתו, but the “nun” of נחתו, and so ותנחת, is not a radical but is sometimes dropped, like the “nun” of נגף, to smite; נשך, to bite; נדר, to vow; נקם, to avenge. And when it is passive we say: נִגַּף, smitten; נִשַׁךְ, bitten; נִדַּר, vowed; נִקַּם, avenged, like נִנְקַם, נִנְדַּר, נִנְשַׁךְ, נִנְגַּף. The “dagesh” in the word replaces the “nun.” Similarly (in Lev. 26:36), a rattling (נִדַף) leaf, “(in Lam. 3:49),” My eyes stream (נִגְרָה), “like נִנְגְּרָה. So does he say נִחֲתוּ like נִנְחֲתוּ, and so (above 18:35):” and a copper bow was bent (וְנִּחֲתָה), “like וְנִנְחֲתָה. It was customary for the “cheth” to be treated like the letters that do accept a “dagesh” in most places, e.g. (in I Kings 13:18): “He lied (כִּחֶשׁ) to him,” in the form that is punctuated by a “dagesh,” [i.e., the pi’el conjugation,] like דִבֶּר spoke, from the same conjugation as וַיְדַבֶּר, כִּחֶשׁ from the same conjugation as (Gen. 18:15): “And Sarah lied (וַתְּכַחֵשׁ),” and we do not say כֵּחַשׁ as we say from הַמְבָרֵךְ, בֵּרַךְ and we do not say בִּרֵךְ as we say דִּבֵּר, because the power of the “dagesh;” is not recognizable in the “resh,” but in the “cheth” the power of the “dagesh” is recognizable, and so (in Deut. 32:5): ”Have they injured (שִׁחֵת) Him?” like כִּפֵר, atoned, דִּבֵּר, spoke. Here, too, he says, נִחֲתוּ like נִגְּשׁוּ they approached, נִתְּנוּ, they were given, from the roots נחת, נגש, נתן, the “nun” being a defective radical, replaced by a “dagesh” in the passive voice. So is (I Sam. 2:4): “The bows of the mighty are broken (חתים),” from the root נחת and חתת as you say from נסב, סבב, from נשם, שמם; (Lev. 26:22), “and your ways shall become desolate (וְנָשַׁמוּ),” (ibid. verse 32), “shall wonder (וְשָׁמְמוּ) over it.” Similarly, בָּלַל, נָבֹל, (Gen. 11:9) “for there the Lord confused בָּלַל” (ibid. verse 7) “and let us confuse (וְנָבְלָה) their language there.” So does he say נחת and חתת in the active voice.

rashi.heb:
*ותנחת עלי ידך.* 
פירש לחציך נחתו בי וכן פתרונו מה דרך בקשת לירות החצים יד שלך היא נחתה בקשת להפיל עלי חצים ותנחת לשון ותרד ובזה הנו"ן שורש בתבה וכן (לעיל י"ח) ונחתה קשת נחושה אין הנו"ן שורש בתיבה (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *and Your hand has come down upon me.* This is the explanation of “Your arrows have been shot into me.” And this is its interpretation: What bent the bow to shoot the arrows? Your hand has come down upon the bow to shoot arrows at me. ותנחת is an expression of ותרד, it came down, and in this the “nun” is a radical.
