rashi.eng: *And wine.* which cheers man’s heart, that too He brings forth from the earth, and oil to cause the face to radiate.

rashi.heb:
*ולחם.* 
אשר לב אנוש יסעד:
rashi.eng: *and bread.* which sustains man’s heart.

notes.3578: (sn): The trees of the Lord are the cedars of Lebanon (see the next line), which are viewed as special because of their great size and grandeur. The Lebanon forest was viewed elsewhere in the OT as the “garden of God” (see Ezek 31:8).
notes.3579: (tn, Heb): “are satisfied,” which means here that they receive abundant rain (see v. 13).

rashi.heb:
*עצי ה'.* 
בגן עדן:
rashi.eng: *The Lord’s trees.* in the Garden of Eden.

notes.3580: (tn, Heb): “[the] heron [in the] evergreens [is] its home.” The cedars and evergreens of the Lebanon forest are frequently associated (see, for example, 2 Chr 2:8; Isa 14:8; 37:24; Ezek 31:8).

rashi.heb:
*צפרים יקננו.* 
ישראל ישכנו שם יקננו לשון קן צפור:
rashi.eng: *birds nest.* Israel will dwell there. יְקַנֵנוּ is an expression of a bird’s nest (קן צפור).

notes.3581: (tn, Heb): “the high mountains [are] for the goats.”

rashi.heb:
*הרים הגבוהים.* 
ברא ליעלים:
rashi.eng: *The lofty mountains.* He created for the ibexes.

rashi.heb:
*מחסה.* 
כל לשון מחסה לשון צל ומחבא שאדם מתכסה שם מן הזרם ומן המט' אבר"י בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *shelter.* Every expression of מַחְסֶה is an expression of a shadow and a hiding place, where a person covers himself from flood and rain.

notes.3582: (tn, Heb): “he made [the] moon for appointed times.” The phrase “appointed times” probably refers to the months of the Hebrew lunar calendar.

rashi.heb:
*למועדים.* 
למנות בו זמנים ורגלים:
rashi.eng: *He made the moon for the appointed seasons.* To count with it the times and the festivals.

rashi.heb:
*שמש ידע מבואו.* 
אבל ירח לא ידע מבואו פעמים שבא בארוכה פעמים שבא בקצרה:
rashi.eng: *the sun knows its setting.* But the moon does not know its setting, because sometimes it comes through a long way and sometimes it comes through a short way.

notes.3584: (tn, Heb): “you make darkness, so that it might be night.”

rashi.heb:
*תשת חשך ויהי לילה.* 
בכל יום אתה מחשיך ומעריב את השמש והיה לילה ובו תרמוש כל חיתו יער:
rashi.eng: *You make darkness and it is night.* Every day You darken and block out the sun and it becomes night, when all the beasts of the forest move about.

notes.3585: (sn): The lions’ roaring is viewed as a request for food from God.

rashi.heb:
*תזרח השמש יאספון.* 
במסתרים ונחבאים שם מבני אדם ואז כל אדם יוצא לפעלו:
rashi.eng: *When the sun rises they gather in.* into the secret places and hide there from the sons of men; then every man goes forth to his work.

notes.3587: (tn, Heb): “man goes out to his work, and to his labor until evening.”

notes.3588: (tn, Heb): “How many [are] your works, O Lord.” In this case the Lord’s “works” are the creatures he has made, as the preceding and following contexts make clear.
notes.3589: (tn, Heb): “all of them with wisdom you have made.”

rashi.heb:
*קניניך.* 
מקנה קנין שלך כמו (בראשית י״ד:י״ט) קונה שמים וארץ הכל קנוי לך:
rashi.eng: *Your possessions.* Heb. קנינך, the acquisition that you have acquired, like (Gen. 14:19): “Owner (קנה) of heaven and earth.” All is acquired by You.

notes.3590: (tn, Heb): “this [is] the sea, great and broad of hands [i.e., “sides” or “shores”].”
notes.3591: (tn, Heb): “where [there are] swimming things, and without number.”

rashi.heb:
*ורחב ידים.* 
רחב מקום לריי"ש בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *and wide.* Heb. ורחב ידים. Wide of place, large in French, broad.

notes.3592: (tn, Heb): “[and] this Leviathan, [which] you formed to play in it.” Elsewhere Leviathan is a multiheaded sea monster that symbolizes forces hostile to God (see Ps 74:14; Isa 27:1), but here it appears to be an actual marine creature created by God, probably some type of whale.

rashi.heb:
*לשחק בו.* 
שלש שעות ביום כך אמרו רבותינו במסכת ע"א וכך מפורש בספר איוב התשחק בו כצפור:
rashi.eng: *with which to sport.* three hours during the day. So did our Sages say in tractate Avodah Zarah (3b), and so it is written explicitly in the Book of Job (40:29): “Will you play with him like a bird?”

notes.3593: (tn, Heb): “All of them.” The pronoun “them” refers not just to the sea creatures mentioned in vv. 25-26, but to all living things (see v. 24). This has been specified in the translation as “all of your creatures” for clarity.
notes.3594: (tn, Heb): “to give their food in its time.”

notes.3596: (tn, Heb): “you hide your face, they are terrified.”

rashi.heb:
*תוסף רוחם.* 
לשון כליון כמו (לעיל עג) ספו תמו:
rashi.eng: *You gather in their spirit.* Heb. תסף, an expression of destruction, as (above 73:19): “They were completely consumed (ספו).”

rashi.heb:
*תשלח רוחך.* 
בתחיית המתים:
rashi.eng: *You will send forth Your spirit.* with the resurrection of the dead.

rashi.heb:
*יגע בהרים ויעשנו.* 
כמו שמפורש בסיני (שמות י"ט) והר סיני עשן כולו:
rashi.eng: *He touches the mountains and they emit smoke.* as is depicted of Sinai (Exod. 19:18): “And Mount Sinai was all in smoke.”

rashi.heb:
*בעודי.* 
כמו בעודני חי (דברים ל"א):
rashi.eng: *as long as I exist.* Heb. בעדי, like (Deut. 31:27): “When I am still (בעודני) alive.”

notes.3600: (tn): That is, the psalmist’s thoughts as expressed in his songs of praise.

notes.3602: (sn): Psalm 105. The psalmist summons Israel to praise God because he delivered his people from Egypt in fulfillment of his covenantal promises to Abraham. A parallel version of vv. 1-15 appears in 1 Chr 16:8-22.

rashi.heb:
*יתמו חטאים.* 
חוטאים:
rashi.eng: *Sinners will be destroyed.* Heb. חטאים, sinners [rather than sins, but see Tal. Ber. 10a].

rashi.heb:
*עלילותיו.* 
מעלליו:
rashi.eng: *His deeds.* Heb. עלילותיו, His deeds.

rashi.heb:
*התהללו בשם קדשו.* 
התפארו במעוז שם קדשו שיש לכם פטרון כמוהו, התהללו פורוונטי"ץ וו"ש בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *Boast of His holy name.* Boast of the stronghold of His holy name that you have a patron like Him. התהללוּ is “porvontez vous” in Old French, [vantez vous in modern French, boast].

notes.3603: (tn, Heb): “and the judgments of his mouth.”

notes.3605: (tc): Some mss have “Israel,” which appears in the parallel version of this psalm in 1 Chr 16:13.
notes.3606: (tn, Heb): “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.3608: (tn, Heb): “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

notes.3609: (tn, Heb): “in all the earth [are] his judgments.”

notes.3610: (tn, Heb): “[the] word he commanded.” The text refers here to God’s unconditional covenantal promise to Abraham and the patriarchs, as vv. 10-12 make clear.

rashi.heb:
*דבר צוה לאלף דור.* 
התורה אשר צוה להודיעה בעולם לאחר אלף דור וראה שאין העולם מתקיים בלא תורה והעביר מהם תשע מאות ושבעים וארבעה דורות, ויש לפתו' כפשוטו זכר לישרא' את בריתו אשר צוה והבטיח לשמור להם לאלף דור כענין שומר הברית והחסד לאהביו ולשומרי מצותיו לאלף דור:
rashi.eng: *the word He had commanded to the thousandth generation.* The Torah, which He commanded to make known in the world after a thousand generations, but He saw that the world could not exist without Torah, so he skipped 974 generations of them. It may also be interpreted according to its simple meaning: He remembered for Israel His covenant, which He commanded and promised to keep for them for a thousand generations, as the matter of (Deut. 7:9): “Who keeps the covenant and the kindness for those who love Him and who keep His commandments, to a thousand generations.”

rashi.heb:
*לאמר לך אתן את ארץ כנען וגו'.* 
הוא הברית אשר כרת להם:
rashi.eng: *Saying, “To you I shall give, etc.”.* That is the covenant that He made for them.

notes.3613: (tn, Heb): “and from a kingdom to another nation.”

rashi.heb:
*ויתהלכו מגוי אל גוי.* 
אברהם גר בארץ פלשתים ובמצרים ובארץ כנען וכן יצחק וכן יעקב כולם גלו מגרות לגרות:
rashi.eng: *And they walked from nation to nation.* Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines, in Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, and so Isaac, and so Jacob, they all were exiled from one strange place to another strange place.

rashi.heb:
*ויוכח עליהם מלכים.* 
וינגע ה' את פרעה (בראשית י״ב:י״ז) כי עצור עצר ה' בעד כל רחם לבית אבימלך (שם כ):
rashi.eng: *and He reproved kings on their account.* (Gen. 12:17): “And the Lord plagued Pharaoh;” (ibid. 20:18), “For the Lord had closed up every womb of the house of Abimelech.”

notes.3614: (tn): The word “saying” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*אל תגעו במשיחי.* 
בגדולי, כל משיחה ל' שררה וגדולה:
rashi.eng: *My anointed ones.* My great ones. Every [expression of] anointing is an expression of rulership and greatness.

notes.3616: (tn, Heb): “and every staff of food he broke.” The psalmist refers to the famine that occurred in Joseph’s time (see v. 17 and Gen 41:53-57).

rashi.heb:
*ויקרא רעב.* 
כדי להגלותם למצרים (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *He called a famine.* in order to exile them to Egypt (I found).

notes.3617: (tn): After the reference to the famine in v. 16, v. 17 flashes back to events that preceded the famine (see Gen 37).

rashi.heb:
*שלח לפניהם איש.* 
(שם מ"ה) וישלחני אלהים לפניכם ואיזה איש יוסף שנמכר:
rashi.eng: *He sent a man before them.* (Gen. 45:5): “And God sent me before you.” Now who was the man? Joseph, who was sold.

notes.3618: (tn, Heb): “they afflicted his feet with shackles.”
notes.3619: (tn, Heb): “his neck came [into] iron.” The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) with the suffix could mean simply “he” or “his life.” But the nuance “neck” makes good sense here (note the reference to his “feet” in the preceding line). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 38.

rashi.heb:
*ברזל באה נפשו.* 
א"ר הונא בר אידי שרתוע עשתה לו תחת זקנו שאם ירכין פניו השרתוע מכהו, שרתוע פי' שפוד:
rashi.eng: *his soul was placed in irons.* Said Rav Huna the son of Idi: She [Potiphar’s wife] made him a “shirtua” under his beard, so that if he bent his face over, the “shirtua” would wound him. שרתוע means a forked, suspended spear.

notes.3620: (tn, Heb): “word,” probably referring to Joseph’s prediction about the fate of Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker (see Gen 41:9-14).
notes.3621: (tn): This line may refer to Joseph’s prediction of the famine in response to Pharaoh’s dream. Joseph emphasized to Pharaoh that the interpretation of the dream came from God (see Gen 41:16, 25, 28, 32, 39).

rashi.heb:
*עד עת בא דברו.* 
של הקב"ה לקיים גזירתו שיתגלגל הדבר וירדו ישראל למצרים:
rashi.eng: *Until His word came.* [The word] of the Holy One, blessed be He, to fulfill His decree that the matter should “roll” and Israel should descend to Egypt.

rashi.heb:
*אמרת ה' צרפתהו.* 
בחנתהו ליוסף שנתנסה וכבש את יצרו באשת אדניו ועליה נתייסר ונצרף ביסורין לתתו אל בית הסוהר:
rashi.eng: *the saying of the Lord purified him.* It tried Joseph, for he was tested and he overcame the temptation [to sin] with his master’s wife, and he was tortured because of her and purified with tortures to place him in the dungeon.

notes.3623: (tn, Heb): “[the] king sent and set him free.”

rashi.heb:
*שלח מלך ויתירהו.* 
שלח פרעה מלך מצרים שלוחיו ויתירהו, שלח מושל עמים הוא פרעה ויפתחהו:
rashi.eng: *A king sent and released him.* Pharaoh, king of Egypt, sent his messengers and released him. A ruler of peoples, viz. Pharaoh, [sent] and loosed his bonds.

notes.3624: (tn, Heb): “he made him master of his house.”

notes.3625: (tn, Heb): “to bind his officials by his will.”
notes.3626: (tn, Heb): “and his elders he taught wisdom.”

rashi.heb:
*לאסור שריו בנפשו.* 
לשון חבה הוא זה כמו (שמואל א י״ח:א׳) ונפש יהונתן נקשרה בנפש דוד, כשפתר החלום חבבוהו כלם, אמר רבי אידי שרו כתיב זה היה פוטיפר:
rashi.eng: *To bind up his princes with his soul.* This is an expression of endearment, as (I Sam. 18:1): “that Jonathan’s soul had become attached to David’s soul.” When he interpreted the dream, they all loved him. Said Rabbi Idi: It is written שָׂרוֹ, his prince. This was Potiphar.

notes.3629: (tn, Heb): “and he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*ויפר.* 
הקב"ה את עמו, הפרה והרבה אותם:
rashi.eng: *And He made… fruitful.* The Holy One, blessed be He, [made] His people [fruitful]. He made them fruitful and caused them to multiply.

notes.3633: (tn): Or “to deal deceptively.” The Hitpael of נָכַל (nakhal) occurs only here and in Gen 37:18, where it is used of Joseph’s brothers “plotting” to kill him.

notes.3634: (tn): Apparently the pronoun refers to “his servants” (i.e., the Israelites, see v. 25).

notes.3635: (tn, Heb): “he sent darkness and made it dark.” He made it dark. The psalmist begins with the ninth plague (see Exod 10:21-29).
notes.3636: (tn, Heb): “they did not rebel against his words.” Apparently this refers to Moses and Aaron, who obediently carried out God’s orders.

rashi.heb:
*ולא מרו את דברו.* 
המכות שצוה עליהם באו במצותיו ולא שינו את דברו:
rashi.eng: *And they did not disobey His word.* The plagues, that He commanded upon them, came according to His commandments and did not deviate from His word.

rashi.heb:
*שרץ ארצם צפרדעים.* 
אמר רבי יוחנן בכל מקום שהיו רובצים מים היו רובצים צפרדעים:
rashi.eng: *Their land swarmed with frogs.* Said Rabbi Johanan: Wherever water would lie, frogs would lie.

notes.3639: (tn, Heb): “fire of flames [was] in their land.”

notes.3642: (tn, Heb): “the beginning of all their strength,” that is, reproductive power (see Ps 78:51). Verses 28-36 recall the plagues in a different order than the one presented in Exodus: v. 28 (plague 9), v. 29 (plague 1), v. 30 (plague 2), v. 31a (plague 4), v. 31b (plague 3), vv. 32-33 (plague 7), vv. 34-35 (plague 8), v. 36 (plague 10). No reference is made in Ps 105 to plagues 5 and 6.

notes.3643: (tn, Heb): “them”; the referent (the Lord’s people) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
notes.3644: (tn): The word “enriched” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

notes.3645: (tn, Heb): “for fear of them had fallen upon them.”

notes.3647: (tn, Heb): “he [i.e., his people] asked.” The singular form should probably be emended to a plural שָׁאֲלוּ (sha’alu, “they asked”), the vav (ו) having fallen off by haplography (note the vav at the beginning of the following form).
notes.3648: (tn): Or “bread of heaven.” The reference is to manna (see Exod 16:4, 13-15).

rashi.heb:
*שאל ויבא שליו.* 
שאל ישראל בשר ויבא לו הקב"ה שלוים:
rashi.eng: *They asked, and He brought quails.* Israel asked for meat, and the Holy One, blessed be He, brought them quails.

rashi.heb:
*הלכו בציות נהר.* 
הלכו נהרות מן הבאר בארץ ציה:
rashi.eng: *in the deserts ran rivers.* Rivers flowed from the well in an arid land.

rashi.heb:
*כי זכר.* 
הקב"ה את דבר קדשו אשר עם אברהם עבדו שהבטיחו (בראשית ט"ו) ואחרי כן יצאו ברכוש גדול ודור רביעי ישובו הנה:
rashi.eng: *For He remembered.* The Holy One, blessed be He, [remembered] His holy word, which was with Abraham His servant, which He promised him (Gen. 15:14, 17): “and afterwards they will go out with many possessions… and a fourth generation will return here.”

notes.3651: (tn, Heb): “and he led his people out with joy, with a ringing cry, his chosen ones.”

notes.3652: (tn, Heb): “and the [product of the] work of peoples they possessed.”

notes.3654: (sn): Psalm 106. The psalmist recalls Israel’s long history of rebellion against God, despite his mighty saving deeds on their behalf.

notes.3656: (tn, Heb): “[or] cause to be heard all his praise.”

rashi.heb:
*ברצון עמך.* 
בהרצותך לעמך:
rashi.eng: *when You favor Your people.* When You show goodwill to Your people.

notes.3658: (tn, Heb): “in order that [I may] rejoice with the rejoicing of your nation.”

notes.3662: (tn, Heb): “Reed Sea” (also in vv. 9, 22). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression יָם סוּף (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in Exod 13:18. They rebelled. The psalmist recalls the people’s complaint recorded in Exod 14:12.

rashi.heb:
*וימרו על ים.* 
היו מקטני אמנה אמרו כשם שאנו עולים מכאן מצד זה אף המצריים עולים מצד אחר ויבואו אחרינו עד שרמז הקב"ה לים והקיאם ליבשה אז וירא ישראל את מצרים מת על שפת הים (שמות י"ד:ל') לפיכך ויאמינו בה', אבל מתחלה לא האמינו (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *and they were rebellious by the sea.* They had little faith; they said, “Just as we ascend from here, from this side, the Egyptians also are ascending from another side, and they will come after us,” until the Holy One, blessed be He, hinted to the sea, and it vomited them out onto the dry land. Then (Exod. 15:30) “Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.” Therefore (ibid. verse 31) “they believed in the Lord,” but in the beginning, they did not believe. I found this.

notes.3663: (tn, Heb): “his name,” which here stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

rashi.heb:
*ויוליכם בתהומות כמדבר.* 
ים סוף היה במדבר דכתיב סגר עליהם המדבר וגו' (שם י"ד) דרך שלשת ימים וגו' (במדבר י׳:ל״ג):
rashi.eng: *and He led them in the depths in the desert.* The Sea of Reeds was in the desert, for it is written (Exod. 14:13): “the desert has closed upon them, etc.;” (Exod. 3:18): “three days’ journey in the desert.”

rashi.heb:
*לא חכו לעצתו.* 
לא קוו לו:
rashi.eng: *they did not await His counsel.* They did not hope for Him.

notes.3672: (sn): They had an insatiable craving. This is described in Num 11:4-35.

rashi.heb:
*ויתאוו תאוה.* 
מי יאכילנו בשר (שם י"א):
rashi.eng: *They craved a lust.* (Num. 11:4) “Who will give us meat to eat?”

notes.3675: (tn, Heb): “and he sent leanness into their being.” Disease. See Num 11:33-34, where this plague is described.

rashi.heb:
*וישלח רזון בנפשם.* 
ואף ה' חרה בעם (שם י"א):
rashi.eng: *but He sent emaciation into their soul.* (Num. 11:33) “and the Lord’s wrath was kindled against the people.”

notes.3677: (tn, Heb): “the holy one of the Lord.”

rashi.heb:
*ויקנאו למשה.* 
במדבר הכעיסוהו כמו קנאוני בלא אל (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *They angered Moses.* Heb. ויקנאו. In the desert they angered him, like (Deut. 32:21): “They angered Me (קנאוני) with a no-god.” I found this.

rashi.heb:
*תפתח ארץ וגו'.* 
נראה שחלק כבוד לבני קרח מלהזכיר אביהם תלה הקלקלה בדתן ואבירם:
rashi.eng: *The earth opened up, etc..* It appears that [the Psalmist] bestowed honor upon the sons of Korah [by refraining] from mentioning their father. He attributed the sin to Dathan and Abiram.

notes.3680: (sn): Verses 16-18 describe the events of Num 16:1-40.

rashi.heb:
*ותבער אש.* 
ותאכל את מקריבי הקטרת (במדבר טז):
rashi.eng: *And fire burned.* (Num. 16: 35) “and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who burnt the incense. ”

notes.3681: (tn, Heb): “their glory.” According to an ancient Hebrew scribal tradition, the text originally read “his glory” or “my glory.” In Jer 2:11 the Lord states that his people (Israel) exchanged “their glory” (a reference to the Lord) for worthless idols.

rashi.heb:
*אוכל עשב.* 
אין לך מתועב ומשוקץ מן השור בשעה שהוא אוכל עשב שהוא מוציא פרש רבה והוא מלוכלך בה, ס"א רירו:
rashi.eng: *eating grass.* There is nothing as disgusting and repugnant as an ox. When it eats grass, it emits much dung, with which it sullies itself. Other books read: its saliva.

notes.3685: (tn, Heb): “if not,” that is, “[and would have] if [Moses] had not.”
notes.3686: (tn, Heb): “stood in the gap before him.”
notes.3687: (tn, Heb): “to turn back his anger from destroying.” Verses 19-23 describe the events of Exod 32:1-35.

notes.3688: (tn, Heb): “a land of delight” (see also Jer 3:19; Zech 7:14).

rashi.heb:
*וימאסו בארץ חמדה.* 
בשלוח מרגלים והוציאו דבה על הארץ (שם יג):
rashi.eng: *They rejected the desirable land.* when the spies were sent out, and they brought calumny on the land (Num. 13:32).

notes.3690: (sn): They grumbled in their tents. See Deut 1:27.
notes.3691: (tn, Heb): “did not listen to the voice of.”

notes.3692: (tn, Heb): “and he lifted his hand to [or “concerning”] them.” The idiom “to lift a hand” here refers to swearing an oath. One would sometimes solemnly lift one’s hand when making such a vow (see Ezek 20:5-6, 15).

rashi.heb:
*וישא ידו.* 
בשבועה:
rashi.eng: *He raised His hand.* with an oath.

notes.3695: (tn, Heb): “and to cause their offspring to fall.” Some emend the verb to “scatter” to form tighter parallelism with the following line (cf. NRSV “disperse”).
notes.3696: (tn, Heb): “among the lands.” The word “foreign” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*ולהפיל זרעם בגוים.* 
מאותו שעה נגזר עליהם חורבן הבית שהרי ליל ט' באב בכו ואמר הקב"ה הם בכו בכיה של חנם ואני אקבע להם בכיה לדורות:
rashi.eng: *And to cast their seed among the nations.* From that time, the destruction of the Temple was decreed upon them, for on the night of the ninth of Ab they went, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “They wept for nothing, and I shall establish for them weeping for generations.”

notes.3697: (tn, Heb): “joined themselves to.” They worshiped Baal of Peor. See Num 25:3, 5. Baal of Peor was a local manifestation of the Canaanite deity Baal located at Peor.
notes.3698: (tn): Here “the dead” may refer to deceased ancestors (see Deut 26:14). Another option is to understand the term as a derogatory reference to the various deities which the Israelites worshiped at Peor along with Baal (see Num 25:2 and L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 49).

notes.3699: (tn, Heb): “They made angry [him].” The pronominal suffix is omitted here, but does appear in a few medieval Hebrew mss. Perhaps it was accidentally left off, an original וַיַּכְעִיסוּהוּ (vayyakh’isuhu) being misread as וַיַּכְעִיסוּ (vayyakh’isu). In the translation the referent of the pronominal suffix (the Lord) has been specified for clarity to avoid confusion with Baal of Peor (mentioned in the previous verse).

notes.3700: (sn): The intervention of Phinehas is recounted in Num 25:7-8.

notes.3701: (tn, Heb): “and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, to a generation and a generation forever.” The verb חָשַׁב (khashav, “to reckon”) is collocated with צְדָקָה (ts�daqah, “righteousness”) only in Ps 106:31 and Gen 15:6, where God rewards Abram’s faith with a land grant. Brought him a reward. See Num 25:12-13.

notes.3703: (tn): The Hebrew text vocalizes the form as הִמְרוּ (himru), a Hiphil from מָרָה (marah, “to behave rebelliously”), but the verb fits better with the object (“his spirit”) if it is revocalized as הֵמֵרוּ (hemeru), a Hiphil from מָרַר (marar, “to be bitter”). The Israelites “embittered” Moses’ “spirit” in the sense that they aroused his temper with their complaints.
notes.3705: (tn): The Hebrew text adds “with his lips,” but this has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons. Verses 32-33 allude to the events of Num 20:1-13.

rashi.heb:
*כי המרו.* 
משה ואהרן:
rashi.eng: *For they rebelled.* Moses and Aaron.

rashi.heb:
*את רוחו.* 
בשמעו נא המורים:
rashi.eng: *against His spirit.* with (Num. 20:10) “Hear now, you rebels!”

rashi.heb:
*ויבטא בשפתיו.* 
שבועה לכן לא תביאו את הקהל הזה וגו' (שם כ):
rashi.eng: *and He uttered with His lips.* an oath (Num. 20:12): “Therefore you shall not bring this community, etc.”

notes.3706: (tn): That is, the nations of Canaan.

rashi.heb:
*לא השמידו.* 
בימי יהושע:
rashi.eng: *They did not destroy.* in the days of Joshua.

rashi.heb:
*את העמים.* 
אשר אמר ה' להם (דברים כ׳:ט״ז) לא תחיה כל נשמה לא ישבו בארצך והם הניחום לשבת בקרבם למס עובד:
rashi.eng: *the peoples whom the Lord had told them.* (Deut. 20:16): “You shall not allow a soul to remain alive;” (Exod. 23:33), “They shall not remain as residents in your land,” but they allowed them to dwell in their midst, paying tribute.

notes.3709: (sn): Became a snare. See Exod 23:33; Judg 2:3.

notes.3710: (tn): The Hebrew term שֵׁדִים (shedim, “demons”) occurs only here and in Deut 32:17. Some type of lesser deity is probably in view.

notes.3711: (sn): Num 35:33-34 explains that bloodshed defiles a land.

notes.3712: (tn, Heb): “and they committed adultery in their actions.” This means that they were unfaithful to the Lord (see Ps 73:27).

notes.3713: (tn, Heb): “the anger of the Lord burned against his people.”

notes.3715: (tn, Heb): “gave them into the hand of.”

rashi.heb:
*ויתנם ביד גוים.* 
בימי השופטים בין שופט לשופט כגון עגלון וכושן רשעתים וסיסרא ופלשתים ומדין, (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *And He delivered them into the hands of nations.* in the days of the Judges between one judge and another, e.g. Eglon, Cushan-rishathaim, Sisera, the Philistines, and Midian. (I found.)

notes.3716: (tn, Heb): “they were subdued under their hand.”

notes.3717: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is either preterite or imperfect, in which case it is customary, describing repeated action in past time (“he would deliver”).
notes.3718: (tn, Heb): “but they rebelled in their counsel.” The prefixed verbal form is either preterite or imperfect, in which case it is customary, describing repeated action in past time (“they would have a rebellious attitude”).
notes.3719: (tn, Heb): “they sank down.” The Hebrew verb מָכַךְ (makhakh, “to lower; to sink”) occurs only here in the Qal.

rashi.heb:
*פעמים רבות יצילם.* 
כמה פעמים מכעיסים והוא מאריך אפו ומצילם:
rashi.eng: *Many times He saved them.* Many times they provoked Him; yet He was slow to anger and saved them.

rashi.heb:
*וימכו בעונם.* 
נעשו שפלים בעונם:
rashi.eng: *and they were humbled because of their iniquity.* Heb. וימכו, and they were humbled because of their iniquity.

rashi.heb:
*וירא בצר.* 
מתוך תפלה:
rashi.eng: *But He looked upon their distress.* On account of prayer.

rashi.heb:
*בשמעו את רנתם.* 
מתוך זכות אבות:
rashi.eng: *when He heard their cries.* On account of the merit of the Patriarchs.

notes.3720: (tn): The Niphal of נָחַם (nakham) refers here to God relenting from a punishment already underway.

rashi.heb:
*ויזכור להם בריתו.* 
מתוך תשובה:
rashi.eng: *And He remembered His covenant.* On account of repentance.

rashi.heb:
*וינחם כרב חסדיו.* 
מתוך הקץ בשמעו הושיענו וגו' אף משה כללם בפסוק אחד בצר לך ומצאוך וגו' (דברים ד׳:ל׳):
rashi.eng: *and He relented in accordance with His abundant kindness.* On account of the end, when He heard, “Save us, etc.” Moses, too, included them in one verse (Deut. 4:30): “In this distress that will befall you etc.”

notes.3722: (tn, Heb): “to give thanks.” The infinitive construct indicates result after the imperative.

rashi.heb:
*הושיענו.* 
גם עתה ה' אלהינו:
rashi.eng: *save us.* now also, O Lord, our God.

notes.3727: (sn): The final verse (v. 48) is a conclusion to this fourth “book” (or major editorial division) of the Psalter. Similar statements appear at or near the end of each of the first, second and third “books” of the Psalter (see Pss 41:13; 72:18-19; 89:52, respectively).
notes.3728: (sn): Psalm 107. The psalmist praises God for his kindness to his exiled people.

rashi.heb:
*מן העולם ועד העולם.* 
מן עלמא הדין ועד עלמא דאתי (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *from world to world.* From this world to the world to come.

rashi.heb:
*הודו לה'.* 
:
rashi.eng: *Give thanks to the Lord because He is good, etc..*

notes.3730: (tn): Or “let the redeemed of the Lord say [so].”

rashi.heb:
*יאמרו גאולי ה'.* 
כשיפדם מיד צר:
rashi.eng: *Those redeemed by the Lord shall say it.* when He redeems them from the hands of an oppressor.

notes.3733: (tn, Heb): “from lands.” The word “foreign” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*תעו במדבר וגו'.* 
והולכי מדברות אף הם צריכין להודות שהרי פעמים שהם תועים ורעבים וצמאים:
rashi.eng: *They strayed in the desert, on a road of desolation, etc..* Those who travel in the deserts must also give thanks because sometimes they stray and suffer from hunger and thirst.

notes.3734: (tn, Heb): “and their soul in them fainted.”

rashi.heb:
*וידריכם.* 
וינהגם לפיכך יודו לה' חסדו:
rashi.eng: *And He led them.* And He led them; therefore, they shall give thanks to the Lord for His kindness.

notes.3736: (tn, Heb): “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.”

notes.3737: (tn, Heb): “[the] longing throat.” The noun נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh), which frequently refers to one’s very being or soul, here probably refers to one’s parched “throat” (note the parallelism with נֶפֱשׁ רְעֵבָה, nefesh r�’evah, “hungry throat”).
notes.3738: (tn, Heb): “and [the] hungry throat he has filled [with] good.”

notes.3739: (tn, Heb): “those who sat in darkness and deep darkness.” Synonyms are joined here to emphasize the degree of “darkness” experienced by the exiles. The Hebrew term צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet, “deep darkness”) has traditionally been understood as a compound noun, meaning “shadow of death” (צֵל + מָוֶת [tsel + mavet]; see BDB 853 s.v. צַלְמָוֶת; cf. NASB). Other authorities prefer to vocalize the form צַלְמוּת (tsalmut) and understand it as an abstract noun (from the root צלם) meaning “darkness.” An examination of the word’s usage favors the latter derivation. It is frequently associated with darkness/night and contrasted with light/morning (see Job 3:5; 10:21-22; 12:22; 24:17; 28:3; 34:22; Ps 107:10, 14; Isa 9:1; Jer 13:16; Amos 5:8). In some cases the darkness described is associated with the realm of death (Job 10:21-22; 38:17), but this is a metaphorical application of the word and does not reflect its inherent meaning. In Ps 107:10 the word refers metonymically to a dungeon, which in turn metaphorically depicts the place of Israel’s exile (see vv. 2-3).
notes.3740: (tn, Heb): “those bound in suffering and iron.” “Suffering and iron” is a hendiadys (like English “good and angry”), where both words contribute to one idea. In this case the first word characterizes the second; the iron (chains) contribute to the prisoners’ pain and suffering.

rashi.heb:
*יושבי חשך וצלמות.* 
אף האסורים בבית הסוהר צריכים להודות כשיוצאין מבית אסוריהם:
rashi.eng: *Those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death.* Also those imprisoned in a dungeon are required to give thanks when they emerge from their prison.

notes.3742: (tn, Heb): “the counsel of the Most High.”

rashi.heb:
*כי המרו אמרי אל.* 
אין פורענות באה על האדם אלא בעונו:
rashi.eng: *For they rebelled against the words of God.* Trouble does not befall a person except because of his iniquity.

notes.3743: (tn, Heb): “and he subdued with suffering their heart.”

notes.3744: (tn, Heb): “darkness and deep darkness.” See the note on the word “darkness” in v. 10.

notes.3745: (tn, Heb): “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

notes.3746: (sn): The language of v. 16 recalls Isa 45:2.

rashi.heb:
*כי שבר דלתות נחשת.* 
שהיו נעולים בפניהם:
rashi.eng: *For He broke copper doors.* that were shut before them.

notes.3747: (tn, Heb): “fools [they were] because of the way of their rebellion.”

rashi.heb:
*אוילים מדרך פשעם.* 
אשר מעונותיהם יתענו ביסורי חלאים אף הם מן הצריכין להודות, יש סמניות בפ' זו (כלומר כתיבות שש נוני"ן הפוכין) ובאין לידרש במקום אכין ורקין למעט, לומר צעקו קודם גזר דין נענין לאחר גזר דין אינם נענין:
rashi.eng: *Fools, because of the way of their transgression and because of their iniquities, are afflicted.* with the agonies of illnesses. They too are among those who are required to give thanks. There are markers in this chapter (i.e., six inverted “nuns” are written) and they come to be expounded upon instead of “buts” and “onlys” to limit [the power of the verse] meaning that if they [the prisoners] cry out before the verdict has been promulgated, they are answered; after the verdict has been promulgated, they are not answered.

notes.3749: (tn, Heb): “he sent his word.” This probably refers to an oracle of assurance which announced his intention to intervene (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 59).
notes.3750: (tn, Heb): “he rescued from their traps.” The Hebrew word שְׁחִית (shekhit, “trap”) occurs only here and in Lam 4:20, where it refers to a trap or pit in which one is captured. Because of the rarity of the term and the absence of an object with the verb “rescued,” some prefer to emend the text of Ps 107:20, reading מִשַׁחַת חַיָּתָם (mishakhat khayyatam, “[he rescued] their lives from the pit”). Note also NIV “from the grave,” which interprets the “pit” as Sheol or the grave.

notes.3751: (tn, Heb): “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

notes.3752: (tn, Heb): “and let them proclaim his works with a ringing cry.”

notes.3753: (sn): Verses 23-30, which depict the Lord rescuing sailors from a storm at sea, do not seem to describe the exiles’ situation, unless the word picture is metaphorical. Perhaps the psalmist here broadens his scope and offers an example of God’s kindness to the needy beyond the covenant community.
notes.3755: (tn, Heb): “doers of work on the mighty waters.”

notes.3756: (tn, Heb): “he spoke and caused to stand a stormy wind.”
notes.3757: (tn, Heb): “and it stirred up its [i.e., the sea’s, see v. 23] waves.”

notes.3759: (tn, Heb): “their being”; traditionally “their soul” (referring to that of the sailors). This is sometimes translated “courage” (cf. NIV, NRSV).

notes.3762: (tn): Only here does the Hebrew verb חָגַג (khagag; normally meaning “to celebrate”) carry the nuance “to sway.”
notes.3763: (tn): The Hitpael of בָלַע (vala’) occurs only here in the OT. Traditionally the form is derived from the verbal root בלע (“to swallow”), but HALOT 135 s.v. III בלע understands a homonym here with the meaning “to be confused.”

rashi.heb:
*יחוגו.* 
לשון שבר הוא וכן בחגוי הסלע (שיר השירים ב׳:י״ד) וכן והיתה אדמת יהודה למצרים לחגא (ישעיהו י״ט:י״ז):
rashi.eng: *They were frightened.* Heb. יחוגו. This is an expression of breaking. Similarly (Song 2:14): “in the clefts of (בחגוי) the rock;” and similarly (Isa. l9:17), “And the land of Judah will be to Egypt for a dread (לחגא).”

notes.3765: (tn, Heb): “their waves.” The antecedent of the third masculine plural pronominal suffix is not readily apparent, unless it refers back to “waters” in v. 23.

notes.3766: (tn, Heb): “they”; the referent (the sailors) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.3767: (tn, Heb): “they”; the referent (the waves) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.3768: (tn): The Hebrew noun occurs only here in the OT.

rashi.heb:
*וישמחו כי ישתקו.* 
הגלים:
rashi.eng: *They rejoiced that they were stilled.* The waves.

rashi.heb:
*וינחם.* 
וינהגם:

*מחוז.* 
לשון גבול, ומנחם חברו עם וחזותכם את שאול (שם כ"ח) גבולינו שלא יכנס בגבולינו וכן מחזה אל מחזה שלש פעמים (מלכים א ז') בתנחומא, מצאתי:
rashi.eng: *the region.* Heb. מחוז, an expression of a border, and Menachem (p. 86) associated it with (Isa. 28:18): “and your limit (וחזותכם) with the grave,” your limit, that it should not enter our boundary. Similarly (I Kings 7:4): “an edge (מחזה מול מחזה) opposite an edge,” three times. In Tanchuma, I found [this].

notes.3769: (tn, Heb): “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

notes.3770: (tn, Heb): “in the seat of the elders.”

rashi.heb:
*וירוממוהו בקהל עם.* 
צריך לאודויי באפי בי עשרה:
rashi.eng: *And they shall exalt Him in an assembly of people.* He must give thanks in the presence of ten.

rashi.heb:
*ובמושב זקנים.* 
ותרין מנייהו צורבא מרבנן:
rashi.eng: *and in a sitting of elders.* And two of them must be rabbinical scholars.

notes.3771: (tn): The verbal form appears to be a preterite, which is most naturally taken as narrational. (The use of prefixed forms with vav [ו] consecutive in vv. 36-37 favor this.) The psalmist may return to the theme of God’s intervention for the exiles (see vv. 4-22, especially vv. 4-9). However, many regard vv. 33-41 as a hymnic description which generalizes about God’s activities among men. In this case it would be preferable to use the English present tense throughout (cf. NEB, NRSV).

rashi.heb:
*ישם נהרות למדבר.* 
כלומר נותן יישובי האומות לחרבן:
rashi.eng: *He makes rivers into a desert.* That is to say that He makes the settlements of the nations into ruins.

rashi.heb:
*למלחה.* 
להיות כארץ מלחה מעשות פרי:
rashi.eng: *into a salty waste.* To be like a salty land insofar as it does not produce fruit.

notes.3773: (tn): The words “As for his people” are not included in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. The psalmist contrasts God’s judgment on his enemies with his blessing of his people. See the note on the word “enemies” in v. 39 for further discussion.
notes.3774: (tn): The verbal form appears to be a preterite, which is most naturally taken as narrational. See the note on the word “turned” in v. 33.

rashi.heb:
*ישם מדבר לאגם מים.* 
נותן יישוב חרב לבניין ומחזירו לקדמותו:
rashi.eng: *He makes a desert into a pool of water.* He makes a ruined settlement into a building and restores it to its original state.

notes.3777: (tn): “Bless” here carries the nuance “endue with sexual potency, make fertile.” See Gen 1:28, where the statement “he blessed them” directly precedes the command “be fruitful and populate the earth” (see also 1:22). The verb “bless” carries this same nuance in Gen 17:16 (where God’s blessing of Sarai imparts to her the capacity to bear a child); 48:16 (where God’s blessing of Joseph’s sons is closely associated with their having numerous descendants); and Deut 7:13 (where God’s blessing is associated with fertility in general, including numerous descendants). See also Gen 49:25 (where Jacob uses the noun derivative in referring to “blessings of the breast and womb,” an obvious reference to fertility) and Gen 27:27 (where the verb is used of a field to which God has given the capacity to produce vegetation).
notes.3778: (tn): The verbal form in this line appears to be an imperfect, which may be taken as customary (drawing attention to typical action in a past time frame) or as generalizing (in which case one should use the English present tense, understanding a move from narrative to present reality).

notes.3779: (tn): The words “As for their enemies” are not included in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. Without such clarification, one might think that v. 39 refers to those just mentioned in v. 38 as objects of divine blessing, which would contradict the point just emphasized by the psalmist. The structure of vv. 33-42 is paneled (A-B-A-B). In vv. 33-34 the psalmist describes God’s judgment upon his enemies (perhaps those who had enslaved his people). In vv. 35-38 he contrasts this judgment with the divine blessing poured out on God’s people. (See the note on the word “people” in v. 35.) In vv. 39-40 he contrasts this blessing with the judgment experienced by enemies, before returning in vv. 41-42 to the blessing experienced by God’s people.

rashi.heb:
*וימעטו וישוחו.* 
והם מתחלה היו שוחין ומועטין מעוצר רעה ויגון:
rashi.eng: *Whereas they were few and they sank down.* But they, from the beginning, sank down and were few because of dominion, trouble, and sorrow.

notes.3781: (tn): The active participle is understood as past durative here, drawing attention to typical action in a past time frame. However, it could be taken as generalizing (in which case one should translate using the English present tense), in which case the psalmist moves from narrative to present reality. Perhaps the participial form appears because the statement is lifted from Job 12:21.

rashi.heb:
*וישם כצאן משפחות.* 
וישם האביון משפחת זרעו כצאן רבים:
rashi.eng: *and made him families like flocks.* He made [for] the needy the families of his children as numerous as flocks.

notes.3783: (tn, Heb): “all evil,” which stands metonymically for those who do evil.

rashi.heb:
*קפצה.* 
סתמה כמו לא תקפוץ את ידך (דברים ט״ו:ז׳):
rashi.eng: *shuts.* Heb. קפצה, closes up, like (Deut. 15:7): “and not close up (תקפץ) your hand.”

notes.3784: (sn): Psalm 108. With some minor variations, this psalm is a composite of Ps 57:7-11 (see vv. 1-5) and Ps 60:5-12 (see vv. 6-13).

notes.3785: (tn, Heb): Or perhaps “confident”; “my heart is steadfast.” The “heart” is viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s volition and/or emotions.
notes.3786: (tn, Heb): “also my glory,” but this makes little sense in the context. Some view the term כָּבוֹד (“glory”) here as a metonymy for man’s inner being (see BDB 459 s.v. II כָּבוֹד 5), but it is preferable to emend the form to כְּבֵדִי (k�vodiy, “my liver”). Like the heart, the liver is viewed as the seat of one’s emotions. See also Pss 16:9; 30:12; 57:9; as well as H. W. Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 64, and M. Dahood, Psalms (AB), 3:93. For an Ugaritic example of the heart/liver as the source of joy, see G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 47-48: “her [Anat’s] liver swelled with laughter, her heart was filled with joy, the liver of Anat with triumph.”

notes.3787: (tn): BDB 1007 s.v. שַׁחַר takes “dawn” as an adverbial accusative, though others understand it as a personified direct object. “Dawn” is used metaphorically for the time of deliverance and vindication the psalmist anticipates. When salvation “dawns,” the psalmist will “wake up” in praise.

rashi.heb:
*נכון לבי.* 
נאמן עמך:
rashi.eng: *My heart is steadfast.* faithful with You.

rashi.heb:
*אף כבודי.* 
הוא מה שאני משורר לך ד"א:
rashi.eng: *even my glory.* Even my glory is what I sing to You. Another explanation:

rashi.heb:
*אף כבודי.* 
אף לפי כבודי לא אמנע לשורר לו ולא אחלק לעצמי כבוד:
rashi.eng: *Even my glory.* Even according to my honor, I shall not hesitate to sing to Him, and I shall not take glory for myself.

rashi.heb:
*אעירה שחר.* 
דרך שאר מלכים השחר מעוררם ואני מעורר את השחר שאני קם חצות לילה שהנבל והכנור מעוררני כמו שאמרו רבותינו כנור היה תלוי למעלה ממטתו של דוד כיון שהגיע חצי הלילה רוח צפונית מנשבת בו והוא מנגן מאליו:
rashi.eng: *I shall awaken the dawn.* It is the custom of other kings that the dawn awakens them, but I awaken the dawn, for I rise at midnight, when the psaltery and the harp awaken me, as our Rabbis said (Ber. 3b): A harp was suspended above David’s bed. As soon as midnight arrived, the north wind would blow on it and it would play by itself.

notes.3789: (tn, Heb): “for great upon the sky [or “heavens”] [is] your loyal love.”

notes.3791: (tn, Heb): “over all the earth [be] your splendor.” Though no verb appears, the tone of the statement is a prayer or wish. (Note the imperative form in the preceding line.)

rashi.heb:
*מעל שמים.* 
וכתוב אחד אומר (לעיל נ"ז) עד שמים פירשו רבותינו כאן בעושין לשמה כאן בעושין שלא לשמה:
rashi.eng: *above the heavens.* and one verse says (above 57:11): “is up to the heavens.” Our Rabbis explained: This one speaks of those who perform [a commandment] for its sake [i.e., for the sole purpose of obeying the Torah], and that one deals with those who perform [the commandments] with ulterior motives.

notes.3793: (tn): Or “may be rescued.” The lines are actually reversed in the Hebrew text: “So that the ones you love may be rescued, deliver by your power and answer me.”

notes.3795: (sn): Shechem stands for the territory west of the Jordan River; the valley of Succoth represents the region east of the Jordan.

rashi.heb:
*וענני.* 
שכל עמך וידידיך תלוין בי:
rashi.eng: *and answer me.* for all Your people and Your beloved ones are dependent upon me.

notes.3796: (tn): Gilead was located east of the Jordan River. Half of the tribe of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan in the region of Bashan.
notes.3797: (tn, Heb): “the protection of my head.” Ephraim, one of Joseph’s sons, was one of two major tribes located west of the Jordan River. By comparing Ephraim to a helmet, the Lord suggests that the Ephraimites played a primary role in the defense of his land.
notes.3798: (sn): Judah, like Ephraim, was the other major tribe west of the Jordan River. The Davidic king, symbolized here by the royal scepter, came from this tribe.

rashi.heb:
*אלהים דבר בקדשו.* 
שאמלוך ויבא העת ואעלוז בדברו, (עיין לעיל פרשה ס' פסוק ח):
rashi.eng: *God spoke with His holiness.* that I would reign and that the time would come that I would rejoice in His word.

rashi.heb:
*אחלקה שכם.* 
אחלקה ארץ אויבי לישראל, שכם חלק כמו (בראשית מ״ח:כ״ב) שכם אחד על אחיך, (ועמק סכות אמדד):
rashi.eng: *that I would allot a portion.* I shall divide the land of my enemies to Israel, like (Gen. 48:22): “one portion (שכם) more than your brethren.”

notes.3799: (sn): The metaphor of the wash basin, used to rinse one’s hands and feet, suggests that Moab, in contrast to Israel’s elevated position (vv. 7-8), would be reduced to the status of a servant.
notes.3800: (tn, Heb): “over Edom I will throw my sandal.” The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Some interpret this as idiomatic for “taking possession of.” Others translate עַל (’al) as “to” and understand this as referring to a master throwing his dirty sandal to a servant so that the latter might dust it off.

notes.3801: (sn): The psalmist speaks again and acknowledges his need for help in battle. He hopes God will volunteer, based on the affirmation of sovereignty over Edom in v. 9, but he is also aware that God has seemingly rejected the nation of Israel (v. 11).

rashi.heb:
*מואב סיר רחצי.* 
כלומר עבדי ושמשי ככלי תשמיש שמשתמשין בו:
rashi.eng: *Moab is my washbasin.* i.e., my slaves and my servants, like a utensil that people use.

rashi.heb:
*על אדום אשליך.* 
עבודתי שיהיו מלכיהם נוטלין מנעלי ברגלי:
rashi.eng: *on Edom I shall cast.* my servitude, that their kings should put my shoes on my feet.

rashi.heb:
*אתרועע.* 
אריע להם קול ליראם מפני:
rashi.eng: *I shall shout.* I shall raise my voice to them to frighten them.

rashi.heb:
*מי יובילני.* 
לימות המשיח לפשוט יד בעשו בערי מבצרים:
rashi.eng: *Who will bring me.* in the time of the Messiah, to stretch forth my hand upon Esau in his fortified cities?

rashi.heb:
*מי שנחני.* 
כבר על אדום שהכיתי בהם בגיא מלח שמנה עשר אלף:
rashi.eng: *He Who.* Who led us already upon Edom, that I smote them in the Valley of Salt, eighteen thousand.

notes.3802: (tn, Heb): “and futile [is] the deliverance of man.”

notes.3803: (tn, Heb): “in God we will accomplish strength.” The statement refers here to military success (see Num 24:18; 1 Sam 14:48; Pss 60:12; 118:16-16).
notes.3804: (sn): On the expression trample down our enemies see Ps 44:5.
notes.3805: (sn): Psalm 109. Appealing to God’s justice, the psalmist asks God to vindicate him and to bring severe judgment down upon his enemies.

rashi.heb:
*אלהי תהלתי אל תחרש.* 
על כל ישראל נאמר:
rashi.eng: *O God of my praise, be not silent.* This was said regarding all Israel.

notes.3807: (tn, Heb): “for a mouth of evil and a mouth of deceit against me they open, they speak with me [with] a tongue of falsehood.”

rashi.heb:
*כי פי רשע.* 
עשו:
rashi.eng: *For the mouth of a wicked man.* Ishmael.

notes.3808: (tn, Heb): “and [with] words of hatred they surround me.”

notes.3809: (tn, Heb): “in place of my love they oppose me.”

rashi.heb:
*תחת אהבתי.* 
אותך ישטנוני:
rashi.eng: *Instead of my love.* for You, they hinder me.

rashi.heb:
*ואני תפלה.* 
ואני מתפלל אליך תמיד (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *but I am at prayer.* But I pray to You constantly. I found:

notes.3811: (tn, Heb): “and they set upon me evil in place of good.”

rashi.heb:
*רעה תחת טובה.* 
שבעים פרים אני מקריב בכל שנה בשביל שבעי' אומו' ומבקש לגשמים והם מריעים לי (בשוחר טוב):
rashi.eng: *evil instead of good.* I sacrifice seventy bulls every year for the seventy nations, and we request rain, yet they harm us. Shocher Tov (109:4).

notes.3812: (sn): In vv. 6-19 the psalmist calls on God to judge his enemies severely. Some attribute this curse-list to the psalmist’s enemies rather than the psalmist. In this case one should paraphrase v. 6: “They say about me, ‘Appoint an evil man, etc.’” Those supporting this line of interpretation point out that vv. 2-5 and 20 refer to the enemies’ attack on the psalmist being a verbal one. Furthermore in vv. 1-5, 20 the psalmist speaks of his enemies in the plural, while vv. 6-19 refer to an individual. This use of the singular in vv. 6-19 could be readily explained if this is the psalmist’s enemies’ curse on him. However, it is much more natural to understand vv. 6-19 as the psalmist’s prayer against his enemies. There is no introductory quotation formula in v. 6 to indicate that the psalmist is quoting anyone, and the statement “may the Lord repay my accusers in this way” in v. 20 most naturally appears to be a fitting conclusion to the prayer in vv. 6-19. But what about the use of the singular in vv. 6-19? Often in the psalms the psalmist will describe his enemies as a group, but then speak of them as an individual as well, as if viewing his adversaries collectively as one powerful foe. See, for example, Ps 7, where the psalmist uses both the plural (vv. 1, 6) and the singular (vv. 2, 4-5) in referring to enemies. Perhaps by using the singular in such cases, the psalmist wants to single out each enemy for individual attention, or perhaps he has one especially hostile enemy in mind who epitomizes the opposition of the whole group. This may well be the case in Ps 109. Perhaps we should understand the singular throughout vv. 6-19 in the sense of “each and every one.” For a lengthy and well-reasoned defense of the opposite view – that vv. 6-19 are a quotation of what the enemies said about the psalmist – see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 72-73.
notes.3814: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive here (note the imperative in the preceding line).

notes.3815: (tn): The prefixed verbal form could be taken as a jussive, but the use of the imperfect form in the following line suggests that v. 7 anticipates the outcome of the accusation envisioned in v. 6.
notes.3816: (tn, Heb): “he will go out [as] a criminal” (that is, guilty).

rashi.heb:
*בהשפטו.* 
לפניך יצא מדינך מחויב ורשע:
rashi.eng: *When he is judged.* before You, may he emerge from Your judgment guilty and wicked.

notes.3817: (tn): The prefixed verbal forms (except those with vav [ו] consecutive) in vv. 8-20 are taken as jussives of prayer. Note the distinct jussive forms used in vv. 12-13, 15, 19.
notes.3818: (tn): The Hebrew noun פְּקֻדָּה (p�quddah) can mean “charge” or “office,” though BDB 824 s.v. suggests that here it refers to his possessions.

rashi.heb:
*פקודתו.* 
גדולתו פרבושטיא"ה בלע"ז כמו ויפקד המלך פקידים (אסתר ב ד):
rashi.eng: *his office of dignity.* Heb. פקדתו, his greatness, provostie or pruvote in Old French, like (Esther 2:3): “And let the king appoint officers (פקידים).”

notes.3821: (tn, Heb): “and roaming, may his children roam and beg, and seek from their ruins.” Some, following the LXX, emend the term וְדָרְשׁוּ (v�doreshu, “and seek”) to יְגֹרְשׁוּ (y�goreshu; a Pual jussive, “may they be driven away” [see Job 30:5; cf. NIV, NRSV]), but דָּרַשׁ (darash) nicely parallels שִׁאֵלוּ (shi’elu, “and beg”) in the preceding line.

rashi.heb:
*ושאלו ודרשו מחרבותיהם.* 
הכל ישאלו עליה' מה נהיתה בפלוני ופלוני מתוך קול חורבה שיצא עליהם ודרשו 
משמע מאת אחרים שהרי נקוד חטף קמץ וכן ושאלו מפי אחרים הוא משמע שישאלו אחרים עליהם, ויש לפתור ושאלו ממשקל חזק יהיו משאלים על הפתחים:
rashi.eng: *and [people] should ask and search from their ruins.* Everyone will ask about them, what happened to So-and-so and So-and-so, because of the rumor of ruin that emerged about them. And “search” (וְדָרְשוּ) means from others, because it is vowelized with a short “kamatz,” and וְשִׁאֵלוּ also means from others, that others should ask about them. This can also be interpreted as וְשִׁאֵלוּ, of the intensive conjugation, meaning that they will go around by the doors [to beg for alms].

rashi.heb:
*ינקש נושה לכל אשר לו.* 
אדם הטורח מחזיר ולהוט לעשות דבר נופל בו לשון מתנקש כלומר מוטרף ומתלבט כמו (דניאל ה׳:ו׳) וארכובתיה דא לדא נקשן וכן פן תנקש אחריהם אף כאן יהיה הנושה בעשו את עבודתו שנאמר ורב יעבד צעיר, ל"א יהיה הנושה נוגע ונקרב לכל אשר לו ינקש שייטאצופי"ץ בלע"ז יהי משפט הנושה נוקש ונשען על כל ממונו וזהו יעקב הנושה בעשו את עבודתו שנאמר ורב יעבד צעיר מצאתי.
rashi.eng: *May a creditor search out all he has.* Heb. ינקש. A person who toils and searches, and longs passionately to do something is described by the expression מִתְנַקֵשׁ, i.e., shaken and going from place to place, like (Dan. 5:6): “and his knees knocked (נקשן) against each other.”

notes.3824: (tn, Heb): “may there not be for him one who extends loyal love.”
notes.3825: (tn): Perhaps this refers to being generous (see Ps 37:21).

notes.3827: (sn): On the expression cut off see Ps 37:28.
notes.3828: (tn, Heb): “in another generation may their name be wiped out.”

rashi.heb:
*בדור אחר.* 
שיבא אחר כורתו ימח שמו וטבעו שאפילו זכרון לא יפול עליו בפי הדור הנולד בעול' לאחר שנשחת שמו שארטרמיר"א בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *in another generation.* that will come after his being cut off, his name and his fame will be blotted out so that not even a remembrance will remain of him in the mouth of the generation that is born in the world after his name will be destroyed, sa retremure in Old French, its extirpation.

notes.3830: (tn, Heb): “not be wiped out.” According to ancient Israelite theology and its doctrine of corporate solidarity and responsibility, children could be and often were punished for the sins of their parents. For a discussion of this issue see J. Kaminsky, Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible (JSOTSup). (Kaminsky, however, does not deal with Ps 109.)

rashi.heb:
*עון אבותיו.* 
עון שהעוה על אבותיו, לאברהם שגרע חמש שנים מחייו ולאביו גרם כהיון עינים:
rashi.eng: *the iniquity against his forefathers.* The iniquity that he sinned against his forebears, to Abraham, whose life he shortened by five years, and to his father he caused blindness.

rashi.heb:
*וחטאת אמו.* 
שהשחית רחמה ושגרם להעלים יום קבורתה מן הבריות שלא יקללוה שיצא מכריסה עשו כמו שנאמר (בראשית ל״ה:ח׳) ותמת דבורה מינקת רבקה וגומר אלון בכות בלשון יוני קורין לאחר אלון שאבל אחר היה ליעקב עם של דבורה שמתה אמו והעלימו מיתתה:
rashi.eng: *and the sin against his mother.* that he destroyed her womb, and that he caused the day of her burial to be concealed from the people, lest they curse her for Esau emerged from her womb, as it is said (Gen. 35:8): “Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, died… the Plain of Weeping.” In Greek, another is called “allon,” for Jacob had another mourning along with that of Deborah, for his mother died and they concealed her death.

notes.3831: (tn, Heb): “may they [that is, the sins mentioned in v. 14] be before the Lord continually.”
notes.3832: (tn, Heb): “their memory.” The plural pronominal suffix probably refers back to the children mentioned in v. 13, and for clarity this has been specified in the translation.

rashi.heb:
*יהיו.* 
העונו' האלה נגד ה' תמיד:
rashi.eng: *May they be.* [May] these iniquities [be] before the Lord constantly.

rashi.heb:
*ויכרת מארץ זכרם.* 
של עשו ואלופיו:
rashi.eng: *and may He cut off their remembrance from the earth.* [the remembrance] of Esau and his chieftains.

notes.3833: (tn, Heb): “he did not remember to do loyal love.”
notes.3834: (tn, Heb): “and he chased an oppressed and needy man, and one timid of heart to put [him] to death.”

rashi.heb:
*יען אשר לא זכר עשות חסד.* 
לעסוק באבל אביו כמו שעשה יעקב נזיד עדשים לנחם את יצחק שבאותו היום מת אברהם:
rashi.eng: *Because he did not remember to do kindness.* to engage in the mourning of his father, as Jacob had made a pottage of lentils to console Isaac, for on that day Abraham had died.

rashi.heb:
*איש עני.* 
ישראל:
rashi.eng: *a poor… man.* Israel.

notes.3835: (sn): A curse in OT times consists of a formal appeal to God to bring judgment down upon another. Curses were sometimes justified (such as the one spoken by the psalmist here in vv. 6-19), but when they were not, the one pronouncing the curse was in danger of bringing the anticipated judgment down upon himself.
notes.3836: (tn, Heb): “and he loved a curse and it came [upon] him.” A reference to the evil man experiencing a curse seems premature here, for the psalmist is asking God to bring judgment on his enemies. For this reason some (cf. NIV, NRSV) prefer to repoint the vav (ו) on “it came” as conjunctive and translate the verb as a jussive of prayer (“may it come upon him!”). The prefixed form with vav consecutive in the next line is emended in the same way and translated, “may it be far from him.” However, the psalmist may be indicating that the evil man’s lifestyle has already begun to yield its destructive fruit.
notes.3837: (tn, Heb): “and he did not delight in a blessing and it is far from him.”

rashi.heb:
*ויאהב קללה.* 
קללתו של הקדוש ברוך הוא שכפר בו:
rashi.eng: *And he loved a curse.* [Esau loved] the curse of the Holy One, blessed be He, Whose existence he denied.

notes.3838: (tn, Heb): “he put on a curse as [if it were] his garment.”
notes.3839: (tn, Heb): “and it came like water into his inner being, and like oil into his bones.” This may refer to this individual’s appetite for cursing. For him cursing was as refreshing as drinking water or massaging oneself with oil. Another option is that the destructive effects of a curse are in view. In this case a destructive curse invades his very being, like water or oil. Some who interpret the verse this way prefer to repoint the vav (ו) on “it came” to a conjunctive vav and interpret the prefixed verb as a jussive, “may it come!”

rashi.heb:
*וילבש קללה.* 
הכניס עצמו בקללה ונוחה לו פריקת עול הקרבן וברכת כהנים וקללת האומות:
rashi.eng: *And he donned a curse.* He brought himself into a curse and was satisfied with breaking off the yoke of the sacrifice and the priestly blessing and the curse of the heathens.

notes.3840: (tn, Heb): “may it be for him like a garment one puts on.”
notes.3841: (tn): The Hebrew noun מֵזַח (mezakh, “belt; waistband”) occurs only here in the OT. The form apparently occurs in Isa 23:10 as well, but an emendation is necessary there.

rashi.heb:
*תהי לו.* 
הקללה מעטה כבגד (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *May it be to him.* [May] the curse [be to him] as an envelopment like a garment. [This] I found.

rashi.heb:
*ולמזח תמיד.* 
חגורה, וכן ומזיח אפיקים רפה (איוב י״ב:כ״א) אזור החזקים פתח:
rashi.eng: *and as a girdle… constantly.* Heb. ולמזח, a girdle, and so, (Job 12:21): “and loosens the belt (מזיח) of the strong.” He loosens the belt of the strong.

notes.3842: (tn, Heb): “[may] this [be] the repayment to my accusers from the Lord.”
notes.3844: (tn): The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “being; soul”) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 4.a).

notes.3845: (tn, Heb): “but you, Lord, Master, do with me for the sake of your name.” Here “name” stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

notes.3846: (tc): The verb in the Hebrew text (חָלַל, khalal) appears to be a Qal form from the root חלל meaning “pierced; wounded.” However, the Qal of this root is otherwise unattested. The translation assumes an emendation to יָחִיל (yakhil), a Qal imperfect from חוּל (khul, “tremble”) or to חֹלַל (kholal), a polal perfect from חוּל (khul). See Ps 55:4, which reads לִבִּי יָחִיל בְּקִרְבִּי (libbiy yakhil b�qirbbiy, “my heart trembles [i.e., “beats violently”] within me”).

notes.3847: (tn, Heb): “like a shadow when it is extended I go.” He is like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness. See Ps 102:11.

rashi.heb:
*כצל כנטותו.* 
לעת ערב:
rashi.eng: *Like a shadow when it lengthens.* at eventide.

rashi.heb:
*ננערתי.* 
לשון תשנוק וטרוף ואוטם כארבה שהוא נודד ונע ומטורף, (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *I was stirred up.* an expression of stirring and mixing and astonishment, like a locust, which wanders to and fro and is stirred up. [This] I found:

notes.3849: (tn, Heb): “and my flesh is lean away from fatness [i.e., “lean so as not to be fat”].”

notes.3850: (tn, Heb): “as for me, I am a reproach to them.”
notes.3851: (sn): They shake their heads. Apparently shaking the head was a taunting gesture. See also Job 16:4; Ps 22:7; Lam 2:15.

notes.3852: (tn, Heb): “deliver me according to your faithfulness.”

notes.3853: (tn): After the preceding imperative, the prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose or result.

notes.3855: (tn): Another option is to translate the imperfect as a prayer/request (“may you bless”).
notes.3856: (tn): The verbal sequence is perfect + prefixed form with vav (ו) consecutive. Since the psalmist seems to be anticipating the demise of his enemies, he may be using these forms rhetorically to describe the enemies’ defeat as if it were already accomplished. Some emend the text to קָמוּ יֵבֹשׁוּ (qamu yevoshu, “may those who attack me be humiliated”). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 75.

notes.3857: (tn, Heb): “clothed.” Another option is to translate the prefixed verbal forms in this line and the next as jussives (“may my accusers be covered with shame”).

rashi.heb:
*ויעטו כמעיל.* 
העוטה ועוטף כל הגוף לכל לבוש:
rashi.eng: *and enwrap themselves… like a cloak.* which enwraps and envelops the entire body.

notes.3858: (tn, Heb): “I will thank the Lord very much with my mouth.”

notes.3861: (sn): Psalm 110. In this royal psalm the psalmist announces God’s oracle to the Davidic king. The first part of the oracle appears in v. 1, the second in v. 4. In vv. 2-3 the psalmist addresses the king, while in vv. 5-7 he appears to address God.

notes.3862: (tn): The word נְאֻם (n�’um) is used frequently in the OT of a formal divine announcement through a prophet.
notes.3863: (sn): My lord. In the psalm’s original context the speaker is an unidentified prophetic voice in the royal court. In the course of time the psalm is applied to each successive king in the dynasty and ultimately to the ideal Davidic king. NT references to the psalm understand David to be speaking about his “lord,” the Messiah. (See Matt 22:43-45; Mark 12:36-37; Luke 20:42-44; Acts 2:34-35).
notes.3864: (tn): To sit at the “right hand” of the king was an honor (see 1 Kgs 2:19). In Ugaritic myth (CTA 4 v. 108-10) the artisan god Kothar-and Khasis is described as sitting at the right hand of the storm god Baal. See G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 61-62. The Lord’s invitation to the Davidic king to sit down at his right hand reflects the king’s position as the Lord’s vice-regent.
notes.3865: (sn): When the Lord made his covenant with David, he promised to subdue the king’s enemies (see 2 Sam 7:9-11; Ps 89:22-23).

rashi.heb:
*נאם ה' לאדני.* 
רבותינו דרשוהו באברהם אבינו ואני אפרשנו כדבריהם נאם ה' לאברהם שקראוהו העולם אדוני שמעני אדוני (בראשית כ״ג:י״א):
rashi.eng: *The word of the Lord to my master.* Our Rabbis interpreted it as referring to Abraham our father, and I shall explain it according to their words (Mid. Ps. 110:1): The word of the Lord to Abraham, whom the world called “my master,” as it is written (Gen. 23:6): “Hearken to us, my master.”

rashi.heb:
*שב לימיני.* 
התעכב לתשועתי והתחולל לה' אין ישיבה אלא עכבה וכן הוא אומר ותשבו בקדש (דברים א׳:מ״ו):
rashi.eng: *“Wait for My right hand”.* Wait for My salvation and hope for the Lord. [The root] ישיבה means only waiting, as Scripture states (Deut. 1:46): “And you stayed (ותשבו) in Kadesh for many days.”

rashi.heb:
*לימיני.* 
לתשועת ימיני:
rashi.eng: *for My right hand.* For the salvation of My right hand.

rashi.heb:
*עד אשית אויביך.* 
אמרפל וחביריו:
rashi.eng: *until I make your enemies.* Amraphel and his allies.

notes.3866: (tn): Since the Lord is mentioned in the third person (note the use of the first person in v. 1), it is likely that these are the psalmist’s words to the king, not a continuation of the oracle per se.
notes.3867: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing, though it could be taken as future.
notes.3868: (tn, Heb): “your strong scepter,” symbolic of the king’s royal authority and dominion.

rashi.heb:
*מטה.* 
לשון משען כמו (לעיל ק"ה) כל מטה לחם:
rashi.eng: *The staff of.* [This is] an expression of support, as (above 105:16): “every staff of bread.”

rashi.heb:
*מטה עוזך ישלח ה' מציון.* 
כשתשוב מן המלחמה ואנשיך עייפים ורודפים ישלח לך ה' את מלכי צדק מלך שלם להוציא לחם ויין (בראשית י״ד:י״ז-י״ח):
rashi.eng: *The staff of your might the Lord will send from Zion.* When you return from the war and your men are weary and in pursuit, the Lord will send you Malchizedek, king of Salem, to bring out bread and wine (Gen. 14:14).

rashi.heb:
*רדה.* 
במלחמה:
rashi.eng: *rule.* in the war.

rashi.heb:
*בקרב אויביך.* 
לבטח:
rashi.eng: *in the midst of your enemies.* safely.

notes.3869: (tn, Heb): “your people, free will offerings.” Perhaps the people, in their willingness to volunteer, are compared metaphorically to freewill offerings. Following the LXX, some revocalize the text and read “with you is nobility.”
notes.3870: (tn, Heb): “in the day of your power.”
notes.3871: (tc, Heb): “in splendor of holiness.” The plural construct form הַדְרֵי (hadrey, from הָדַר, hadar, “splendor”) occurs only here; it may indicate degree or perhaps refer by metonymy to garments (see Pss 29:2 and 96:9, where the phrase הַדְרַת קֹדֶשׁ [hadrat qodesh] refers to “holy attire”). If one retains the reading of the MT, this phrase should probably be taken with the preceding line. However, because of the subsequent references to “dawn” and to “dew,” it is better to emend the text to הַרְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ (harrey qodesh, “mountains of holiness”), a reading found in many medieval Hebrew mss and in some other ancient witnesses (see Joel 2:2; Ps 133:3, as well as L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 80). The “mountains of holiness” are probably the hills surrounding Zion (see Ps 87:1; 125:2; 133:3).
notes.3872: (tn, Heb): “from the womb of dawn.” The Hebrew noun רֶחֶם (rekhem, “womb”) is probably used here metonymically for “birth.” The form מִשְׁחָר (mishkhar) occurs only here and should be emended to שַׁחַר (shakhar, “dawn”) with the mem (מ) being understood as dittographic (note the final mem [ם] on the preceding word). The phrase “womb [i.e., “birth”] of dawn” refers to sunrise.
notes.3873: (sn): The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. The dew may symbolize the king’s youthful vitality or, more likely (note the parallelism), may refer to his army of strong, youthful warriors.

rashi.heb:
*עמך נדבות ביום חילך.* 
כשתאסוף חיל לרדוף אחריהם יתנדבו עמך ואוהביך לצאת עמך כמו שמצינו (שם) וירק את חניכיו ילידי ביתו ולא יותר וענר ואשכול וממרא התנדבו מאליהם לצאת ללכת אחריו בעזרתו:
rashi.eng: *Your people will volunteer on the day of your host.* When you gather an army to pursue them, your people and your friends will volunteer to go out with you, as we find (Gen. 14:14): “and he armed his trained men, those born in his house,” and no more; and Aner, Eshkol, and Mamre volunteered by themselves to go out to his aid.

rashi.heb:
*בהדרי קודש מרחם משחר.* 
זאת תהיה לך בזכות הדרת קדושה שהיה בך מבטן אמך שהכיר בוראו בן ג' שנים:
rashi.eng: *because of the beauty of holiness when you fell from the womb.* And this will be to you in the merit of the beauty of holiness that was in you from your mother’s womb, for he recognized his Creator at the age of three.

rashi.heb:
*מרחם משחר.* 
משנפלת מן הרחם כמו משילין פירות דרך ארובה ביו"ט ואיכא דתני משחירין:
rashi.eng: *when you fell from the womb.* Heb. משחר, when you fell from the womb, like (Beizah 35b): “We may let fruit down (משילין) through a skylight on a festival,” and some learn משחירין.

rashi.heb:
*לך טל ילדותיך.* 
לך יחשב ילדותיך דרכי יושר שהנהגת בהם בילדותיך יהיה לך לנועם כטל זה שהוא נעים ונוח:
rashi.eng: *for you, your youth is like dew.* For you will be considered your youth, the ways of uprightness with which you conducted yourself in your youth will be for you as pleasantness, like this dew, which is pleasant and comforting.

notes.3876: (tn): Or “will not change his mind.” The negated Niphal imperfect of נָחַם (nakham) is a way of marking an announcement as an irrevocable decree. See 1 Sam 15:29; Ezek 24:14, as well as R. B. Chisholm, “Does God ‘Change His Mind’?” BSac 152 (1995): 387-99.
notes.3877: (sn): You are an eternal priest. The Davidic king exercised a non-Levitical priestly role. The king superintended Judah’s cultic ritual, had authority over the Levites, and sometimes led in formal worship. David himself instructed the Levites to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11-15), joined the procession, offered sacrifices, wore a priestly ephod, and blessed the people (2 Sam 6:12-19). At the dedication of the temple Solomon led the ceremony, offering sacrifices and praying on behalf of the people (1 Kgs 8).
notes.3878: (tn): The phrase עַל־דִּבְרָתִי (’al-divratiy) is a variant of עַל־דִּבְרָת (’al-divrat; the final yod [י] being an archaic genitival ending), which in turn is a variant of עַל דָּבַר (’al davar). Both phrases can mean “concerning” or “because of,” but neither of these nuances fits the use of עַל־דִּבְרָתִי in Ps 110:4. Here the phrase probably carries the sense “according to the manner of.” See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 81.
notes.3879: (sn): The Davidic king’s priestly role is analogous to that of Melchizedek, who was both “king of Salem” (i.e., Jerusalem) and a “priest of God Most High” in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:18-20). Like Melchizedek, the Davidic king was a royal priest, distinct from the Aaronic line (see Heb 7). The analogy focuses on the king’s priestly role; the language need not imply that Melchizedek himself was “an eternal priest.”

rashi.heb:
*נשבע ה' ולא ינחם.* 
לפי שהיה מתירא שלא יענש על האוכלסין שהרג נאמר לו (שם ט"ו) אל תירא אברם וגו' לא ינחם על הטובה אשר דבר עליך:
rashi.eng: *The Lord swore and will not repent.* Since Abraham was afraid lest he be punished for the troops that he had killed, it was said to him (Gen. 15:1): “Fear not, Abraham, etc.”

rashi.heb:
*אתה כהן לעולם על דברתי מלכי צדק.* 
ממך תצא הכהונה ומלכות להיות בניך יורשין את שם אבי אביך הכהונה והמלכות שנתנו לו:
rashi.eng: *and will not repent.* over the good that He spoke about you.

rashi.heb:
*דברתי מלכי צדק.* 
יו"ד יתירה כמו רבתי עם (איכה א), על דברת מלכי צדק על פקודת מלכי צדק אתה כהן. יש במשמע כהן כהונה ושררה כמו (שמואל ב מ) ובני דוד כהנים היו:
rashi.eng: *you are a priest forever because of the speech of Malchizedek.* From you will emerge the priesthood and the kingship that your children will inherit from Shem your progenitor, the priesthood and the kingship, which were given to him. דִבְרָתִי מלכי-צדק. The “yud” is superfluous, like (Lam. 1:1): “the city that was once so populous (רבתי).” Because of the speech of Malchizedek, because of the command of Malchizedek. You are a priest, Heb. כהן. The word כהן bears the connotation of priesthood and rulership, as (II Sam. 8:18): “and David’s sons were chief officers.”

notes.3880: (tn): As pointed in the Hebrew text, this title refers to God (many medieval Hebrew mss read יְהוָה, yehveh, “Lord” here). The present translation assumes that the psalmist here addresses the Lord as he celebrates what the king is able to accomplish while positioned at God’s “right hand.” According to this view the king is the subject of the third person verb forms in vv. 5b-7. (2) Another option is to understand the king as the addressee (as in vv. 2-3). In this case “the Lord” is the subject of the third person verbs throughout vv. 5-7 and is depicted as a warrior in a very anthropomorphic manner. In this case the Lord is pictured as being at the psalmist’s right hand (just the opposite of v. 1). See Pss 16:8; 121:5. (3) A third option is to revocalize אֲדֹנָי (’adonay, “Lord”) as אֲדֹנִי (’adoniy, “my lord”; see v. 1). In this case one may translate, “My lord, at his [God’s] right hand, strikes down.” In this case the king is the subject of the third person verbs in vv. 5b-7.
notes.3881: (tn): The perfect verbal forms in vv. 5-6 are understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing. Another option is to take them as rhetorical. In this case the psalmist describes anticipated events as if they had already taken place.
notes.3882: (tn, Heb): “in the day of his anger.”

rashi.heb:
*אדני.* 
אשר היה על ימינך במלחמה:
rashi.eng: *The Lord.* Who was on your right hand in battle.

rashi.heb:
*מחץ ביום אפו מלכים.* 
את ארבעה מלכים הוא:
rashi.eng: *has crushed kings on the day of His wrath.* The four kings. He…

notes.3883: (tn): The imperfect verbal forms in vv. 6-7 are understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing, though they could be taken as future.
notes.3885: (tn, Heb): “he fills [with] corpses,” but one expects a double accusative here. The translation assumes an emendation to גְוִיּוֹת גֵאָיוֹת(בִּ) מִלֵּא or מִלֵּא גֵאָיוֹת גְּוִיוֹת (for a similar construction see Ezek 32:5). In the former case גֵאָיוֹת(ge’ayot) has accidentally dropped from the text due to homoioteleuton; in the latter case it has dropped out due to homoioarcton.
notes.3886: (tn, Heb): “he strikes [the verb is מָחַץ (makhats), translated “strikes down” in v. 5] head[s] over a great land.” The Hebrew term רַבָּה (rabbah, “great”) is here used of distance or spatial measurement (see 1 Sam 26:13).

rashi.heb:
*ידין בגוים מלא גויות.* 
זו היא בשורת ברית בין הבתרים שנאמר לו על מצרים וגם את הגוי אשר יעבודו דן אנכי (בראשית ט״ו:י״ד):
rashi.eng: *will execute justice upon the nations [into] a heap of corpses.* This is the tidings of the ‘covenant between the segments,’ [in] which was stated to him concerning Egypt (Gen. 15:14): “But also that nation whom they will serve do I judge.”

rashi.heb:
*מלא גויות.* 
אסיפת פגרים, מלא לשון אסיפה כמו (ירמיה י"ד) קראו אחריך מלא, אשר יקרא עליו מלא רועים (ישעיהו ל״א:ד׳), והיכן דן מלא גויות את מצרים על שפת הים (שמות ט"ו):
rashi.eng: *a heap of corpses.* Heb. מלא, a heap of corpses. מלא is an expression of gathering, as (Jer. 12:6): “have called a gang (מלא) after you;” (Isa. 31:4), “although a band (מלא) of shepherds gather against him.” Now where did He execute justice, making them a heap of corpses? (Exod. 14:30), “the Egyptians dead on the seashore.”

rashi.heb:
*מחץ ראש על ארץ רבה.* 
זו היא דוגמת נבואת (חבקוק ג׳:י״ג) מחצת ראש מבית רשע ראש פרעה שהיה ראש ושר על ארץ גדולה וחשובה על כל הארצות כמו שנאמר (לעיל ק"ה) מושל עמים ויפתחהו שהיו כל האומות תחת ממשלת מצרים:
rashi.eng: *He crushed the head on a great land.* This resembles the prophecy of Habakkuk (3:12): “You have crushed the head of the house of the wicked.” [This refers to] the head of Pharaoh, who was the head and the prince of a land greater and more esteemed than all the lands, as is said (above 102:20): “a ruler of peoples [sent] and loosed his bonds,” for all the nations were under the rule of Egypt.

notes.3887: (tn): Here the expression “lifts up the head” refers to the renewed physical strength and emotional vigor (see Ps 3:3) provided by the refreshing water. For another example of a victorious warrior being energized by water in the aftermath of battle, see Judg 15:18-19 (see also 1 Sam 30:11-12, where the setting is different, however).
notes.3888: (sn): Psalm 111. The psalmist praises God for his marvelous deeds, especially the way in which he provides for and delivers his people. The psalm is an acrostic. After the introductory call to praise, every poetic line (twenty-two in all) begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

rashi.heb:
*מנחל בדרך ישתה וגו'.* 
מנילוס הנהר בדרך הליכתו היתה ארצו שותה ולא היתה צריכה למי גשמים על כן היה מרים ראש ומתפאר (יחזקאל כ״ט:ג׳) לי יאורי ואני עשיתני, ענין אחר יש לפרש המזמור הזה בדוד:
rashi.eng: *From the stream on the way he would drink, etc..* From the Nile River, on the way of its course, his land would drink, and it was not in need of rain water. Therefore, he would raise his head and boast (Ezek. 29:3): “My river is my own, and I made myself.” In another manner, this psalm can be explained regarding David:

rashi.heb:
*נאם ה' לאדני.* 
על עסקי אדוני שאול כשהייתי נרדף מפניו:
rashi.eng: *[Verse 1] The word of the Lord about my master.* Concerning my master, Saul, when I was pursued by him.

rashi.heb:
*לאדני.* 
על אדוני כמו ואמר פרעה לבני ישראל (שמות י״ד:ג׳), וישאלו אנשי המקום לאשתו (בראשית כ״ו:ז׳):
rashi.eng: *about my master.* Heb. לאדני, about my master, as (Exod. 14:3): “Then Pharaoh will say concerning the children of (לבני) Israel;” (Gen. 26:7), “The people of the place asked him about his wife (לאשתו).”

rashi.heb:
*שב לימיני.* 
התעכב והמתן לישועתי:
rashi.eng: *“Wait for My right hand”.* Stay and wait for My salvation.

rashi.heb:
*מטה עזך ישלח ה' מציון.* 
מעשים טובים המצויינין בידך, ד"א עוד תמלוך בציון ושם ישולח לך מטה עז ואז תרדה בקרב אויביך:
rashi.eng: *[Verse 2] The staff of your might the Lord will send from Zion.* The exceptional good deeds in your hand. Another explanation: You will yet reign in Zion, and there a staff of might will be sent to you, and then you will rule in the midst of your enemies.

rashi.heb:
*עמך נדבות ביום חילך.* 
עם ישראל יתנדבו לעזרתך ביום שתעשה חיל כמו שמפורש (בדברי הימים א י״ב:כ״א) שהיו נקבצים עליו מכל שבט ושבט בלכתו אל צקלג נפלו עליו ממנשה וגומר ומן הגדי נבדלו אל דוד וגומר (שם):
rashi.eng: *[Verse 3] Your people will volunteer on the day of your host.* The people of Israel will volunteer to your aid on the day that you form an army, as it is delineated in (I) Chronicles (12:21); that they were joining him from every tribe: “When he went to Ziklag, there deserted to him of Manasseh, etc.;” (ibid. verse 8): “And from the Gadites there separated themselves to David, etc.”

rashi.heb:
*בהדרי קודש מרחם משחר.* 
בשביל הדרת קדושה שהיה בך מנעוריך:
rashi.eng: *because of the beauty of holiness when you fell from the womb.* Because of the beauty of holiness that was in you from your youth.

rashi.heb:
*לך טל ילדותך.* 
ילדות טובה ופרק נאה שהיה בך תהיה לך כטל שהוא נעים יערב ותעשה לך פירות להצליחך:
rashi.eng: *your youth is like dew.* A good youth and a good period of maturity that you had will be to you like dew, which is pleasant and sweet, and will produce fruit for you to make you prosper.

rashi.heb:
*נשבע ה' וגו'.* 
שהמלכות תהא שלך עולמית:
rashi.eng: *[Verse 4] The Lord has sworn, etc..* that the kingdom will be yours forever.

rashi.heb:
*אתה כהן לעולם.* 
ואיזו מן הכהונות כהונה שהיא למעלה מכהונת מלכי צדק וזהו המלכות שהיא למעלה מכהונה גדולה בשלשים מעלות:
rashi.eng: *You are a priest forever.* And which of the priesthoods? A priesthood that is above the priesthood of Malchizedek, and that is the kingdom, which is above the high priesthood in thirty steps.

rashi.heb:
*על דברתי מלכי צדק.* 
למעלה מכהונת מלכי צדק שהיה כהן לאל עליון וא"ת אף הוא מלך היה, מלוכת מלכי צדק אינה מלוכה חשובה כנגד ישראל:
rashi.eng: *above the charge of Malchizedek.* above the priesthood (Some mss. read: above the charge) of Malchizedek, who was a priest to the Most High God. Now if you challenge that he too was a king, [we answer that] the kingdom over the nations was not an esteemed kingdom when compared to Israel.

rashi.heb:
*אדני.* 
יהיה תמיד על ימינך להושיעך:
rashi.eng: *[Verse 5] The Lord.* will always be on your right hand to save you, Who…

rashi.heb:
*אשר מחץ ביום אפו מלכים.* 
שנלחמו עם אברהם ועם יהושע ועם ברק:
rashi.eng: *crushed kings on the day of His wrath.* Those who fought with Abraham and with Joshua and with Barak.

rashi.heb:
*ידין בגוים מלא גויות.* 
ועוד בימי יחזקיהו בנך ידין באוכלסי סנחריב קבוץ פגרים מתים וימחץ בסנחריב שהוא ראשה של נינוה ואשור שהיא ארץ רבה:
rashi.eng: *[Verse 6] He will execute justice upon the nations [into] a heap of corpses.* And further, in the days of Hezekiah your son, He will execute justice upon the armies of Sennacherib [making them] a heap of dead corpses, and He will crush Sennacherib, who is the head of Nineveh and Assyria, which is a great land, who

rashi.heb:
*אשר מנחל בדרך.* 
היה שותה שנתפאר ששתו אוכלסיו מימי הירדן שנאמר (ישעיהו ל״ז:כ״ה) אני קרתי ושתיתי מים ואחריב וגו':
rashi.eng: *[Verse 7] From the stream on the way.* he was drinking, for he boasted that his armies drank from the waters of the Jordan, as it is said (Isa. 37:25): “I dug and drank water, and I dry up, etc.”

rashi.heb:
*על כן ירים ראש.* 
היה משתבח ומתפאר בגודלו:
rashi.eng: *therefore, he raised his head.* He praised himself and boasted of his greatness.

rashi.heb:
*הללויה וגו'.*
