rashi.eng: *The commencement of Your words enlightens.* The beginning of your words enlightened the heart of Israel, that You understated the simple, by Your statement (Exod. 20:2): “I am… Who took you out.” You let them know the favor that You did for them, that You acquired them from the house of bondage to know that You are their Master, and they should accept Your kingdom upon themselves. (Exod. 20:3): “You shall not have another god, etc.” and afterwards You made Your decrees (Cf. Mechilta ad loc.). Another explanation:

rashi.heb: *פתח דבריך יאיר.* תחילת דבריך במעשה בראשית יהי אור:
rashi.eng: *The commencement of Your words enlightens.* The beginning of Your words in the Creation was (Gen. 1:3): “Let there be light.”

rashi.heb:
*מבין פתיים.* 
משם יבינו הכל ויפתחו (להתחיל ולפתוח) בדברי תורה, תנחומא
rashi.eng: *You make the simple understand.* From there, everyone will understand and will commence with words of Torah. Tanchuma (Vayakhel 6).

notes.4200: (tn): The verb occurs only here in the OT.

rashi.heb:
*ואשאפה.* 
ל' בליעה כמו (ירמיהו ב׳:כ״ד) שאפה רוח.
rashi.eng: *and panted.* Heb. ואשאפה, an expression of swallowing, as (Jer. 2:24): “snuffs up (שאפה) the wind.”

notes.4201: (tn, Heb): “according to custom toward the lovers of your name.” The “lovers of” God’s “name” are the Lord’s loyal followers. See Pss 5:11; 69:36; Isa 56:6.

notes.4202: (tn): God’s “word” refers here to his law (see v. 11).

notes.4204: (tn): The cohortative verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

rashi.heb:
*פדני מעושק אדם.* 
מיצר הרע העושק את הבריות בפירושים אחרים מצאתי.
rashi.eng: *Redeem me from the oppression of man.* From the evil inclination, which oppresses the people. In other commentaries I found:

rashi.heb: *פדני מעושק אדם.* פדני מעושקו של אדם.
rashi.eng: *Redeem me from the oppression of man.* Redeem me so that no man oppress me.

notes.4206: (tn, Heb): “[with] flowing streams my eyes go down.”
notes.4207: (tn, Heb): “they”; even though somewhat generic, the referent (people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*צמתתני קנאתי.* 
הקנאה שאני מקנא לשמך על השוכחי דבריך היא צומתה אותי ומקנטת אותי בהם, (מצאתי).
rashi.eng: *My zeal incenses me.* Heb. קנאתי. The zeal with which I am zealous for Your name against those who forget Your words, cuts me and incenses me against them.

rashi.heb:
*צעיר אנכי ונבזה.* 
כד"א (שמואל א י״ז:י״ד) ודוד הוא הקטן, נבזה אני להקטין עצמי אצל עוסקי תורה להתלמד כי פקודיך לא שכחתי מלסלסל ומלפלפל בהם בצדקתך שבתוכן צדק ואמת עולמית ואף כי מצאוני צרות היו הם עסקי ולעולם הבינני צדקם ואחיה בהם כי היא חייך וגומר (דברי' ל'):
rashi.eng: *I am young and despised.* As it is stated (I Sam. 17:14): “And David was the youngest.” I am despised to the extent that I humble myself beside those who engage in the Torah, to learn, for I have not forgotten Your precepts; [nor have I refrained] from searching and debating with them about Your righteousness that is within them [the precepts], which is righteousness and truth to eternity; and even though troubles have befallen me, they were my occupation. And forever enable me to understand their righteousness and I shall live by them (Deut. 30:20): “for it [the Torah] is your life and the length of your days.”

notes.4216: (tn): The cohortative verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

notes.4217: (tn): The cohortative verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

rashi.heb:
*ואשמרה.* 
הסימן של עדותיך דמה בן פר"ץ הוי"ו חולם אבל משאר עדותיך הדלי"ת חולם
rashi.eng: *and I shall keep.* (The acronym of, עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ is דמה בן פֶרֶץ; the “vav” is vowelized with a “holam,” but in the other instances, it is עֵדֹתֶיךָ; the “daleth” is vowelized with a “holam.”)

rashi.heb:
*אשמרות.* 
חצי הלילה שתי אשמורות, ולדברי האומר שלש משמרות הוי לילה היה דוד עומד ממטתו בשליש הלילה הראשונה ועוסק בתורה עד חצות כמו שנאמר לשיח באמרתך, ומחצות ולהלן עוסק בשירות ותושבחות כמו שנאמר חצות לילה אקום להודות לך:
rashi.eng: *watches.* Half the night, two watches, and according to one who says that the night consists of three watches, David would rise from bed at the first third of the night and engage in Torah until midnight, as it is said: “to speak of Your word.” From midnight on, he would engage in songs and praises, as it is said (verse 62): “At midnight, I rise to give thanks to You.”

rashi.heb:
*קרבו רודפי זמה.* 
עצת חטאים הולכים בעצת חטאיהם, ומתרחקים מתורתך ליקרב אל עצת רעתם:
rashi.eng: *Pursuers of lewdness have drawn near.* a counsel of sins. They follow the counsel of their sins and distance themselves from your Torah to draw near to the counsel of their evil.

rashi.heb:
*קרוב אתה.* 
לרחוקים הללו המתרחקים מתורתך אם ישובו מדרכם.
rashi.eng: *You are near.* to these faraway people, who distance themselves from Your Torah, if they repent of their way.

notes.4223: (tn, Heb): “long ago I knew concerning your rules, that forever you established them.” See v. 89 for the same idea. The translation assumes that the preposition מִן (min) prefixed to “your rules” introduces the object of the verb יָדַע (yada’), as in 1 Sam 23:23. Another option is that the preposition indicates source, in which case one might translate, “Long ago I realized from your rules that forever you established them” (cf. NIV, NRSV).

rashi.heb:
*קדם ידעתי מעדותיך.* 
קודם היות הדבר ידעתיו מתוך עדותיך קדם ירשו את הארץ צוית להם על הבכורים ותרומות ומעשרות וקדם הניחות להם מאויביהם צוית להם והיה בהניח ה' אלהיך לך וגו' (שם כ"ה) להעמיד מלך ולהכרית עמלק ולבנות בית הבחירה:
rashi.eng: *From before, I knew from Your testimonies.* Before the thing came about, I knew it from Your testimonies. Before they inherited the land, You commanded them about the first fruits, heave offerings, and tithes, and before You gave them rest from their enemies, You commanded them (Deut. 25:19): “And it will be, when the Lord Your God gives you rest, etc.” to appoint a king, to annihilate Amalek, and to build the Temple.

rashi.heb:
*כי לעולם יסדתם.* 
כי על כל הדברים העתידים להיות לסוף העולם יסדת עדותיך:
rashi.eng: *to the world.* For You established Your testimonies concerning all things destined to be until the end of the world.

notes.4225: (tn, Heb): “and redeem me.” The verb “redeem” casts the Lord in the role of a leader who protects members of his extended family in times of need and crisis (see Ps 19:14).

notes.4228: (tn, Heb): “many [are] those who chase me and my enemies.”

notes.4230: (tn, Heb): “the head of your word is truth, and forever [is] all your just regulation.” The term “head” is used here of the “sum total” of God’s instructions.

rashi.heb:
*ראש דברך אמת.* 
סוף דברך הוכיח על הראש שהוא אמת שכששמעו האומות אנכי ולא יהיה לך ולא תשא אמרו הכל להנאתו ולכבודו כיון ששמעו כבד, לא תרצח, לא תנאף, הודו על ראש דברך שהוא אמת
rashi.eng: *The beginning of Your word is true.* And the end of Your word is not true? Rather, the end of Your word proves that the beginning of Your word is true. For, when the nations heard, “I am the Lord your God,” and “You shall not have [another god],” and “You shall not take, etc.,” they said, “Everything is for His benefit and for His glory.” As soon as they heard, “Honor, etc.; You shall not murder; You shall not commit adultery,” they admitted [that they had erred] about the beginning of Your word, that it is true.

notes.4231: (tn, Heb): “and because of your instructions my heart trembles.” The psalmist’s healthy “fear” of the consequences of violating God’s instructions motivates him to obey them. See v. 120.

notes.4232: (tn, Heb): “like one who finds great plunder.” See Judg 5:30. The image is that of a victorious warrior who finds a large amount of plunder on the field of battle.

rashi.heb:
*שש אנכי על אמרתך.* 
על הבטחתך הבטחתני, ד"א על אחת מאמרותיך הסתומות כשאני מבין בה, ורבותינו דרשו על המילה שהיה דוד בבית המרחץ וראה עצמו בלא ציצית ובלא תפילין ובלא תורה אמר אוי לי שאני ערום מכל מצות כיון שנסתכל במילה שמח ואמר בצאתו (מבית המרחץ) שש אנכי על אמרתך המילה שמתחלה נתנה במאמר ולא בדבור שנאמ' (בראשית י״ז:ט׳) ויאמר אלהים אל אברהם ואתה את בריתי תשמור.
rashi.eng: *I rejoice over Your word.* Over Your promise that You promised me. Another explanation: Over one of Your enigmatic statements, when I understand it. Our Rabbis, however, interpreted it as referring to circumcision, for [when] David was in the bathhouse and saw himself without zizith, without tefillin, and without Torah, he said, “Woe is to me, for I am naked of all commandments.” As soon as he thought of the circumcision, he rejoiced and said when he emerged (from the bathhouse), “I rejoice over Your word.” [This refers to] circumcision, which was first given with a saying (אמירה), and not with speaking (דיבור) , as it is said (Gen. 17:9): “And God said (ויאמר) to Abraham, ‘And you shall keep My covenant.’”

notes.4233: (tn): The number “seven” is use rhetorically to suggest thoroughness.

rashi.heb:
*שבע ביום.* 
שחרית שתים לפני קריאת שמע ואחת לאחריה ובערב שתים לפניה ושתים לאחריה:
rashi.eng: *Seven times a day.* In the morning, twice before the reading of “Shema” and once after it, and in the evening, twice before it and twice after it.

rashi.heb:
*על משפטי צדקך.* 
על ק"ש שהיא דברי תורה:
rashi.eng: *for Your righteous judgments.* For the reading of the Shema, which consists of words of Torah.

notes.4234: (tn, Heb): “great peace [is] to the lovers of your law.”
notes.4235: (tn, Heb): “and there is no stumbling to them.”

rashi.heb:
*שברתי* 
הוחלתי:

notes.4237: (tn, Heb): “for all my ways [are] before you.”

rashi.heb:
*כל דרכי נגדך.* 
אתה יודע כל דרכי:
rashi.eng: *for all my ways are before You.* You know all my ways.

notes.4238: (tn, Heb): “may my cry approach before you.”

rashi.heb:
*כדברך הבינני.* 
דברי תורתך כהלכתן וכהווייתן:
rashi.eng: *according to Your word, enable me to understand.* the words of Your Torah; according to their law and in the order in which they stand.

notes.4239: (tn, Heb): “may my appeal for mercy come before you.”

rashi.heb:
*תבענה.* 
תדברנה:
rashi.eng: *will utter.* will speak.

rashi.heb:
*תען לשוני.* 
כל עניה לשון קול רם הוא ואב לכולם וענו הלוים ואמרו (דברים כ״ז:י״ד):
rashi.eng: *My tongue will proclaim.* Heb. תען. Every [expression of] עַנִיָה is an expression of a loud voice, and the “father” of them all is (Deut. 27:14): “And the Levites shall proclaim (וענו) and say [to all Israel with a loud voice].”

notes.4242: (tn): The words “to obey” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarity.

notes.4244: (tn): God’s regulations will “help” the psalmist by giving him moral and ethical guidance.

notes.4245: (tn, Heb): “I stray like a lost sheep.” It is possible that the point of the metaphor is vulnerability: The psalmist, who is threatened by his enemies, feels as vulnerable as a straying, lost sheep. This would not suggest, however, that he has wandered from God’s path (see the second half of the verse, as well as v. 110).
notes.4246: (sn): Psalm 120. The genre and structure of this psalm are uncertain. It begins like a thanksgiving psalm, with a brief notice that God has heard the psalmist’s prayer for help and has intervened. But v. 2 is a petition for help, followed by a taunt directed toward enemies (vv. 3-4) and a lament (vv. 5-7). Perhaps vv. 2-7 recall the psalmist’s prayer when he cried out to the Lord.
notes.4247: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*שיר המעלות.* 
שיאמרו הלוים אותו על חמש עשרה מעלות היורדות מעזרת ישראל עד עזרת נשים ויש כאן ט"ו מזמורים של שיר המעלות ורבותינו אמרו שיסדן דוד להעלות את התהום כמו שמפורש במסכת סוכה, ולפי אגדה פתרונו שיר למאה עולות:
rashi.eng: *A song of ascents.* which the Levites will recite on the fifteen steps that go down from the Israelites’ court to the Women’s court, and there are fifteen psalms entitled “A song of ascents” (Suc. 5:4, Mid 2:5). And our Rabbis said that David composed them to raise the deep, as is explained in Tractate Succah (53a). And according to the Aggadah (Yerushalmi Sanh. 10:2, 52b), it is to be interpreted: A song for a hundred steps (שיר למאה עולות).

notes.4248: (tn): The words “I said” are supplied in the translation for clarification. See the introductory note for this psalm.

rashi.heb:
*משפת שקר.* 
זרעו של הרשע שצדין את הבריות בפיהם בעלילות רשע:
rashi.eng: *from false lips.* The arm of those who hunt people with their mouth with wicked accusations.

notes.4252: (tn, Heb): “What will he give to you, and what will he add to you, O tongue of deception?” The psalmist addresses his deceptive enemies. The Lord is the understood subject of the verbs “give” and “add.” The second part of the question echoes a standard curse formula, “thus the Lord/God will do … and thus he will add” (see Ruth 1:17; 1 Sam 3:17; 14:44; 20:13; 25:22; 2 Sam 3:9, 35; 19:13; 1 Kgs 2:23; 2 Kgs 6:31).

rashi.heb:
*מה יתן לך.* 
הקב"ה:
rashi.eng: *What can He give you.* [What can] the Holy One, blessed be He [give you]?

rashi.heb:
*ומה יוסיף לך.* 
שמירה ומחיצות הרי את נתונה לפנים משתי מחיצות:
rashi.eng: *and what can He add to you.* [What] safeguard and walls? Behold you are placed within two walls.

notes.4253: (tn): The words “here’s how” are supplied in the translation as a clarification. In v. 4 the psalmist answers the question he raises in v. 3.
notes.4254: (tn, Heb): “with coals of the wood of the broom plant.” The wood of the broom plant was used to make charcoal, which in turn was used to fuel the fire used to forge the arrowheads.

rashi.heb:
*חצי גבור שנונים.* 
והרי את הורגת במקום רחוק כחץ:
rashi.eng: *Sharpened arrows of a mighty man.* Behold you kill in a distant place like an arrow.

rashi.heb:
*עם גחלי רתמים.* 
כל הגחלים כבו מבחוץ כבו מבפנים ואלו כבו מבחוץ ולא מבפנים ד"א מה יתן לך מה סופו של הקב"ה לגזור עליך חצי גבורים עם גחלי רתמים חצים מלמעלה וגיהנם מלמטה:
rashi.eng: *with coals of brooms.* All coals, when extinguished on the outside, are extinguished on the inside, but these extinguish themselves on the outside but not on the inside (ibid.). Another explanation: What will He give you? What is the Holy One, blessed be He, destined to decree upon you? Arrows of a mighty man with coals of brooms. His arrows from above and Gehinnom from below.

notes.4255: (tn): Or “woe to me.” The Hebrew term אוֹיָה (’oyah, “woe”) which occurs only here, is an alternate form of אוֹי (’oy).
notes.4256: (tn, Heb): “I live as a resident alien.”
notes.4257: (sn): Meshech was located in central Anatolia (modern Turkey). Kedar was located in the desert to east-southeast of Israel. Because of the reference to Kedar, it is possible that Ps 120:5 refers to a different Meshech, perhaps one associated with the individual mentioned as a descendant of Aram in 1 Chr 1:17. (However, the LXX in 1 Chr 1:17 follows the parallel text in Gen 10:23, which reads “Mash,” not Meshech.) It is, of course, impossible that the psalmist could have been living in both the far north and the east at the same time. For this reason one must assume that he is recalling his experience as a wanderer among the nations or that he is using the geographical terms metaphorically and sarcastically to suggest that the enemies who surround him are like the barbarians who live in these distant regions. For a discussion of the problem, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 146.

rashi.heb:
*אויה לי.* 
אמרה כנסת ישראל כי כבר לקית בגליות רבים הרי גרתי משך עם בני יפת במלכות פרס ויון ומשך:
rashi.eng: *Woe is to me.* says the congregation of Israel, for I have already suffered in many exiles. Behold I sojourned in Meshech with the sons of Japheth in the kingdom of Persia, Greece, and Meshech.

notes.4258: (tn): The singular participial form probably has a representative function here. The psalmist envisions the typical hater of peace who represents the entire category of such individuals.

notes.4261: (sn): Psalm 121. The psalm affirms that the Lord protects his people Israel. Unless the psalmist addresses an observer (note the second person singular forms in vv. 3-8), it appears there are two or three speakers represented in the psalm, depending on how one takes v. 3. The translation assumes that speaker one talks in vv. 1-2, that speaker two responds to him with a prayer in v. 3 (this assumes the verbs are true jussives of prayer), and that speaker three responds with words of assurance in vv. 4-8. If the verbs in v. 3 are taken as a rhetorical use of the jussive, then there are two speakers. Verses 3-8 are speaker two’s response to the words of speaker one. See the note on the word “sleep” at the end of v. 3.
notes.4262: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*אני שלום.* 
עמהם:
rashi.eng: *I am at peace.* With them.

rashi.heb:
*וכי אדבר.* 
עליהם שלום המה באים להלחם בי:
rashi.eng: *but when I speak.* peacefully with them, they come to wage war with me.

notes.4264: (tn): The Hebrew term מֵאַיִן (me’ayin) is interrogative, not relative, in function. Rather than directly stating that his source of help descends from the hills, the psalmist is asking, “From where does my help come?” Nevertheless, the first line does indicate that he is looking toward the hills for help, probably indicating that he is looking up toward the sky in anticipation of supernatural intervention. The psalmist assumes the dramatic role of one needing help. He answers his own question in v. 2.

rashi.heb:
*(שיר למעלות.* 
הפשט כשהיו הלוים מתחילין לעלות במעלות אמרו שיר זה אע"פ שזה השיר לא נכתב בראשונה אין מוקדם ומאוחר) (ס"א מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *A song for ascents.* The simple meaning is that when the Levites began to ascend the steps, they recited this song. Although this song is not written first, there is no chronological sequence.) (In other books I found:

rashi.heb:
*שיר למעלות.* 
רמז במזמור שני למעלות העולות לצדיקים לעתיד לבא מתחת עץ החיים לכסא הכבוד דתניא בספרי שיר המעלות אין כתוב כאן אלא שיר למעלות שיר למי שעתיד לעשות מעלות לצדיקים לעתיד לבא, וזהו שיסד הקליר (בסילוק דיוצר של יום ב' דסוכות שיסד ר' אליעזר הקליר שהוא בנו של רשב"י בחגיגה פ' אין דורשין ע"ש) ומתחתיה שלשים מעלות זו למעלה מזו עד כסא הכבוד טסות ועולות בשיח נעימות שיר המעלות:
rashi.eng: *A song for ascents.* [The Psalmist] alludes, in the second psalm, to the steps that ascend for the righteous in the future from beneath the tree of life to the Throne of Glory, as we learned in Sifrei (Ekev 47): “It does not say here, ‘A song of ascents’ but, ‘A song for ascents’; a song for the One Who is destined to make ascents for the righteous in the future.” This is what the Kalir established (in the concluding poem of the morning service for the second day of Succoth, which was composed by Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Simon the son of Yochai in Chagigah, chapter “We may not expound,” see there): “And from beneath them thirty steps, one above the other until the Throne of Glory, flying and ascending with the pleasant speech of the song of ascents.”

notes.4265: (tn, Heb): “my help [is] from with the Lord.”

notes.4268: (tn): The prefixed verbal forms following the negative particle אל appear to be jussives. As noted above, if they are taken as true jussives of prayer, then the speaker in v. 3 would appear to be distinct from both the speaker in vv. 1-2 and the speaker in vv. 4-8. However, according to GKC 322 �109.e), the jussives are used rhetorically here “to express the conviction that something cannot or should not happen.” In this case one should probably translate, “he will not allow your foot to slip, your protector will not sleep,” and understand just one speaker in vv. 4-8.

notes.4270: (sn): One hardly thinks of the moon’s rays as being physically harmful, like those of the sun. The reference to the moon may simply lend poetic balance to the verse, but it is likely that the verse reflects an ancient, primitive belief that the moon could have an adverse effect on the mind (note the English expression “moonstruck,” which reflects such a belief). Another possibility is that the sun and moon stand by metonymy for harmful forces characteristic of the day and night, respectively.

notes.4271: (tn, Heb): “your going out and your coming in.”
notes.4272: (sn): Psalm 122. The psalmist expresses his love for Jerusalem and promises to pray for the city’s security.
notes.4273: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4274: (tn, Heb): “in the ones saying to me.” After the verb שָׂמַח (samakh), the preposition בְּ (bet) usually introduces the reason for joy.

rashi.heb:
*שמחתי באומרים לי.* 
שמעתי בני אדם שאומרים מתי ימות אותו זקן וימלוך שלמה בנו ויבנה בית המקדש ונעלה לרגל ואני שמח:
rashi.eng: *I rejoiced when they said to me.* I heard people saying, “When will that old man die, and his son Solomon reign and build the Temple, and we shall go up on the festival pilgrimages?” And I am happy.

rashi.heb:
*עומדות היו רגלינו.* 
במלחמה בכל מקום בשביל שעריך ירושלים שעוסקין בהן בתורה:
rashi.eng: *Our feet were standing.* in battle everywhere because of the gates of Jerusalem, where they were engaged in Torah.

notes.4276: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
notes.4277: (tc, Heb): “Jerusalem, which is built like a city which is joined to her together.” The meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear. Many regard this as a description of the compact way in which the city was designed or constructed. The translation assumes an emendation of the verb חֻבְּרָה (khubb�rah, “is joined”) to a noun חֶבְרָה (khevrah, “association; company”). The text then reads literally, “Jerusalem, which is built like a city which has a company together.” This in turn can be taken as a reference to Jerusalem’s role as a city where people congregated for religious festivals and other civic occasions (see vv. 4-5).

rashi.heb:
*ירושלים הבנויה.* 
כשיבנה שלמה בני בית המקדש בתוכה תהא בנוי' בשכינה ומקדש וארון ומזבח:
rashi.eng: *The built-up Jerusalem.* When my son Solomon builds the Temple within it [Jerusalem], it will be built with the Shechinah, the Temple, the Ark, and the altar.

rashi.heb:
*כעיר שחוברה לה.* 
כשילה שדימה הכתוב זו לזו שנאמר (דברים י״ב:ט׳) אל המנוחה ואל הנחלה מנוחה זו שילה נחלה זו ירושלים, ורבותינו אמרו יש ירושלים הבנויה בשמים ועתידה ירושלים של מטה להיות כמותה:
rashi.eng: *is like a city that was joined together within itself.* Like Shiloh, for Scripture compared them to one another, as it is said (Deut. 12:9): “to the rest and to the inheritance.” The rest is Shiloh. The inheritance is Jerusalem (see Sifrei Re’eh 66). And our Rabbis said (Ta’an. 5a): There is a Jerusalem in heaven, and the Jerusalem on Earth is destined to be like it.

notes.4279: (tn, Heb): “which is where the tribes go up.”
notes.4280: (tn, Heb): “[it is] a statute for Israel to give thanks to the name of the Lord.”

rashi.heb:
*ששם עלו שבטים.* 
אשר שם בשילה עלו שבטים כשעלו ממצרים ונקבע המשכן בתוכה:
rashi.eng: *There ascended the tribes.* For there in Shiloh the tribes ascended when they went up from Egypt, and the Tabernacle was established in its midst.

rashi.heb:
*שבטי יה.* 
שהוא עדות לישראל. לפי שהיו האומות מליזין אחריהם כשיצאו ממצרים ואומרים עליהם שהם ממזרים אם בגופם היו שולטין המצרים בנשותיהם לא כל שכן אמר הקב"ה אני מעיד עליהם שהם בני אבותיהם הטיל שמו עליהם הראובני השמעוני (במדבר כ"ו) הוסיף עליהם אותיות השם אחת מכאן ואחת מכאן נמצא השם הזה יה עדות לישראל:
rashi.eng: *the tribes of God.* Heb. י-ָהּ, which is testimony to Israel, for the heathens were talking about them when they left Egypt, and they would say about them that they were the offspring of adulterous unions. If the Egyptians ruled over their own bodies, surely [they ruled] over their wives. Said the Holy One, blessed be He, “I attest that they are the sons of their fathers.” He bestowed His name upon them: the Reubenites (הראובני), the Simeonites (השמעוני) (Num. 26). He added the letters of the name, one on this side and one on that side. The result is that this name י-ָהּ is testimony to Israel.

notes.4283: (tn, Heb): “Indeed, there they sit [on] thrones for judgment, [on] thrones [belonging] to the house of David.”

rashi.heb:
*כי שמה ישבו וגו'.* 
כי גם בירושלים תשרה השכינה וישבו שם כסאות לשפוט בהם את האומו' וכסאות מלוכה לבית דוד:
rashi.eng: *For there were set thrones, etc..* For also in Jerusalem the Shechinah will rest, and thrones will sit there upon which to judge the nations, and the royal thrones of the house of David.

rashi.heb:
*שאלו שלום ירושלים.* 
ואמרו לה ישליו אהביך ויהי שלום בחילך:
rashi.eng: *Request the welfare of Jerusalem.* and say to her, “May those who love you enjoy tranquility, and let there be peace in your wall.”

notes.4287: (tn): The psalmist uses second feminine singular pronominal forms to address personified Jerusalem.

rashi.heb:
*למען.* 
ישראל אחי ורעי:
rashi.eng: *For the sake of.* Israel, my brethren and my companions

rashi.heb:
*אדברה נא.* 
אני דוד המלך שלום בך:
rashi.eng: *I shall now speak.* I, King David, [shall now speak] of peace in you.

notes.4288: (tn, Heb): “I will seek good for you.” The psalmist will seek Jerusalem’s “good” through prayer.
notes.4289: (sn): Psalm 123. The psalmist, speaking for God’s people, acknowledges his dependence on God in the midst of a crisis.
notes.4290: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4292: (tn, Heb): “sitting.” The Hebrew verb יָשַׁב (yashav) is here used metonymically of “sitting enthroned” (see Pss 9:7; 29:10; 55:19; 102:12).

rashi.heb:
*שיר וגו' היושבי.* 
יו"ד יתירה:
rashi.eng: *Who dwell.* Heb. הישבי.The “yud” is superfluous.

notes.4293: (sn): Servants look to their master for food, shelter, and other basic needs.

notes.4294: (tn, Heb): “for greatly we are filled [with] humiliation.”

notes.4295: (tn, Heb): “greatly our soul is full to it.”
notes.4296: (sn): Psalm 124. Israel acknowledges that the Lord delivered them from certain disaster.
notes.4297: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*הלעג השאננים.* 
לעג הגוים השאננים שבענו:
rashi.eng: *the ridicule of the complacent.* [With] the ridicule of the complacent heathens we are sated.

rashi.heb:
*הבוז.* 
שבזו את גיא היונים היא ירושלים:
rashi.eng: *the contempt.* that they despised the valley of doves, which is Jerusalem.

rashi.heb:
*לגאיונים.* 
כתיב חד וקרינן תרין:
rashi.eng: *the complacent.* Heb. לגאיונים. It is written as one word and read as two.

rashi.heb:
*בחרות אפם בנו.* 
כשחרה אפם בנו. בחרות. כמו בעשות:
rashi.eng: *when their anger was kindled against us.* Heb. בחרות, “when their anger was kindled against us,” is the same form as בעשות, “when he made.”

notes.4301: (tn, Heb): “our being.” The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 4.a).

rashi.heb:
*נחלה.* 
לשון חולי:
rashi.eng: *illness.* Heb. נחלה, an expression of illness (חלי).

notes.4302: (tn, Heb): “then they would have passed over our being, the raging waters.”

rashi.heb:
*נפשינו [ כצפור ] נמלטה.* 
מהם כצפור אשר נמלטה מפח יוקשים:
rashi.eng: *Our soul escaped like a bird.* [It escaped] from them like a bird that escaped from the hunter’s snare.

notes.4306: (tn, Heb): “our help [is] in the name of the Lord.”
notes.4308: (sn): Psalm 125. The psalmist affirms his confidence in the Lord’s protection and justice.
notes.4309: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*שיר המעלות הבוטחים בה'.* 
לא ימוטו כהר ציון אשר לא ימוט כי כאשר ירושלים הרים סביב לה כן הקב"ה סביב לעמו:
rashi.eng: *Those who trust in the Lord.* will not falter, like Mount Zion, which will not falter, for just as Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains, so is the Holy One, blessed be He, around His people.

notes.4310: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

notes.4312: (tn, Heb): “a scepter of wickedness.” The “scepter” symbolizes royal authority; when collocated with “wickedness” the phrase refers to an oppressive foreign conqueror.
notes.4314: (tn, Heb): “so that the godly might not stretch out their hands in wrongdoing.” A wicked king who sets a sinful example can have an adverse moral and ethical effect on the people he rules.

rashi.heb:
*כי לא ינוח שבט הרשע על גורל הצדיקים.* 
(כי לא יתן הקב"ה את ממשלת הרשעים לנוח על הצדיקים) למען כי הצדיקים נזהרין מלשלוח ידיהם בעולה:
rashi.eng: *For the rod of wickedness will not rest on the lot of the righteous.* For the Holy One, blessed be He, will not allow the rule of the wicked to rest on the righteous because the righteous are careful not to stretch out their hand in wrongdoing.

notes.4315: (tn, Heb): “pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 36:10; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).

notes.4316: (tn, Heb): “and the ones making their paths twisted.” A sinful lifestyle is compared to a twisting, winding road.
notes.4317: (tn, Heb): “lead them away.” The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive of prayer here (note the prayers directly before and after this). Another option is to translate, “the Lord will remove them” (cf. NIV, NRSV).
notes.4319: (tn, Heb): “peace [be] upon Israel.” The statement is understood as a prayer (see Ps 122:8 for a similar prayer for peace).
notes.4320: (sn): Psalm 126. Recalling the joy of past deliverance, God’s covenant community asks for a fresh display of God’s power and confidently anticipate their sorrow being transformed into joy.
notes.4321: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*והמטים עקלקלותם.* 
על הבריות למצוא עלילות רשע יוליכם ה' את פועלי און:
rashi.eng: *and those who turn their crooked ways.* on the people to find wicked accusations, may the Lord lead them away with the workers of iniquity.

notes.4322: (tn, Heb): “turns with a turning [toward] his people.” The Hebrew noun שִׁיבַת (shivat) occurs only here in the OT. For this reason many prefer to emend the form to the more common שְׁבִית (shevit) or שְׁבוּת (sh�vut), both of which are used as a cognate accusative of שׁוּב (shuv; see Ps 14:7). However an Aramaic cognate of שְׁבִית appears in an eighth century b.c. Old Aramaic inscription with the verb שׁוּב. This cognate noun appears to mean “return” (see J. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Treaties of Sefire [BibOr], 119-20) or “restoration” (see DNWSI 2:1125). Therefore it appears that שְׁבִית should be retained and understood as a cognate accusative of שׁוּב. In addition to Fitzmyer (119-20) see L. C. Allen, who offers the literal translation, “turn with a turning toward” (Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 170). Allen takes שְׁבִית as construct and understands “Zion” as an objective genitive.
notes.4323: (tn, Heb): “we were like dreamers.” This could mean the speakers were so overcome with ecstatic joy (see v. 3b) that they were like those who fantasize about pleasurable experiences in their sleep (see Isa 29:7-8). Since dreams are more commonly associated in the OT with prophetic visions, the community may be comparing their experience of God’s renewed favor to a prophet’s receiving divine visions. Just as a prophetic dream sweeps the individual into a different dimension and sometimes brings one face-to-face with God himself (see Gen 28:11-15; 1 Kgs 3:5-15), so the community was aware of God’s presence in a special way in the day of Zion’s restoration. Though the MT as it stands makes good sense, some choose to understand a homonymic root here meaning “to be healthy; to be strong” (see BDB 321 s.v. I חָלַם) and translate, “we were like those restored to health.” This reading appears to have the support of several ancient translations as well as 11QPsa. See L. C. Allen (Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 170-71) for a discussion of the viewpoints.

rashi.heb:
*בשוב ה' את שיבת ציון.* 
מגלות בבל היינו כחולמים:
rashi.eng: *When the Lord returns the returnees to Zion.* from the Babylonian exile, we were like dreamers.

notes.4324: (tn, Heb): “then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with a shout.”

notes.4326: (tn, Heb): “like the streams in the Negev.” The streams in the arid south. Y. Aharoni writes of the streams in the Negev: “These usually dry wadis collect water on rainy days from vast areas. The situation is also aggravated by floods from the desert mountains and southern Judah. For a day or two or, more frequently, for only a few hours they turn into dangerous torrents” (Y. Aharoni, The Land of the Bible, 26). God’s people were experiencing a “dry season” after a time of past blessing; they pray here for a “flash flood” of his renewed blessing. This does not imply that they are requesting only a brief display of God’s blessing. Rather the point of comparison is the suddenness with which the wadis swell during a rain, as well as the depth and power of these raging waters. The community desires a sudden display of divine favor in which God overwhelms them with blessings.

rashi.heb:
*כאפיקים בנגב.* 
כאפיקי מים בארץ יבשה שמלחלחין אותה כך נהיה מרטיבין בשובך את שבותינו אשר הזורעים בה בארץ ציה בדמעה דואגים שסבורים שמא לא תצמח, ברנה קוצרין על ידי אפיקי המים כשהם משולחין בה:
rashi.eng: *like rivulets in arid land.* Like rivulets in arid land, which moisten it, so shall we be moistened [freshened] when You return [us from] our captivity, for those who sow in an arid land, with tears, worrying that it will not grow, reap with song through the rivulets of water, when they are directed into it [that land].

notes.4327: (sn): O. Borowski says regarding this passage: “The dependence on rain for watering plants, the uncertainty of the quantity and timing of the rains, and the possibility of crop failure due to pests and diseases appear to have kept the farmer in a gloomy mood during sowing” (Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 54). Perhaps the people were experiencing a literal drought, the effects of which cause them to lament their plight as they plant their seed in hopes that the rain would come. However, most take the language as metaphorical. Like a farmer sowing his seed, the covenant community was enduring hardship as they waited for a new outpouring of divine blessing. Yet they are confident that a time of restoration will come and relieve their anxiety, just as the harvest brings relief and joy to the farmer.

notes.4328: (tn): The noun occurs only here and in Job 28:18 in the OT. See HALOT 646 s.v. I מֶשֶׁךְ which gives “leather pouch” as the meaning.
notes.4329: (tn): The Hebrew noun אֲלֻמָּה (’alummah, “sheaf”) occurs only here and in Gen 37:7 in the OT. Verse 6 expands the image of v. 5. See the note on the word “harvest” there.
notes.4330: (sn): Psalm 127. In this wisdom psalm the psalmist teaches that one does not find security by one’s own efforts, for God alone gives stability and security.
notes.4331: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*הלוך ילך ובכה וגו'.* 
כך ישראל זורעין לפני הקב"ה צדקה בדמעה בגלות וברנה יקצורו כשתשלם משכורתם לעתיד:
rashi.eng: *He will go along weeping, etc..* So do Israel in exile sow charity in tears, and they will reap it when You pay their reward in the future.

notes.4332: (sn): The expression build a house may have a double meaning here. It may refer on the surface level to a literal physical structure in which a family lives, but at a deeper, metaphorical level it refers to building, perpetuating, and maintaining a family line. See Deut 25:9; Ruth 4:11; 1 Sam 2:35; 2 Sam 7:27; 1 Kgs 11:38; 1 Chr 17:10, 25. Having a family line provided security in ancient Israel.
notes.4333: (sn): The city symbolizes community security, which is the necessary framework for family security.

rashi.heb:
*שיר המעלות לשלמה.* 
שיר זה אמר דוד על שלמה בנו שצפה ברוח הקודש שעתיד לבנות בית המקדש ובו ביום ישא שלמה את בת פרעה ועל זה נאמר (ירמיהו ל״ב:ל״א) כי על אפי ועל חמתי היתה לי העיר הזאת למן היום אשר בנו אותה לכך אמר המזמור הזה למה לך בני לבנות בית ולסור מאחרי המקום מאחר שאינו חפץ בה לשוא עמלו בוניו בו:
rashi.eng: *A song of ascents about Solomon.* This song David recited about his son, Solomon, for he saw through the holy spirit that he [Solomon] was destined to build the Temple, and on that very day, Solomon would marry Pharaoh’s daughter, and concerning this was said (Jer. 32:31): “For this city has aroused My anger and My wrath since the day they built it.” Therefore, he recited this song. My son, why should you build a house and turn away from following the Omnipresent? Since He does not desire it, its workers have toiled at it in vain.

rashi.heb:
*שוא שקד שומר.* 
על חנם צופה בה השומר:
rashi.eng: *[its] watcher keeps his vigil in vain.* The watchman watches it in vain.

notes.4334: (tn, Heb): “[it is] vain for you, you who are early to rise, who delay sitting, who eat the food of hard work.” The three substantival participles are parallel and stand in apposition to the pronominal suffix on the preposition. See לָכֶם (lakhem, “for you”).
notes.4335: (tn): Here the Hebrew particle כֵּן (ken) is used to stress the following affirmation (see Josh 2:4; Ps 63:2).
notes.4336: (tn, Heb): “he gives to his beloved, sleep.” The translation assumes that the Hebrew term שֵׁנָא (shena’, “sleep,” an alternate form of שֵׁנָה, shenah) is an adverbial accusative. The point seems to be this: Hard work by itself is not what counts, but one’s relationship to God, for God is able to bless an individual even while he sleeps. (There may even be a subtle allusion to the miracle of conception following sexual intercourse; see the reference to the gift of sons in the following verse.) The statement is not advocating laziness, but utilizing hyperbole to give perspective and to remind the addressees that God must be one’s first priority. Another option is to take “sleep” as the direct object: “yes, he gives sleep to his beloved” (cf. NIV, NRSV). In this case the point is this: Hard work by itself is futile, for only God is able to bless one with sleep, which metonymically refers to having one’s needs met. He blesses on the basis of one’s relationship to him, not on the basis of physical energy expended.

rashi.heb:
*שוא לכם.* 
בעלי האומניות המשכימים ומאחרים למלאכתם ומתפרנסים בעצבון וביגיעה בלחם העצבים של טורח:
rashi.eng: *It is futile for you.* The craftsmen, who rise early and stay late at their work and sustain themselves with toil and labor, with bread of toil, [i.e.,] of the toil of work.

rashi.heb:
*כן יתן.* 
הקב"ה פרנסה למי שמנדד שנת מעיניו בשביל לעסוק בתורה:
rashi.eng: *so will the Lord give.* The Holy One, blessed be He, [will give] sustenance to him who banishes his sleep from his eyes in order to engage in the Torah.

rashi.heb:
*לידידו שנא.* 
למנדד מעיניו שינה:
rashi.eng: *to one who banishes sleep.* Heb. לידידו שנא. to one who banishes (מנדד) sleep from his eyes.

notes.4338: (tn): Some prefer to translate this term with the gender neutral “children,” but “sons” are plainly in view here, as the following verses make clear. Daughters are certainly wonderful additions to a family, but in ancient Israelite culture sons were the “arrows” that gave a man security in his old age, for they could defend the family interests at the city gate, where the legal and economic issues of the community were settled.

rashi.heb:
*הנה נחלת ה'.* 
לאותו האיש:
rashi.eng: *Behold, the heritage of the Lord.* for that man [who banishes sleep from his eyes].

rashi.heb:
*בנים.* 
אלו התלמידים שהוא מעמיד שהם לו כבנים:
rashi.eng: *sons.* These are the disciples whom he sets up, who are to him like sons.

rashi.heb:
*שכר פרי הבטן.* 
שכר פרי התורה שבלב שנאמר (משלי כ״ב:י״ח) כי נעים כי תשמרם בבטנך:
rashi.eng: *the reward is the fruit of the innards.* The reward is the fruit of the Torah that is in his heart as it is said (Prov. 22:18): “For it is pleasant that you guard them in your innards.”

notes.4339: (tn, Heb): “like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so [are] sons of youth.” Arrows are used in combat to defend oneself against enemies; sons are viewed here as providing social security and protection (see v. 5). The phrase “sons of youth” is elliptical, meaning “sons [born during the father’s] youth.” Such sons will have grown up to be mature adults and will have children of their own by the time the father reaches old age and becomes vulnerable to enemies. Contrast the phrase “son of old age” in Gen 37:3 (see also 44:20), which refers to Jacob’s age when Joseph was born.

rashi.heb:
*כחצים ביד גבור.* 
להלחם בם את אויביו:
rashi.eng: *Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man.* with which to battle his enemies.

rashi.heb:
*כן בני הנעורים.* 
התלמידים שאדם מעמיד מנעוריו:
rashi.eng: *so are the sons of one’s youth.* The disciples that a man sets up in his youth.

notes.4340: (tn): Being “put to shame” is here metonymic for being defeated, probably in a legal context, as the reference to the city gate suggests. One could be humiliated (Ps 69:12) or deprived of justice (Amos 5:12) at the gate, but with strong sons to defend the family interests this was less likely to happen.
notes.4342: (sn): Psalm 128. The psalmist observes that the godly individual has genuine happiness because the Lord rewards such a person with prosperity and numerous children.
notes.4343: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*אשרי הגבר אשר מלא את אשפתו.* 
מאותם חצים, אשפה תיק החיצים שקורין קויכרי"ן בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *Praiseworthy is the man who has filled his quiver.* with those arrows. אשפה is the arrowcase, called cuyvre in Old French.

rashi.heb:
*לא יבושו כי ידברו את אויבים בשער.* 
תלמידי חכמים שמנצחין זה את זה בהלכה ונראים כאויבים זה לזה (תוספות):
rashi.eng: *they will not be ashamed when they talk to the enemies in the gate.* Torah scholars who defeat one another in halachah and appear as enemies to one another (addendum).

notes.4345: (tn, Heb): “the one who walks in his ways.”

rashi.heb:
*שיר המעלות אשרי כל ירא ה'.* 
כל אלו תוכחות ומוסרים לפי שכתוב אשרי האיש אשרי איש, לכך נאמר כאן כל לרבות אשה:
rashi.eng: *A song of ascents. Praiseworthy is every man who fears the Lord.* All of these are admonitions and disciplines. Because it is written, “Praiseworthy is the man”, “Praiseworthy is a man,” it therefore says here “every,” to include a woman.

notes.4346: (tn): The psalmist addresses the representative God-fearing man, as indicated by the references to “your wife” (v. 3) and “the man” (v. 4), as well as the second masculine singular pronominal and verbal forms in vv. 2-6.
notes.4347: (tn, Heb): “the work of your hands, indeed you will eat.”
notes.4348: (tn, Heb): “how blessed you [will be] and it will be good for you.”

rashi.heb:
*יגיע כפיך.* 
הנהנה מיגיע כפו נוחל שני עולמות (במס' ברכות):
rashi.eng: *If… the toil of your hands.* He who benefits from the toil of his hands inherits two worlds. In Tractate Berachoth (8a).

notes.4349: (sn): The metaphor of the fruitful vine pictures the wife as fertile; she will give her husband numerous children (see the next line).
notes.4350: (tn): One could translate “sons” (see Ps 127:3 and the note on the word “sons” there), but here the term seems to refer more generally to children of both genders.

rashi.heb:
*כגפן פוריה.* 
בניה מרובין:
rashi.eng: *as a fruitful vine.* Every woman whose blood is abundant will have many children.

rashi.heb:
*בירכתי ביתך.* 
לפי שדרך תשמיש להיות בצנעה. דבר אחר:
rashi.eng: *in the innermost parts of your house.* Because it is customary to have marital relations in secret. Another explanation:

rashi.heb:
*בירכתי.* 
אם אשתך נידה תשימנה בירכתי ביתך שלא תתרגל אצלה:
rashi.eng: *in the innermost parts.* If your wife is menstruating, put her into the innermost parts of your house so that you will not become accustomed to being with her.

rashi.heb:
*בניך כשתילי זיתים.* 
מה זיתים אין להם הרכבה כך אין בבניך פסול:
rashi.eng: *your sons will be like olive shoots.* Just as olive trees cannot be grafted, so will your sons not have any disqualification.

notes.4351: (tn, Heb): “look, indeed thus will the man, the fearer of the Lord, be blessed.”

notes.4352: (tn): The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive of prayer (note the imperatives that are subordinated to this clause in vv. 5b-6a). Having described the blessings that typically come to the godly, the psalmist concludes by praying that this ideal may become reality for the representative godly man being addressed.
notes.4353: (tn): The imperative with prefixed vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding jussive.
notes.4354: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

rashi.heb:
*מציון.* 
שהוא שער השמים:
rashi.eng: *from Zion.* which is the gate of heaven. Moreover, in the merit of Zion they would be fruitful and multiply, as it is written (I Kings 4:20): “Judah and Israel [were] many.”

rashi.heb:
*בטוב ירושלים.* 
ושמחת בכל הטוב:
rashi.eng: *the good of Jerusalem.* And you shall rejoice with all the good.

notes.4355: (tn): The imperative with prefixed vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the jussive in v. 5a.
notes.4357: (tn, Heb): “peace [be] upon Israel.” The statement is understood as a prayer (see Ps 125:5).
notes.4358: (sn): Psalm 129. Israel affirms God’s justice and asks him to destroy the enemies of Zion.
notes.4359: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*וראה בנים לבניך.* 
ולא יבואו לקטטה עבור חליצה ואז שלום על ישראל תוספות:
rashi.eng: *And may you see children [born] to your children.* and they shall not come to quarrel about halitzah, [since that is performed only if there are no children,] and then there will be peace upon Israel (addendum).

rashi.heb:
*בנים לבניך.* 
ירשו נחלה ואין אשה זקוקה ליבם אז שלום בעולם:
rashi.eng: *children [born] to your children.* They will inherit the estate, and no woman will be subject to the levir [in a levirate marriage]. Then there will be peace in the world.

rashi.heb:
*חרשים האריכו למעניתם.* 
הוא תלם המחרישה כבחצי מענה צמד שדה:
rashi.eng: *the plowmen… they lengthened their furrow.* That is the hill of the plowshare, as (I Sam. 13:14): “about half a furrow (מענה) [which] a yoke [of oxen plow in] a field.”

notes.4360: (tn): The background of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Perhaps the “ropes” are those used to harness the ox for plowing (see Job 39:10). Verse 3 pictures the wicked plowing God’s people as if they were a field. But when God “cut the ropes” of their ox, as it were, they could no longer plow. The point of the metaphor seems to be that God took away the enemies’ ability to oppress his people. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 187.

notes.4361: (tn): The Hebrew verb שָׁלַף (shalaf) normally means “to draw [a sword]” or “to pull.” BDB 1025 s.v. suggests the meaning “to shoot up” here, but it is more likely that the verb here means “to pluck; to pull up,” a nuance attested for this word in later Hebrew and Aramaic (see Jastrow 1587 s.v. שָׁלַף).

rashi.heb:
*שקדמת שלף יבש.* 
שקודם שישלפוהו ויתלשוהו ממקומו הוא יבש:
rashi.eng: *which, before it is plucked, withers.* Which, before they pluck it and uproot it from its place, is withered.

rashi.heb:
*וחצנו.* 
כמו (ישעיהו מ״ט:כ״ב) והביאו בניך בחוצן איישי"לא בלע"ז, וכן גם חצני נערתי:
rashi.eng: *his arm.* Like (Isa. 49:22): “and they will bring your sons in [their] arms (בחצן) ,” aisselle in French, and so (Neh. 5:13): “Also I shook out my arm (חצני).”

notes.4362: (tn): The perfect verbal form is used for rhetorical effect; it describes an anticipated development as if it were already reality.
notes.4363: (sn): Psalm 130. The psalmist, confident of the Lord’s forgiveness, cries out to the Lord for help in the midst of his suffering and urges Israel to do the same.
notes.4364: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4365: (tn, Heb): “depths,” that is, deep waters (see Ps 69:2, 14; Isa 51:10), a metaphor for the life-threatening danger faced by the psalmist.

notes.4367: (tn, Heb): “may your ears be attentive to the voice of.”

notes.4369: (tn): The words “before you” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The psalmist must be referring to standing before God’s judgment seat. The rhetorical question expects the answer, “No one.”

rashi.heb:
*כי עמך הסליחה.* 
לא נתת רשות לשליח לסלוח כמו שנאמר (שמות כ״ג:כ״א) כי לא ישא לפשעכם:
rashi.eng: *For forgiveness is with You.* You did not give permission to an agent to forgive, as it is said (Exod. 23:21): “for he will not forgive your transgression.”

rashi.heb:
*למען תורא.* 
על זאת שלא יהא אדם בטוח על סליחת אחר:
rashi.eng: *in order that You be feared.* for this, so that no man will rely on the forgiveness of another. (I found this.)

rashi.heb:
*קויתי ה' קותה נפשי.* 
קווי אחר קווי כעין (לעיל כ"ז) קוה אל ה' חזק ויאמץ לבך וקוה כעין משומרים לבקר שומרים לבקר:
rashi.eng: *I hoped, O Lord; yea, my soul hoped.* one hope after another hope, similar to (above 27:14): “Hope for the Lord, be strong and He will give your heart courage, and hope,” and similar to “among those who await the morning, those who await the morning.”

notes.4378: (tn, Heb): “more than watchmen for the morning, watchmen for the morning.” The words “yes, more” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*נפשי לה' משומרים לבקר.* 
הריני מן המצפים לגאולה:
rashi.eng: *My soul is to the Lord among those who await the morning.* I am among those who look forward to the redemption.

rashi.heb:
*שומרים לבקר.* 
מצפין וחוזרין ומצפין קץ אחר קץ, (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *those who await the morning.* They look forward and repeatedly look forward for one end after another end. (I found this.)

notes.4379: (tn, Heb): “for with the Lord [is] loyal love.”

notes.4382: (tn): The Hebrew noun עָוֹן (’avon) can refer to sin, the guilt sin produces, or the consequences of sin. Only here is the noun collocated with the verb פָּדָה (padah, “to redeem; to deliver”). The psalmist may refer to forgiveness per se (v. 4), but the emphasis in this context is likely on deliverance from the national consequences of sin. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 192.
notes.4383: (sn): Psalm 131. The psalmist affirms his humble dependence on the Lord and urges Israel to place its trust in God.
notes.4384: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4385: (tn, Heb): “and my eyes are not lifted up.”
notes.4386: (tn, Heb): “I do not walk in great things, and in things too marvelous for me.”

rashi.heb:
*ה' לא גבה לבי וגו'.* 
לא נהגתי שררה, לא עשיתי גדולות תענוגות בנינים ונטיעות כעין שעשה בני הנני עליך כמי שאין לו ידים ורגלים כגולם מוטל לנגדך (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *my heart was not haughty, etc..* I did not behave with superiority. I did not make great things pleasures, buildings, and plantings as my son made. Behold I am with You like one who has no hands or feet, like an incomplete form lying before You.

notes.4388: (tn, Heb): “I make level and make quiet my soul.”
notes.4389: (tn, Heb): “like a weaned [one] upon his mother.”
notes.4390: (tn, Heb): “like the weaned [one] upon me, my soul.”

rashi.heb:
*שויתי ודוממתי.* 
עליך נפשי כגמול שהוא נתון עלי אמו, גמול יונק שדים:
rashi.eng: *I calmed and quieted.* my soul upon You, like a suckling who is placed upon his mother. גָמוּל is one who sucks the breasts.

rashi.heb:
*כגמול עלי נפשי.* 
נפשי בקרבי לנגדך כיונק שדי אמו:
rashi.eng: *like a suckling was my soul with me.* My soul within me was before You as an infant sucking its mother’s breasts.

notes.4391: (sn): Psalm 132. The psalmist reminds God of David’s devotion and of his promises concerning David’s dynasty and Zion.
notes.4392: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4393: (tn, Heb): “all his affliction.” This may refer to David’s strenuous and tireless efforts to make provision for the building of the temple (see 1 Chr 22:14). Some prefer to revocalize the text as עַנַוָתוֹ (’anavato, “his humility”).

rashi.heb:
*שיר המעלות זכור ה' לדוד את כל ענותו.* 
ענוי נפשו אשר טרח ועמל למצוא לך מקום:
rashi.eng: *A song of ascents. Remember, O Lord, onto David all his affliction.* The affliction of his soul, how he worked and toiled to find a place for You.

notes.4395: (tn): The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows is David’s vow.
notes.4397: (tn, Heb): “go up upon the bed of my couch.”

notes.4398: (tn): The plural form of the noun may indicate degree or quality; David envisions a special dwelling place (see Pss 43:3; 46:4; 84:1).

rashi.heb:
*עד אמצא מקום.* 
עד שיודע היכן יהיה מקום מקדש (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *Until I find a place.* Until it will be known where the place of His sanctuary will be. (I found this.)

notes.4400: (tn): Rather than having an antecedent, the third feminine singular pronominal suffix here (and in the next line) appears to refer to the ark of the covenant, mentioned in v. 8. (The Hebrew term אָרוֹן [’aron, “ark”] is sometimes construed as grammatically feminine. See 1 Sam 4:17; 2 Chr 8:11.)
notes.4401: (sn): Some understand Ephrathah as a reference to Kiriath-jearim because of the apparent allusion to this site in the next line (see the note on “Jaar”). The ark was kept in Kiriath-jearim after the Philistines released it (see 1 Sam 6:21-7:2). However, the switch in verbs from “heard about” to “found” suggests that Ephrathah not be equated with Jair. The group who is speaking heard about the ark while they were in Ephrath. They then went to retrieve it from Kiriath-jearim (“Jaar”). It is more likely that Ephrathah refers to a site near Bethel (Gen 35:16, 19; 48:7) or to Bethlehem (Ruth 4:11; Mic 5:2).
notes.4402: (tn, Heb): “fields of the forest.” The Hebrew term יָעַר (ya’ad, “forest”) is apparently a shortened alternative name for קִרְיַת יְעָרִים (qiryat y�’arim, “Kiriath-jearim”), the place where the ark was kept after it was released by the Philistines and from which David and his men retrieved it (see 1 Chr 13:6).

rashi.heb:
*שמענוה.* 
הבשורה:
rashi.eng: *we heard it.* The tidings.

rashi.heb:
*באפרתה.* 
במקום החשוב והמעולה כמו (שמואל א א׳:א׳) בן תחו בן צוף אפרתי חשוב אבגינוס, ד"א:
rashi.eng: *in Ephrath.* In the most esteemed and superior place, like (I Sam. 1:1): “the son of Toku, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite,” an important person, a palace dweller. Another explanation:

rashi.heb: *שמענוה באפרתה.*  בספר יהושע (ט"ו) שבא מאפרים, בכל התחומין הוא אומר (שם) ועלה הגבול ותאר הגבול וכאן הוא אומר ועלה הגבול אל כתף היבוסי ירושלים נמצאת ירושלים גבוה מכל הארצות והוא ראוי לבית המקדש שנאמר (דברים י״ז:ח׳) וקמת ועלית אל המקום וגו' מלמד שבית המקדש גבוה מכל ארץ ישראל כך נדרש בשחיטת קדשים:
rashi.eng: *We heard it in Ephrath.* In the Book of Joshua (ch. 15), who came from Ephraim. In all the boundaries he says, “And the border went up… and the border circled,” but here he says, “And the border went up by the valley of the son of Hinnon… Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is [therefore] found to be higher than all the lands, and it is fit for the Temple, as it is said (Deut. 17:8): “and you shall arise and ascend to the place, etc.” This teaches [us] that the Temple is higher than the whole land of Israel. So it is expounded upon in tractate Zevahim (54b).

rashi.heb:
*מצאנוה בשדי יער.* 
בגבול בנימן שנמשל לחית העיר שנאמר בנימין זאב יטרף (בראשית מ״ט:כ״ז):
rashi.eng: *we found it in the fields of the forest.* In the boundary of Benjamin, who was likened to a beast of the forest, as it is said (Gen. 49:27): “Benjamin is a devouring wolf.”

rashi.heb:
*נבואה.* 
שמה למשכנותיו:
rashi.eng: *Let us come.* there to His Tabernacles.

notes.4405: (tn, Heb): “do not turn away the face of your anointed one.”

rashi.heb:
*אל תשב פני משיחך.* 
שלמה בבואו להכניס שם את הארון:
rashi.eng: *turn not away the face of Your anointed.* Solomon, when he comes to place the Ark therein.

notes.4406: (tn, Heb): “the Lord swore an oath to David [in] truth.”
notes.4407: (tn, Heb): “he will not turn back from it.”
notes.4408: (tn): The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.

rashi.heb:
*ועדותי זו אלמדם.* 
זו אשר אלמדם:
rashi.eng: *and this, My testimony, which I shall teach them.* This which I shall teach them.

notes.4411: (tn, Heb): “he desired it for his dwelling place.”

notes.4412: (tn): The words “he said” are added in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.

notes.4414: (tn, Heb): “I will greatly bless her provision.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.
notes.4415: (tn, Heb): “her poor I will satisfy [with] food.”

rashi.heb:
*צידה.* 
מזונה:
rashi.eng: *its provision.* its food.

notes.4416: (tn, Heb): “and her priests I will clothe [with] deliverance.”
notes.4417: (tn, Heb): “[with] shouting they will shout.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.

notes.4418: (tn, Heb): “there I will cause a horn to sprout for David.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (cf. Deut 33:17; 1 Kgs 22:11; Pss 18:2; 92:10). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 89:17, 24; 92:10; Lam 2:17). In the ancient Near East powerful warrior-kings would sometimes compare themselves to a goring bull that used its horns to kill its enemies. For examples, see P. Miller, “El the Warrior,” HTR 60 (1967): 422-25, and R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 135-36.
notes.4419: (tn, Heb): “I have arranged a lamp for my anointed one.” Here the “lamp” is a metaphor for the Davidic dynasty (see 1 Kgs 11:36).

notes.4420: (tn, Heb): “his enemies I will clothe [with] shame.”
notes.4421: (sn): Psalm 133. The psalmist affirms the benefits of family unity.
notes.4422: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

rashi.heb:
*יציץ.* 
יאיר כמו ונוצצים כעין נחושת (יחזקאל א׳:ז׳):
rashi.eng: *will shine.* Heb. יציץ, which shine, like (Ezek. 1:7): “and they sparkled (ונצצים) like the color of burnished copper.”

notes.4423: (sn): This statement refers to the extended family structure of ancient Israel, where brothers would often live in proximity to one another (Deut 25:5), giving the family greater social prominence and security. However, in its later application in the Israelite cult it probably envisions unity within the covenant community. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 212-15.

rashi.heb:
*שיר וגו'.* 
הנה מה טוב ומה נעים שבת אחים גם יחד, כשישב הקב"ה בבית הבחירה עם ישראל הקרויין אחים ורעים ויהיה גם הוא יחד עמהם:
rashi.eng: *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers also to dwell together.* When the Holy One, blessed be He, will dwell in the Temple with Israel, who are called brothers and friends, and He too will be together with them.

notes.4424: (tn, Heb): “[it is] like the good oil on the head, going down on the beard.”
notes.4425: (tn, Heb): “which goes down in accordance with his measured things.” The Hebrew phrase מִדּוֹתָיו (middotayv, “his measured things”) refers here to the robes worn by Aaron. HALOT 546 s.v. *מַד derives the form from מַד (midah, “robe”) rather than מִדָּה (middah, “measured thing”). Ugaritic md means “robe” and is pluralized mdt.

rashi.heb:
*כשמן הטוב.* 
שנמשח בו אהרן הכהן:
rashi.eng: *As the good oil.* with which Aaron the priest was anointed.

rashi.heb:
*שיורד.* 
מראשו אל זקנו אל פי ראש הכתונת שלו שהזקן שוכב ע"פ הכתונת כן נעים טל חרמון שגבוה על הררי ציון והטל יורד מחרמון להררי ציון כשם ששמן המשחה לגדולה כך הר ציון לתפאר' ולכבוד לישראל כשם ששמן הטוב כן טל חרמון כזה כן זה כמו והיה כעם ככהן (ישעיהו כ״ד:ב׳), ורבותינו דרשו שבת אחים משה ואהרן לענין מעילה בשמן המשחה במסכת הוריות כל המזמור אבל יש בדברי תורה וקבלה משל ומליצה ודברי חכמים וחידותם ועיקר שיר המעלות על בית המקדש נאמר:
rashi.eng: *which runs down.* from his head to his beard, to the mouth of his tunic, for the beard rests on the mouth of the tunic. So is the dew of Hermon, which is high, pleasant on the mountains of Zion. Just as the anointing oil is for greatness, so is the dew of Zion for glory and distinction for Israel. Just as the good oil is so, so is the dew of Hermon. Like this, so is that, like (Isa. 24:2): “as with the people, so with the priest.” Our Rabbis explained “for brothers to dwell” as concerning Moses and Aaron, regarding unlawful use of the anointment oil, in tractate Horioth (12a) the entire psalm. But [there is], in words of Torah and post-Mosaic Scriptures, an allegory and a figure, and [in the] words of the wise and their riddles, but the primary meaning of the song of ascents is that it was said regarding the Temple.

notes.4426: (sn): Hermon refers to Mount Hermon, located north of Israel.
notes.4427: (sn): The hills of Zion are those surrounding Zion (see Pss 87:1; 125:2). The psalmist does not intend to suggest that the dew from Mt. Hermon in the distant north actually flows down upon Zion. His point is that the same kind of heavy dew that replenishes Hermon may also be seen on Zion’s hills. See A. Cohen, Psalms (SoBB), 439. “Dew” here symbolizes divine blessing, as the next line suggests.
notes.4429: (tn, Heb): “there the Lord has commanded the blessing, life forever.”
notes.4430: (sn): Psalm 134. The psalmist calls on the temple servants to praise God (vv. 1-2). They in turn pronounce a blessing on the psalmist (v. 3).
notes.4431: (sn): The precise significance of this title, which appears in Pss 120-134, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 219-21.

notes.4434: (tn): The pronominal suffix is second masculine singular, suggesting that the servants addressed in vv. 1-2 are responding to the psalmist.
notes.4435: (tn, Heb): “may the Lord bless you from Zion, the maker of heaven and earth.”
notes.4436: (sn): Psalm 135. The psalmist urges God’s people to praise him because he is the incomparable God and ruler of the world who has accomplished great things for Israel.

rashi.heb: *הללויה הללו את שם ה' וגו'.*
rashi.eng: *Hallelujah, praise, etc..*

notes.4438: (tn, Heb): “for [it is] pleasant.” The translation assumes that it is the Lord’s “name” that is pleasant. Another option is to understand the referent of “it” as the act of praising (see Ps 147:1).

notes.4440: (sn): His special possession. The language echoes Exod 19:5; Deut 7:6; 14:2; 26:18. See also Mal 3:17.

rashi.heb:
*ברקים למטר עשה.* 
הם זהרורי הרקיע המבריקים ומאירים לפני המטר שקורין אשליילד"ש בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *He made lightning for the rain.* They are the flashes in the sky, that flash and lighten before the rain; esloyde, esluyde, esludes, esloisdes, aleydonz in Old French.

rashi.heb:
*מוצא.* 
ל' מציאה כלומ' אוצרות תקן לרוח ושם הם מצויים לו לשלחם במשלחתו:
rashi.eng: *He finds.* Heb. מוצא, an expression of finding. i.e., He prepared a treasury for the wind, and there they are accessible to Him to send them on His mission.

notes.4443: (tn): Or “portents”; “omens” (see Ps 71:7). The Egyptian plagues are alluded to here.

rashi.heb:
*בתוככי.* 
כמו בתוכך:
rashi.eng: *in the midst.* Heb. בתוככי, like בתוך in the midst.

notes.4445: (tn, Heb): “O Lord, your remembrance [is] for a generation and a generation.” See Ps 102:12.

rashi.heb:
*ה' שמך לעולם.* 
כגדולתך וכממשלתך אז כן הוא גם עתה והיכולת בידך לדון ולנקום נקמתנו:
rashi.eng: *O Lord, Your name is eternal.* Like Your greatness and Your authority then, so is it also now, and You have the power to judge and to avenge us.

notes.4446: (tn, Heb): “judges,” but here the idea is that the Lord “judges on behalf of” his people. The imperfect verbal forms here and in the next line draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic actions.
notes.4447: (sn): Verse 14 echoes Deut 32:36, where Moses affirms that God mercifully relents from fully judging his wayward people.

rashi.heb:
*כי ידין ה' עמו.* 
ישפוט משפטם מאויביהם:
rashi.eng: *For the Lord will judge His people.* He will judge their judgment from their enemies.

rashi.heb:
*יתנחם.* 
יתעשת (יתעכב):
rashi.eng: *and relent.* He will have another thought.

notes.4448: (tn, Heb): “the work of the hands of man.”

notes.4449: (tn, Heb): “indeed, there is not breath in their mouth.” For the collocation אַף אֵין (’af ’en, “indeed, there is not”) see Isa 41:26. Another option is to take אַף as “nose” (see Ps 115:6), in which case one might translate, “a nose, [but] they have no breath in their mouths.”

rashi.heb:
*אף אין יש רוח בפיהם.* 
גם רוח אין בפיה' אפילו כבהמה זו כל שכן שלא ידברו כאדם ומאחר שאין בהם רוח אין צריך לפרש רוח החוטם, אף זה פתח, ואף להם ולא יריחון קמץ (סא"א):
rashi.eng: *neither is there any breath in their mouth.* There is not even any breath in their mouth like an animal. Now, since they have no breath [in the mouth], he need not explain [that they do not have] the breath of the nose. This אף is vowelized with a “pattah,” whereas (115:6): “they have a nose (אף) but they do not smell,” is vowelized with a “kamatz.” (This is not found in all editions.)

notes.4450: (tn, Heb): “will be.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a prayer, “may those who make them end up like them.” Because the idols are lifeless, they cannot help their worshipers in times of crisis. Consequently the worshipers end up as dead as the gods in which they trust.

notes.4451: (tn, Heb): “house” (here and in the next two lines).

rashi.heb:
*יראי ה'.* 
אלו הגרים (מצאתי):
rashi.eng: *those who fear the Lord.* These are the proselytes (I found this).

notes.4453: (tn, Heb): “praised be the Lord from Zion.”
notes.4454: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
notes.4455: (sn): Psalm 136. In this hymn the psalmist affirms that God is praiseworthy because of his enduring loyal love, sovereign authority, and compassion. Each verse of the psalm concludes with the refrain “for his loyal love endures.”

rashi.heb:
*לעשה נפלאות גדולות לבדו.* 
בראשונה לא נברא מלאך כשעשאן לנפלאות הללו השמים והארץ השמש והירח:
rashi.eng: *To Him Who performs great wonders alone.* In the beginning, no angel was created when He made the wonders: the heaven, the earth, the sun and the moon.

rashi.heb:
*למכה מצרים בבכוריהם.* 
בכוריהם לא נאמר אלא בבכוריהם עמדו בכורים וקפחו שוקן של אביהם המעכבי' בישראל כששמעו נגע עשירי מפי משה:
rashi.eng: *To Him Who smote the Egyptians with their firstborn.* It does not say, “their firstborn,” but “with their firstborn.” The firstborn arose and beat their fathers’ legs because they detained Israel, when they heard about the tenth plague from Moses.

notes.4458: (tn, Heb): “Reed Sea” (also in v. 15). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression יָם סוּף (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in Exod 13:18.

rashi.heb:
*לגזרים.* 
י"ב קרעים לי"ב שבטים:
rashi.eng: *asunder.* In twelve pieces for the twelve tribes.

rashi.heb:
*מלכים גדולים.* 
כאן רמז ל"א מלכים והשוה להם פרעה וחילו ומכת מצרים למלכים אדירים קשים מהם שקול סיחון כנגד כלם כל אחד לעצמו וכן פירש למעלה לסיחון מלך האמרי ולעוג מלך הבשן ולכל ממלכות כנען, כן באגדה:
rashi.eng: *great kings.* Here he alluded to the thirty- one kings, and he compared for them Pharaoh and his host and the plagues of Egypt to mighty kings, harsher than they. Sihon was equal to all of them, [and Og was equal to all of them (Machzor Vitry)], each one individually, and so did he explain above (135:11): “Sihon the king of the Amorites and Og the king of Bashan and all the kingdoms of Canaan.” So it is in the Aggadah.

notes.4461: (tn, Heb): “who, in our low condition, remembered us.”

rashi.heb:
*שבשפלנו זכר לנו.* 
במצרי' זכר לנו:
rashi.eng: *Who remembered us in our humble state.* In Egypt, He remembered us.

rashi.heb:
*ויפרקנו.* 
מתוכם והפליא לנו כל זה:
rashi.eng: *And He rescued us.* from their midst and performed all these wonders for us.

notes.4462: (tn, Heb): “to all flesh,” which can refer to all people (see Pss 65:2; 145:21) or more broadly to mankind and animals. Elsewhere the psalms view God as the provider for all living things (see Pss 104:27-28; 145:15).

rashi.heb:
*נותן לחם.* 
רמז כאן חסד (כל המעשים):
rashi.eng: *Who gives bread.* He alludes here to kindness (to all creatures).

notes.4463: (sn): Psalm 137. The Babylonian exiles lament their condition, vow to remain loyal to Jerusalem, and appeal to God for revenge on their enemies.

rashi.heb:
*הודו לאל השמים.* 
המכין בהם מזון לכל בריה, עשרים וששה כי לעולם חסדו נאמרו במזמור זה כנגד עשרים וששה דורות שהיה העול' בלא תורה ונתקיים בחסדו של הקב"ה:
rashi.eng: *Gives thanks to the God of heaven.* Who prepares therein food for every creature. The expression, “for His kindness is eternal,” appears twenty-six times in this psalm, corresponding to the twenty-six generations that the world was without Torah and existed through the kindness of the Holy One, blessed be He.

notes.4464: (tn, Heb): “there we sit down, also we weep.”

rashi.heb:
*על נהרות בבל שם ישבנו.* 
כשירדנו לגולה ושאלם נבוכדנצר שישירו לו כמו שהיו משוררין על הדוכן:
rashi.eng: *By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat.* when we went down into exile, and Nebuchadnezzar asked them to sing for him as they used to sing on the stage.

rashi.heb:
*על ערבים.* 
ערבי נחל:
rashi.eng: *On willows.* Willows of the brook.

notes.4465: (tn, Heb): “ask us [for] the words of a song.”
notes.4466: (tn, Heb): “our [?] joy.” The derivation and meaning of the Hebrew phrase תוֹלָלֵינוּ (tolalenu, “our [?]”) are uncertain. A derivation from תָּלַל (talal, “to mock”) fits contextually, but this root occurs only in the Hiphil stem. For a discussion of various proposals, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 236.
notes.4467: (tn, Heb): “from a song of Zion.” Most modern translations read, “one of the songs of Zion,” taking the preposition מִן (min, “from”) as partitive and “song” as collective. The present translation assumes the mem (ם) is enclitic, being misunderstood later as the prefixed preposition.

rashi.heb:
*ותוללינו שמחה.* 
מיני כלי זמר על שם שהם תולין (שתולין) אותם, כך פירשו מנחם, ותוללינו שמחה ותוללינו של שמחה, ויש לפתור תוללינו אויבינו שהם מהוללים ומשטים בנו לשון ומהוללי בי נשבעו (לעיל קב):
rashi.eng: *and our tormentors mirth.* Heb. ותוללינו, kinds of musical instruments that they hang up. This is how Menachem interpreted it (p. 184): וְתוֹלָלֵינוּ שמחה, and our musical instruments of joy. וְתוֹלָלֵינוּ can also be interpreted as: our enemies who would scorn and mock and joke with us, an expression of (102:9): “those who scorn me (מהוללי) swear by me.”

notes.4468: (tn, Heb): “may my right hand forget.” In this case one must supply an object, such as “how to move.” The elliptical nature of the text has prompted emendations (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 236). The translation assumes an emendation to תִּכְשַׁח (tikhshakh), from an otherwise unattested root כשׁח, meaning “to be crippled; to be lame.” See HALOT 502 s.v. כשׁח, which cites Arabic cognate evidence in support of the proposal. The corruption of the MT can be explained as an error of transposition facilitated by the use of שָׁכַח (shakhakh, “forget”) just before this.

rashi.heb:
*אם אשכחך ירושלים.* 
כנסת ישראל אומרת כן:
rashi.eng: *If I forget you, O Jerusalem.* The congregation of Israel says this.

notes.4469: (tn, Heb): “if I do not lift up Jerusalem over the top of my joy.”

rashi.heb:
*אם לא אעלה את ירושלים.* 
את זכרון אבל חורבנה אעלה להזכירו בראש כל שמחתי:
rashi.eng: *If I do not bring up Jerusalem.* The remembrance of the mourning of its destruction I shall bring up to mention at the head of every joyous occasion of mine.

notes.4470: (tn, Heb): “remember, O Lord, against the sons of Edom, the day of Jerusalem.”

rashi.heb:
*ערו ערו.* 
לשון חורבן וכן חומות בבל הרחבה ערער תתערער (ירמיה נא נט) וכן ערות יסוד (חבקוק ג') ואינו נופל אלא על דבר שעוקרין שרשיו מהארץ:
rashi.eng: *Raze it.* Heb. עָרוּ is an expression of destruction, and so (Jer. 51:58): “The broad walls of Babylon shall be overthrown (תתערער),” and so (Hab. 3:13): “baring (ערות) the foundation.” It is used only for something whose roots are uprooted from the ground.

notes.4472: (tn, Heb): “O devastated daughter of Babylon.” The psalmist dramatically anticipates Babylon’s demise.
notes.4473: (tn, Heb): “O the happiness of the one who repays you your wage which you paid to us.”

notes.4474: (sn): For other references to the wholesale slaughter of babies in the context of ancient Near Eastern warfare, see 2 Kgs 8:12; Isa 13:16; Hos 13:16; Nah 3:10.
notes.4475: (sn): Psalm 138. The psalmist vows to thank the Lord for his deliverance and protection.

notes.4476: (tn): The referent of the Hebrew term אֱלֹהִים (’elohim) is unclear. It refers either to the angelic assembly (see Gen 3:5; Ps 8:5) or to the pagan gods (see Pss 82:1, 6; 86:8; 97:7), in which case the psalmist’s praise takes on a polemical tone.

rashi.heb:
*נגד אלהים אזמרך.* 
לעיני השרים (מלאכים):
rashi.eng: *before the princes I shall sing Your praises.* before the eyes of the princes (kings).

notes.4477: (tc): The MT reads, “for you have made great over all your name your word.” If retained, this must mean that God's mighty intervention, in fulfillment of his word of promise, surpassed anything he had done prior to this. However, the statement is odd and several emendations have been proposed. Some read, “for you have exalted over everything your name and your word,” while others suggest, “for you have exalted over all the heavens your name and your word.” The translation assumes an emendation of “your name” to “your heavens” (a construction that appears in Pss 8:3 and 144:5). The point is that God has been faithful to his promise and the reliability of that promise is apparent to all. For a fuller discussion of these options, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 244.

rashi.heb:
*כי הגדלת על כל שמך אמרתך.* 
שמך בעל גבורות קנוא ונוקם ואמרת הבטחת טובך וחסדך הגדלת על כל שמך אמרתך שאתה מעביר לנו על מדותיך וסולח לנו:
rashi.eng: *for You magnified Your word over all Your names.* Your name is mighty, jealous, and vengeful, but You magnified Your word, so that You skip over Your standards, over all Your names, and You forgive us.

notes.4479: (tn, Heb): “you made me bold in my soul [with] strength.”

rashi.heb:
*תרהיבני.* 
הגדלתני:

notes.4480: (tn): The prefixed verbal forms here and in the following verse are understood as jussives, for the psalmist appears to be calling upon the kings to praise God. Another option is to take them as imperfects and translate, “the kings of the earth will give thanks…and will sing.” In this case the psalmist anticipates a universal response to his thanksgiving song.

rashi.heb:
*כי שמעו.* 
כששמעו אמרי פיך לא תרצח לא תנאף הודו על אמרי פיך על אנכי ולא יהיה לך כדי הוא להקבילם עול מלכותו עליהם תחלה ואח"כ יגזור כל גזרותיו:
rashi.eng: *for they heard.* When they heard the words of Your mouth: “You shall not murder; You shall not commit adultery,” they acknowledged the words of Your mouth: “I am [the Lord your God]” and “You shall have no [other god].” It is proper to make them first accept the yoke of His kingdom, and then He should levy all His decrees.

rashi.heb:
*יידע.* 
ייסר כמו ויודע בהם את אנשי סכות:
rashi.eng: *He chastises.* Heb. יידע, chastises, like (Jud. 8:16): “and with them he broke (ויודע) the men of Succoth.”

notes.4485: (tn, Heb): “against the anger of my enemies you extend your hand.”

notes.4486: (tn, Heb): “avenges on my behalf.” For the meaning “to avenge” for the verb גָּמַר (gamar), see HALOT 197-98 s.v. גמר.
notes.4487: (tn, Heb): “the works of your hands.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the singular, “work of your hands.”
notes.4488: (sn): Psalm 139. The psalmist acknowledges that God, who created him, is aware of his every action and thought. He invites God to examine his motives, for he is confident they are pure.

rashi.heb:
*יגמור בעדי.* 
יסכים ע"י בקשותי:
rashi.eng: *May the Lord agree with me.* May He agree with my requests.

rashi.heb:
*מעשי ידיך.* 
בבית הבחירה שנאמר בו כוננו ידיך (שמות טו):
rashi.eng: *the works of Your hands.* The Temple, about which is stated (Exod. 15:16): “Your hands established.”

notes.4489: (tn): The statement is understood as generalizing – the psalmist describes what God typically does.

rashi.heb:
*בנתה לרעי מרחוק.* 
בנתה מרחוק למושכני אל רעותך וחבתך:
rashi.eng: *You understand how to attach me from afar.* You understand from afar [how] to attract me to Your friendship and to Your love.

rashi.heb:
*לרעי.*
